q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the marketing-information management function
q.s: Ridgeline Outfitters, a sporting-goods retailer, assigns a marketing analyst to track the prices, promotions and new store openings of three rival chains. Which responsibility of marketing-information management is the analyst carrying out?
q.r: Monitoring the competition. Marketing-information management (MIM) is the marketing function of gathering, accessing, synthesizing, evaluating and sharing information to aid decision making. One of its key responsibilities is keeping track of what competitors are doing so the business can respond and remain competitive. Setting prices belongs to the pricing function, managing distribution channels belongs to channel management, and developing new products belongs to product/service management, although each of those functions relies on the information MIM provides.
w: Setting prices is the pricing function's job; the analyst is only gathering information about rivals, not deciding what Ridgeline charges for its own products.
Managing distribution channels means getting products from producers to customers, but the analyst is watching rival chains rather than moving any merchandise.
Developing new products belongs to product/service management, and nothing in the analyst's work creates a new item; it only tracks what competitors are doing.

q.pt: Explain techniques for processing marketing data
q.s: The process of converting raw survey responses into organized information that managers can use to make decisions is called
q.r: Data processing. Raw data, such as stacks of completed questionnaires, are not useful until they are checked, coded, entered and tabulated. Data processing turns those raw facts into organized information that can be analyzed and applied to marketing decisions. Data mining is searching large databases for hidden patterns, data collection is gathering the raw facts in the first place, and sampling is choosing who will be studied.
w: Data mining does use stored data, but it searches large databases for hidden patterns rather than turning stacks of raw survey forms into organized information.
Data collection is gathering the survey responses in the first place, while this question asks what happens to those responses after they have already been gathered.
Sampling is deciding which people to study before any survey goes out, so it comes long before raw responses are organized for managers.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the marketing-information management function
q.s: What is the scope of the marketing-information management function?
o: It focuses mainly on designing advertising messages
It supports decisions in all the marketing functions
It is concerned chiefly with setting product prices
It deals primarily with storing sales receipts
q.r: It supports decisions in all the marketing functions. Marketing-information management is one of the seven marketing functions, and its scope is broad. The information it gathers and evaluates supports decisions in channel management, market planning, pricing, product/service management, promotion and selling. Designing advertising messages is part of promotion and setting prices is part of pricing; both use MIM's information but are not its focus. Storing sales receipts is only one small source of internal data.
w: Designing ad messages is part of promotion, which uses marketing information, but the scope of marketing-information management is much wider than a single function.
Setting prices belongs to the pricing function; marketing-information management feeds pricing decisions but also supports product, promotion, channel and selling decisions.
Sales receipts are just one internal source of data, so storing them is a tiny task compared with gathering and sharing information for every marketing decision.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the marketing-information management function
q.s: Each week, the marketing manager at Coastline Cosmetics reads trade publications, scans competitors' websites and talks with sales representatives to stay informed about developments in the market. This ongoing activity is called
q.r: Marketing intelligence. Marketing intelligence is the everyday information a business gathers about developments in its marketing environment, such as competitors' actions and industry news. Unlike marketing research, which studies one specific problem, intelligence gathering is continuous and informal. Cause-and-effect (causal) research uses experiments to test cause and effect, test marketing tries a product in a limited area, and data processing converts raw data into usable information.
w: Cause-and-effect research uses planned experiments to test whether one change causes another, but the manager is simply keeping up with market news every week.
Test marketing means selling a new product in a limited area to measure results, and the manager is not trying out any product at all.
Data processing turns raw data such as questionnaires into usable information, while the manager is informally gathering news from publications, websites and sales reps.

q.pt: Describe the need for marketing data
q.s: Online sales at Maplewood Pet Supply have dropped for three straight months. The owner reviews customer reviews, website traffic reports and competitors' prices. What is the owner's main purpose in analyzing this marketing information?
o: To find the cause of a business problem
To meet a legal reporting requirement
To reduce the number of products sold
To justify a planned price increase
q.r: To find the cause of a business problem. Businesses analyze marketing information to solve problems and make informed decisions rather than relying on guesses. By studying reviews, traffic and competitors' prices, the owner can discover why sales are falling and choose the right response. No law requires this analysis, and the owner's goal is not to cut the product line or to defend a decision already made; it is to understand the problem before acting.
w: No law requires a small retailer to study its reviews and traffic reports; the owner is digging into this information because sales keep falling.
Cutting the number of products sold is not the goal; the owner wants to understand why sales are already dropping so the right fix can be chosen.
Justifying a decision already made is not the point here; the owner has not planned a price change and is trying to learn why online sales are falling.

q.pt: Describe the need for marketing data
q.s: Before investing in a new line of plant-based snacks, Golden Acre Foods studies consumer purchasing trends and competitors' sales. The main advantage of using this marketing information is that it helps the company
o: lower its cost of raw materials.
reduce the risk of its decision.
q.r: Reduce the risk of its decision. Every marketing decision involves risk, the possibility that the decision will lead to a loss. Marketing information lets managers predict how customers and competitors are likely to respond, which helps them anticipate and control that risk. Information cannot guarantee success, but it makes failure less likely. Studying trends does not lower ingredient costs or speed up production, and a new product still needs promotion to reach customers.
w: Studying shopping trends and rivals' sales tells Golden Acre about demand, but it does nothing to change what the company pays for ingredients.
Market information helps decide whether to launch the snacks, but it does not make the factory produce them any faster.
Even a well-researched new product still needs promotion so customers learn it exists, so information cannot remove that need.

q.pt: Describe the need for marketing data
q.s: Data from Brightway Bikes' website show that hundreds of visitors each month search for electric bikes, which the store does not carry. This information most likely helps the store
q.r: Identify a market opportunity. A market opportunity is an unmet customer need that a business could profitably satisfy. Frequent searches for a product the store does not sell signal demand it is missing, so the data point to a chance to add electric bikes. The search data say nothing about how productive employees are or whether the credit policy works, and they describe Brightway's own visitors, not what competitors charge.
w: Website search data show what visitors are looking for, not how much work the store's employees get done, so they cannot measure productivity.
Searches for electric bikes reveal product demand, not whether customers pay their bills on time, so they say nothing about the credit policy.
The data come from Brightway's own website visitors and show what they want to buy, not what rival stores charge for their bikes.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing research
q.s: Effective marketing research is best described as
o: informal and based on the researcher's personal opinions.
planned, orderly and completed in time to aid a decision.
exhaustive, collecting every available fact on the topic.
q.r: Planned, orderly and completed in time to aid a decision. Effective marketing research is systematic, meaning it follows a planned, orderly series of steps; objective, meaning it is free of personal bias; and timely, meaning the results arrive before the decision must be made. Research based on personal opinions is not objective. Trying to collect every available fact wastes time and money and leads to information overload. Casual, everyday information gathering describes marketing intelligence, not a research study.
w: Research built on the researcher's personal opinions is biased, and effective research must be objective so managers can trust what it shows.
Trying to gather every possible fact sounds thorough, but it wastes time and money and buries managers in information they may not need before deciding.
Casual information picked up in everyday conversations is marketing intelligence, not research, because it lacks the planned, orderly steps a study requires.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing research
q.s: What is the first step in the marketing-research process?
q.r: Defining the problem. Marketing research begins by defining the problem, a clear statement of what information managers need in order to make a decision. A correctly defined problem guides every later step, including the research design, the sample and the data-collection method. Collecting data, selecting the sample and analyzing the findings all come later; doing them before the problem is defined wastes resources on information that may not be needed.
w: Collecting data is an important step, but without first knowing what question must be answered, the team cannot know which data are worth gathering.
Choosing a sample depends on knowing what the study needs to learn, so it has to wait until the problem has been clearly defined.
Analyzing findings happens near the end of the process, because there are no findings to analyze until data have been collected.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of marketing research problems/issues
q.s: The marketing manager of Lakeshore Candles asks, "Why are younger customers buying fewer of our candles this year?" This is an example of a __________ decision problem.
q.r: Discovery-oriented. Discovery-oriented decision problems ask what or why questions. They seek information that helps managers understand a situation, such as the reasons a customer group is buying less. Strategy-oriented decision problems ask how questions, such as how to price or promote a product. Production-oriented and sales-oriented are business philosophies, not types of research problems.
w: Strategy-oriented problems ask how to act, such as how to price or promote, but the manager's question asks why customers are buying less.
Production orientation is a business philosophy focused on making goods efficiently, not a type of research problem like the manager's why question.
Sales orientation is a business philosophy of pushing products through heavy selling, not a category of research problem for a why question about customers.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of marketing research problems/issues
q.s: Which of the following questions is an example of a strategy-oriented decision problem:
o: Why did our sales decline last quarter?
What do customers think of our packaging?
Why are shoppers choosing a rival brand?
How should we price our new sports drink?
q.r: How should we price our new sports drink? Strategy-oriented decision problems ask how questions. They help managers choose among alternative ways to act, such as which price to charge for a new product. The other questions ask what or why, so they are discovery-oriented decision problems; their purpose is to understand a situation, such as falling sales, opinions about packaging or the appeal of a competitor, before deciding on a strategy.
w: Asking why sales fell is a discovery-oriented question that seeks to understand a situation, not a how question about choosing a course of action.
Asking what customers think of the packaging gathers understanding about opinions, which makes it discovery-oriented rather than a question about how to act.
Asking why shoppers pick a rival brand seeks to explain behavior, so it is discovery-oriented rather than a how question about choosing a strategy.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of marketing research problems/issues
q.s: Sales at Northgate Shoe Company have fallen 12 percent. Before planning research, the marketing manager recognizes that the sales decline is a __________, not the actual problem.
q.r: Symptom. A symptom is an observable sign that something is wrong, not the cause itself. Falling sales could result from higher prices, a new competitor or poor service, so the manager must identify the underlying problem before choosing a research method. Correctly defining the problem is the most important step in marketing research. A hypothesis is a testable statement, a variable is a factor that can change, and a sample is the group studied.
w: A hypothesis is a testable statement about what might be causing a problem, but the sales drop is an observed fact, not a guess to be tested.
A sales figure can be measured as a variable in a study, but the point here is that the decline is only an outward sign of a deeper cause.
A sample is the group of people chosen for a study, and the 12 percent sales drop is not a group of people at all.

q.pt: Describe methods used to design marketing research studies (i.e., descriptive, exploratory, and causal)
q.s: Customer complaints at Summit Paints have increased, but managers are unsure what is causing them. They hold a few informal interviews with customers to clarify the issue before planning a larger study. This is an example of __________ research.
q.r: Exploratory. Exploratory research is used when a problem is vague and needs to be defined before a larger study begins. It is flexible and small-scale, often relying on informal interviews, focus groups or secondary data. Descriptive research measures the characteristics of a market, causal research uses experiments to test cause and effect, and syndicated research is data a research firm collects and sells to many clients.
w: Descriptive research measures the characteristics of a market, usually with large surveys, but Summit Paints is only trying to clarify a vague problem with a few interviews.
Causal research uses experiments to test cause and effect, while the managers are not testing anything yet; they are still trying to figure out what the issue is.
Syndicated research is data a firm collects and sells to many clients, but Summit Paints is talking directly with its own customers about its own complaints.

q.pt: Describe methods used to design marketing research studies (i.e., descriptive, exploratory, and causal)
q.s: Fresh Fold Laundry Products surveys 1,200 shoppers to learn their ages, incomes and how often they buy detergent. Which type of research design is the company using?
q.r: Descriptive. Descriptive research describes the characteristics of a market or group, answering who, what, when, where and how questions. It usually relies on large surveys that produce quantitative data, such as ages, incomes and purchase frequency. Exploratory research clarifies a vague problem, causal research tests whether one variable causes a change in another, and mixed methods research combines qualitative and quantitative approaches, whereas Fresh Fold used a single survey.
w: Exploratory research clarifies a vague problem with small, flexible methods, but Fresh Fold already knows what it wants and is measuring traits across 1,200 shoppers.
Causal research changes one factor to see its effect on another, but Fresh Fold is simply recording ages, incomes and buying habits without changing anything.
Mixed methods research combines qualitative and quantitative approaches, but Fresh Fold used only one large survey that produced numerical data.

q.pt: Describe methods used to design marketing research studies (i.e., descriptive, exploratory, and causal)
q.s: Peak Coffee Roasters sells its beans at the regular price in some stores and at a 10 percent lower price in similar stores to see whether the lower price increases sales. This is an example of __________ research.
q.r: Causal. Causal research tests cause-and-effect relationships, usually through experiments. Here, price is the independent variable the company changes, and sales are the dependent variable it measures to see the effect. Exploratory research clarifies a vague problem, descriptive research describes the characteristics of a market without manipulating anything, and secondary research uses data that already exist rather than new data from an experiment.
w: Exploratory research is used to clarify a vague problem, but Peak Coffee already has a clear question and is running a controlled price test.
Descriptive research describes a market without changing anything, while Peak Coffee deliberately changes the price in some stores to measure the effect on sales.
Secondary research uses data that already exist, but Peak Coffee is creating brand-new data by running its own price experiment in stores.

q.pt: Describe methods used to design marketing research studies (i.e., descriptive, exploratory, and causal)
q.s: Before launching a new granola bar nationwide, Hearth Bakery sells it for three months only in Columbus, Ohio, and measures the results. The city where the company tries the product is called a
q.r: Test market. A test market is a limited geographic area where a new product or marketing tactic is tried before a full launch. Selling the granola bar only in Columbus lets Hearth Bakery measure actual sales and correct problems at low risk, and test markets are often used in causal research. A target market is the group of customers a business aims to serve, a trade area is the region from which a store draws its customers, and a market segment is a group of customers who share similar characteristics.
w: A target market is the group of customers a business wants to serve, not a single city chosen for a temporary trial before a national launch.
A trade area is the region a store draws its customers from, while Columbus was chosen as a place to try out a new product before selling it everywhere.
A market segment is a group of customers who share similar traits, but Columbus is a geographic location used for a limited product trial.

q.pt: Describe methods used to design marketing research studies (i.e., descriptive, exploratory, and causal)
q.s: What distinguishes causal research from other research designs?
o: It is used mainly to clarify a vague research problem
It tests whether changing one variable affects another
It describes who customers are and how they buy
It relies on a few informal, open-ended interviews
q.r: It tests whether changing one variable affects another. Causal research determines cause and effect. Researchers change one variable, such as price or package design, and measure whether it produces a change in another, such as sales. Clarifying a vague problem and relying on informal, open-ended interviews are characteristics of exploratory research. Describing who customers are and how they buy is the purpose of descriptive research.
w: Clarifying a vague problem is the purpose of exploratory research, which happens before a study like a causal experiment is designed.
Describing who customers are and how they buy is the job of descriptive research, which measures a market without changing anything to test an effect.
A few informal, open-ended interviews are typical of exploratory research, whereas causal research relies on controlled experiments that change one factor.

q.pt: Describe options businesses use to obtain marketing research data (i.e., primary and secondary research)
q.s: Tri-County Hardware reviews last year's sales invoices and expense reports to plan its spring promotions. The store is using data that are
q.r: Internal and quantitative. Internal data come from a business's own records, and invoices and expense reports are generated inside the store. Because these records consist of numbers, such as dollar amounts and units sold, they are quantitative. External data come from outside sources, such as government reports or trade associations. Qualitative data describe opinions, feelings and motives, which invoices and expense reports do not capture.
w: Invoices and expense reports come from the store's own records, so they are not external, and they are numbers, not opinions or feelings.
The records are internal because they come from the store itself, but dollar amounts and units sold are numbers, which makes them quantitative rather than qualitative.
These invoices and expense reports are numbers, so they are quantitative, but they come from the store's own files rather than an outside source.

q.pt: Describe options businesses use to obtain marketing research data (i.e., primary and secondary research)
q.s: Qualitative research is most useful for answering which of the following questions?
o: Why do customers prefer our brand?
How many customers bought last month?
What percentage of buyers are teens?
How often do customers visit the store?
q.r: Why do customers prefer our brand? Qualitative research explores people's feelings, opinions and motives, so it answers why questions, such as the reasons customers prefer a brand. It typically uses open-ended questions with small groups, such as focus groups and in-depth interviews. Questions about how many, what percentage and how often call for counts and measurements, which are answered with quantitative research.
w: Counting how many customers bought last month calls for numbers, which is a job for quantitative research rather than open-ended discussion.
Finding what percentage of buyers are teens requires measuring a large group, which quantitative research does better than small qualitative groups.
How often customers visit is a frequency that can be counted, so quantitative research answers it rather than research about feelings and motives.

q.pt: Describe options businesses use to obtain marketing research data (i.e., primary and secondary research)
q.s: Ellis Marketing Group downloads U.S. Census Bureau population figures to estimate the number of households in a client's trade area. The firm is using
q.r: Secondary data. Secondary data already exist because they were collected earlier for another purpose. Census figures were gathered by the government, not by Ellis for this client, so they are secondary data, which are fast and inexpensive to obtain. Primary data and custom research are collected firsthand for the current problem, and a focus group is a primary-data method in which a moderator leads a small group discussion.
w: Primary data are collected firsthand for the current problem, but the census figures were gathered earlier by the government for its own purposes.
Custom research is designed and carried out for one client's specific problem, while Ellis simply downloaded figures the government had already published.
A focus group is a moderated discussion with a small group of people, and Ellis did not talk with anyone; it downloaded existing census figures.

q.pt: Describe options businesses use to obtain marketing research data (i.e., primary and secondary research)
q.s: A small cereal maker buys a report on national breakfast-food sales that a research firm compiled and sells to many different companies. This report is an example of __________ research.
q.r: Syndicated. Syndicated research is data that a research firm collects on its own and then sells to many clients, which makes it a form of secondary data that costs each buyer less than a study of its own. Custom research is designed and conducted for one client's specific problem, primary research is collected firsthand for the current problem, and exploratory research clarifies a vague problem before a larger study.
w: Custom research is designed for one client's specific problem, but this report was compiled by the research firm on its own and sold to many companies.
Primary research is collected firsthand by or for the business with the problem, while the cereal maker bought a report that already existed.
Exploratory research is a small study to clarify a vague problem, while this is a ready-made national sales report sold to many buyers.

q.pt: Describe data-collection methods (e.g., observations, mail, diaries, phone, internet, discussion groups, interviews, scanners, tracking tools)
q.s: To which category of data-collection methods does a focus group belong?
q.r: Interview. A focus group is a type of interview. A trained moderator asks a small group of people open-ended questions and guides their discussion of a product or topic, gathering in-depth qualitative data. Observation records behavior without asking questions, an experiment changes one factor to measure its effect, and a mail survey collects written answers from respondents who never meet a researcher.
w: Observation records what people do without asking them questions, but a focus group is built around a moderator asking questions and guiding discussion.
An experiment changes one factor to measure its effect, while a focus group simply asks people questions and lets them discuss their opinions.
A mail survey collects written answers from people who never meet a researcher, while a focus group brings people together with a live moderator.

q.pt: Describe data-collection methods (e.g., observations, mail, diaries, phone, internet, discussion groups, interviews, scanners, tracking tools)
q.s: Bayview Juice Company held three focus groups of eight teens each to learn how they feel about its new flavors. What is a limitation of the qualitative data the company collected?
o: It is unable to reveal customers' motives
It requires a very large sample to be useful
It consists mostly of numerical ratings
It reflects only a small part of the market
q.r: It reflects only a small part of the market. Qualitative data come from small groups, so they reflect only a small part of the market and cannot reliably be generalized to all customers. Here, 24 teens cannot speak for every juice buyer. Revealing motives is a strength of qualitative data, not a limitation. Large samples and numerical ratings are features of quantitative research, such as surveys.
w: Revealing feelings and motives is actually a strength of focus groups, since participants can explain why they like or dislike the new flavors.
Large samples are a feature of quantitative surveys; focus groups work with small groups like Bayview's 24 teens, which is the source of their limitation.
Numerical ratings belong to quantitative research, while focus groups produce words, feelings and opinions from open discussion.

q.pt: Describe data-collection methods (e.g., observations, mail, diaries, phone, internet, discussion groups, interviews, scanners, tracking tools)
q.s: A grocery chain uses its checkout scanners to record which items shoppers buy together. This data-collection method is
q.r: Mechanical observation. Observation records what people actually do rather than what they say. When devices such as checkout scanners, cameras or website tracking tools do the recording, it is called mechanical observation, and it provides accurate data on actual purchases. A personal interview and a mail survey ask respondents questions, and a consumer diary relies on respondents to write down their own purchases.
w: A personal interview requires asking someone questions face to face, but the scanners simply record purchases without asking shoppers anything.
A consumer diary depends on shoppers writing down their own purchases, while here the checkout scanners record the purchases automatically.
A mail survey sends questions for people to answer in writing, but the grocery chain is capturing actual purchases at the register, not asking questions.

q.pt: Describe data-collection methods (e.g., observations, mail, diaries, phone, internet, discussion groups, interviews, scanners, tracking tools)
q.s: A research firm asks 300 households to write down every snack purchase they make for four weeks. Which data-collection method is the firm using?
q.r: Consumer diaries. A consumer diary is an ongoing record that respondents keep of their purchases or media use over a period of time. Diaries capture details that people might forget in a single survey. Focus groups are moderated group discussions, mechanical observation uses devices such as scanners to record behavior, and telephone interviews collect answers to questions in a single phone conversation.
w: Focus groups are moderated discussions held at one time, not records that households keep on their own for four weeks.
Mechanical observation uses devices like scanners or cameras to record behavior, but here the households themselves write down their snack purchases.
Telephone interviews collect answers in a single phone call, while this firm has households keep an ongoing written record over several weeks.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of sampling plans (i.e., who, how many, how chosen)
q.s: A sampling method in which every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected is called __________ sampling.
q.r: Simple random. In simple random sampling, every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected, which makes it a probability sampling method and helps the sample represent the population. Convenience, judgment and quota sampling are nonprobability methods. Convenience sampling uses whoever is easiest to reach, judgment sampling relies on the researcher's choice of respondents, and quota sampling fills set numbers for each category without random selection.
w: Convenience sampling uses whoever is easiest to reach, so people who are hard to reach have little or no chance of being selected.
Judgment sampling lets the researcher personally pick respondents, so members of the population do not all have the same chance of being chosen.
Quota sampling fills a set number of people for each category, but those people are not chosen randomly, so not everyone has an equal chance.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of sampling plans (i.e., who, how many, how chosen)
q.s: To learn about upcoming trends in hiking gear, a researcher hand-picks ten experienced outdoor-store buyers she believes are the most knowledgeable. This is an example of __________ sampling.
q.r: Judgment. Judgment sampling is a nonprobability method in which the researcher personally selects respondents believed to be experts or representative of the population. It is useful when only knowledgeable people can answer the questions. Convenience sampling uses whoever is easiest to reach. Stratified random sampling and cluster sampling are probability methods that rely on random selection, not the researcher's personal choice.
w: Convenience sampling uses whoever is easiest to reach, but the researcher carefully chose these buyers because of their expertise, not their availability.
Stratified random sampling picks people randomly from each subgroup, while this researcher hand-picked specific buyers based on her own judgment.
Cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups to study, but the researcher personally chose ten individual experts rather than drawing groups at random.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of sampling plans (i.e., who, how many, how chosen)
q.s: A campus bookstore divides its customers into freshmen, sophomores, juniors and seniors, then randomly selects 50 students from each group to survey. Which sampling method is the bookstore using?
q.r: Stratified random sampling. Stratified random sampling divides the population into subgroups, or strata, and then randomly selects respondents from every subgroup so each is represented. Cluster sampling randomly selects entire groups and studies everyone or a sample within only those groups. Quota sampling also fills set numbers per category, but the people are chosen without random selection. Systematic random sampling selects every nth name from a single list of the whole population rather than sampling within each subgroup.
w: Cluster sampling randomly picks entire groups and studies only those, but the bookstore samples from every class year, not just a few selected groups.
Quota sampling also fills set numbers per category, but its people are not chosen randomly, while the bookstore randomly selects 50 from each class.
Systematic random sampling picks every nth name from one list of everyone, but the bookstore first divides students into class groups and samples within each.

q.pt: Explain characteristics of effective data-collection instruments
q.s: What should the introduction of an effective survey tell participants?
q.r: The purpose of the survey. An effective data-collection instrument begins by explaining its purpose, telling participants why the survey is being conducted and how their answers will be used. Knowing the purpose builds trust and encourages honest, complete responses. Sharing other people's answers, the sponsor's expected results or the researcher's opinions would bias respondents toward particular answers and reduce the accuracy of the data.
w: Sharing other people's answers could push participants to copy them, which biases the results instead of preparing participants to answer honestly.
Revealing the results the sponsor hopes for nudges respondents toward those answers, which makes the data less accurate.
Stating the researcher's personal opinions can sway how participants respond, so it introduces bias rather than building trust in the survey.

q.pt: Explain characteristics of effective data-collection instruments
q.s: Partway through Hilltop Home Goods' 40-question survey, many respondents began choosing the same rating for every question. What should the researcher do to keep respondents focused on the next survey?
o: Use one rating scale for every question
Vary the types of questions and answers
Add more questions to each section
Remove the instructions to save space
q.r: Vary the types of questions and answers. Varying the types of questions and answers, such as mixing multiple-choice, rating-scale and short open-ended items, keeps respondents engaged and thinking about each question. Repeating one rating scale invites respondents to fall into a pattern of identical answers. Adding questions makes the survey longer and more tiring, and removing instructions makes it harder to complete accurately.
w: Using one rating scale throughout is part of the problem, because repeating the same format invites respondents to give the same answer without thinking.
Adding more questions makes an already long 40-question survey even more tiring, which would likely make respondents lose focus even sooner.
Removing instructions makes the survey harder to complete correctly and does nothing to stop respondents from falling into a pattern of identical answers.

q.pt: Explain characteristics of effective data-collection instruments
q.s: Before mailing a questionnaire to 2,000 customers, Orchard Lane Market asks 20 shoppers to complete it so the staff can find confusing questions. This trial run is called a
q.r: Pretest. A pretest is a trial run of a data-collection instrument with a small group before it is used in the full study. It reveals confusing wording, missing answer choices and problems with length, so they can be fixed before the questionnaire is sent out. A focus group is a moderated group discussion, a census studies every member of a population, and tabulation counts responses after the data are collected.
w: A focus group is a moderated discussion about a topic, while Orchard Lane is having shoppers fill out the actual questionnaire to find confusing questions.
A census studies every member of a population, but Orchard Lane is testing the questionnaire on only 20 shoppers before the full mailing.
Tabulation is counting responses after the full study's data are collected, while this trial run happens before the questionnaire is even mailed.

q.pt: Evaluate questionnaire design (e.g., types of questions, question wording, routing, sequencing, length, layout)
q.s: A questionnaire that begins with broad questions about a customer's shopping habits and gradually moves to specific questions about one brand is using the
q.r: Funnel approach. The funnel approach orders questions from broad and general to narrow and specific. Starting broadly eases respondents into the survey and keeps early questions from influencing later answers. The inverted funnel approach does the opposite, moving from specific to general. Branching sends respondents past questions that do not apply to them, and a Likert scale measures how strongly respondents agree or disagree with statements.
w: The inverted funnel approach moves from specific questions to broad ones, which is the reverse of the broad-to-specific order this questionnaire follows.
Branching sends respondents past questions that do not apply to them, but this questionnaire is described by its overall order of questions, from general to specific.
A Likert scale measures how strongly people agree or disagree with a statement, and it is a type of answer scale rather than a way of ordering questions.

q.pt: Evaluate questionnaire design (e.g., types of questions, question wording, routing, sequencing, length, layout)
q.s: Which of the following survey questions is double-barreled:
o: How satisfied are you with our prices?
How often do you shop at our store?
How satisfied are you with our prices and service?
Which of our store locations do you visit most often?
q.r: How satisfied are you with our prices and service? A double-barreled question asks about two things but allows only one answer. A customer might be pleased with the service but unhappy with the prices, so a single answer cannot be interpreted accurately. Good questionnaire design splits such items into two separate questions. The other options each ask about only one topic, so respondents can answer them clearly.
w: Asking about satisfaction with prices covers only one topic, so a single answer clearly tells the store how customers feel about prices.
Asking how often someone shops covers only one topic, so respondents can give one clear answer without being forced to combine two ideas.
Asking which location customers visit most covers a single topic, so it does not force two separate ideas into one answer.

q.pt: Explain techniques for processing marketing data
q.s: After a research team collects 500 completed questionnaires, what should it do before tabulating the responses?
o: Check that each form was completed properly
Write the final research report for managers
Select the sample of respondents for the study
q.r: Check that each form was completed properly. The first step in processing data is checking, or editing, the questionnaires to make sure each was completed properly. Researchers look for missing, unreadable or inconsistent answers and set aside or follow up on problem forms so errors do not distort the results. Writing the report and presenting recommendations come after the data are tabulated and analyzed, and the sample is selected before data are collected.
w: The final report can only be written after the responses are tabulated and analyzed, so it cannot come before tabulation.
The sample has to be chosen before any questionnaires are sent out, and this team already has 500 completed forms in hand.
Recommendations to management come at the very end, after the data have been checked, tabulated and analyzed.

q.pt: Explain techniques for processing marketing data
q.s: Why do researchers assign numbers to survey responses, such as 1 for yes and 2 for no?
o: To increase the survey's response rate
To make the questionnaire shorter to complete
To make large amounts of data easier to analyze
To reduce the cost of printing questionnaires
q.r: To make large amounts of data easier to analyze. Coding assigns numbers or symbols to responses so that large amounts of data can be entered into software, counted and analyzed quickly and accurately. Without coding, hundreds of written answers would be difficult to summarize. Coding happens after the data are collected, so it does not affect how many people respond, how long the questionnaire takes to complete or how much it costs to print.
w: Coding happens after the surveys are already returned, so it cannot change how many people chose to respond.
Respondents still answer the same questions in the same way; the numbers are assigned afterward, so the questionnaire does not get shorter for them.
Coding takes place after collection and does not change the printed questionnaire, so it has no effect on printing costs.

q.pt: Explain techniques for processing marketing data
q.s: Focus groups reveal that several participants find the lid of Trailmark's new travel mug hard to open. How should the company best use this finding?
o: Conclude that most buyers dislike the new mug
Predict the exact drop in sales the lid will cause
Discontinue the mug before conducting more research
Investigate the lid as a possible product problem
q.r: Investigate the lid as a possible product problem. Focus-group findings are qualitative data from a small number of people. They are best used to identify possible problems and generate ideas that the company can investigate further, often with quantitative research. Because the groups are small and not randomly selected, the findings cannot show what most buyers think, cannot predict exact sales changes and do not justify a major decision such as discontinuing the product.
w: Several comments in a few small focus groups cannot show what most buyers think, because the groups are too small to represent the whole market.
Focus groups produce opinions and ideas, not numbers, so they cannot predict an exact drop in sales from the lid problem.
Dropping the whole product based on a few small-group comments would be a major decision made on too little evidence; the lid issue first needs checking.

q.pt: Explain techniques for processing marketing data
q.s: A researcher builds a table showing how customers in three age groups rated a new flavor of sparkling water. This data-processing technique is called
q.r: Cross-tabulation. Cross-tabulation is a table that compares responses across two or more variables, such as age group and flavor rating, so researchers can see how different groups answered. Simple tabulation counts the responses to one question at a time without comparing groups. Data coding assigns numbers or symbols to responses, and data editing checks questionnaires for completeness and accuracy; both come before any tabulation.
w: Simple tabulation counts the answers to one question at a time, but this table compares ratings across three different age groups.
Data coding assigns numbers to responses so they can be counted, and it happens before any table like this comparison can be built.
Data editing checks questionnaires for missing or unclear answers, which happens before the researcher builds tables comparing groups.

q.pt: Explain the use of descriptive statistics in marketing decision making
q.s: How do descriptive statistics help marketers make decisions?
o: They predict the behavior of an entire population
They summarize data so results can be compared
They determine which customers to include in a sample
q.r: They summarize data so results can be compared. Descriptive statistics, such as the mean, median, mode and range, summarize a large set of data in a few numbers. Marketers can then quickly compare results, such as ratings for two package designs or sales in two regions. Cause-and-effect relationships are tested with causal research, drawing conclusions about a population from a sample is the role of inferential statistics, and choosing respondents is part of the sampling plan.
w: Proving cause and effect requires an experiment in causal research, while descriptive statistics like the mean and median only summarize data.
Drawing conclusions about a whole population from a sample is the role of inferential statistics, not of numbers that simply summarize the data collected.
Choosing who to include in a sample is part of the sampling plan done before data collection, not something descriptive statistics do.

q.pt: Explain the use of descriptive statistics in marketing decision making
q.s: Eleven customers rated a new smoothie on a 10-point scale: 4, 9, 7, 10, 6, 9, 8, 9, 5, 7, 6. What is the median rating?
q.r: 7. The median is the middle value when data are ranked in order. Sorted, the ratings are 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10. With 11 values, the middle value is the sixth one, which is 7. The mode, the most frequent value, is 9. The mean is 80 divided by 11, or about 7.3. The range, highest minus lowest, is 10 minus 4, or 6.
w: Nine is the mode, the rating that appears most often, but the median is the middle value once all eleven ratings are sorted in order.
About 7.3 is the mean, found by adding the ratings and dividing by 11, not the middle value of the sorted list.
Six is the range, the highest rating minus the lowest, which shows spread rather than the middle value of the list.

q.pt: Assess appropriateness of marketing research for the problem/issue (e.g., research methods, sources of information, timeliness of information, etc.)
q.s: Nova Skincare wants in-depth reactions to the scent and texture of a new moisturizer. What is a key strength of using focus groups for this primary research?
o: The findings relate directly to the product studied
The results represent the views of all customers
The data cost less than published industry reports
The method works without a trained moderator
q.r: The findings relate directly to the product studied. Focus groups are primary research, so the information gathered relates directly to the specific topic or product being studied, and participants can explain their reactions in depth. Because the groups are small, the results do not represent all customers. Primary research usually costs more than existing published reports, and a skilled moderator is essential to keep the discussion focused and unbiased.
w: Focus groups use only a handful of people, so their reactions cannot represent the views of all of Nova's customers.
Primary research like focus groups usually costs more than buying existing industry reports, so lower cost is not one of its strengths.
A trained moderator is essential to keep a focus group on track and unbiased, so the method does not work well without one.

q.pt: Assess appropriateness of marketing research for the problem/issue (e.g., research methods, sources of information, timeliness of information, etc.)
q.s: Kendall Toys plans to use a market study published several years ago to estimate demand for its newest board game. What is the main risk of relying on this secondary information?
o: The data are costly to obtain
The data take months to collect
The data may be out of date
The data focus too narrowly on its game
q.r: The data may be out of date. Secondary data were gathered earlier for another purpose, so a key drawback is that they may be outdated and no longer reflect the current market. Consumer tastes in toys and games change quickly. Secondary data are usually inexpensive and fast to obtain, and because they were not collected for Kendall's specific problem, they tend to be too general rather than too narrow. High cost, slow collection and specific focus describe primary data.
w: Secondary data are usually inexpensive because they already exist, so high cost is not the main risk of using an old published study.
The study was already published, so Kendall can use it right away; slow collection is a drawback of gathering new primary data.
A study done years ago for another purpose is likely too general, not too narrowly focused, since it was not created for Kendall's newest game.

q.pt: Assess appropriateness of marketing research for the problem/issue (e.g., research methods, sources of information, timeliness of information, etc.)
q.s: Lumen Electronics conducts in-depth interviews with 15 customers and then surveys 2,000 customers to measure how widespread their opinions are. This combined approach is called
q.r: Mixed methods research. Mixed methods research combines qualitative and quantitative approaches in one study. In-depth interviews uncover customers' reasons and opinions, and a large survey then measures how common those opinions are, so each method offsets the other's weaknesses. Cause-and-effect (causal) research uses experiments to test cause and effect, secondary research relies on existing data, and syndicated research is purchased from a firm that sells the same data to many clients.
w: Cause-and-effect research changes one factor in an experiment to measure its effect, but Lumen is interviewing and surveying customers without changing anything.
Secondary research relies on data that already exist, while Lumen is gathering new information firsthand through both interviews and a survey.
Syndicated research is bought from a firm that sells the same data to many clients, but Lumen is collecting its own data from its own customers.

q.pt: Assess appropriateness of marketing research for the problem/issue (e.g., research methods, sources of information, timeliness of information, etc.)
q.s: Carver Furniture must decide within two weeks whether to stock a new sofa line, and the expected profit is modest. Which research approach is most appropriate?
o: A quick review of existing sales data
A year-long test market in several cities
A series of price experiments in every store
q.r: A quick review of existing sales data. Research must fit the problem, including how soon the information is needed and whether its value justifies its cost. Reviewing existing sales and supplier data delivers timely information at low cost for a modest decision. A six-month survey, a year-long test market and store-wide experiments would arrive too late to help and would likely cost more than the decision is worth.
w: A six-month survey would deliver results long after the two-week deadline and would probably cost more than a modest-profit decision is worth.
A year-long test market could not finish before the decision is due in two weeks, and its cost would likely exceed the modest expected profit.
Running price experiments in every store takes time and money far beyond what a quick, low-profit stocking decision justifies.

q.pt: Assess appropriateness of marketing research for the problem/issue (e.g., research methods, sources of information, timeliness of information, etc.)
q.s: A marketing manager needs to estimate what percentage of households in a metropolitan area would buy a new meal-kit service. Which research approach is most appropriate?
o: A single focus group of eight people
A survey of a large random sample
Informal talks with several store employees
An in-depth interview with one loyal customer
q.r: A survey of a large random sample. Estimating a percentage for a whole market calls for quantitative research with a sample large enough, and chosen randomly enough, to represent the population. A survey of a large random sample meets both needs. A single focus group and one in-depth interview produce qualitative insights from too few people to project to the market, and employees' opinions are not a substitute for data from actual households.
w: One focus group of eight people gives useful opinions but is far too small to estimate a percentage for an entire metropolitan area.
Store employees can share impressions, but their opinions cannot measure what percentage of actual households would buy the service.
One loyal customer's views can offer insight, but a single person cannot represent all households in the area, so no percentage can be estimated.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in marketing-information management
q.s: A research firm is preparing a client report from a customer survey. Which action reflects ethical marketing-research practice?
o: Adjusting the sample so it favors the client's product
Leaving out findings that the client may dislike
Removing respondents' names before sharing results
Describing a sales call to respondents as a short survey
q.r: Removing respondents' names before sharing results. Ethical marketing research protects respondents' privacy, so removing names and other identifying details before sharing results keeps their answers confidential. Adjusting the sample to favor a product and leaving out unwelcome findings are dishonest because they distort the results. Presenting a sales call as a survey is sugging, a deceptive practice that misleads respondents about the true purpose of the contact.
w: Choosing respondents so the results favor the client's product distorts the findings, which makes the research dishonest rather than ethical.
Hiding findings the client may not like gives a false picture of the results, which breaks the honesty that ethical research requires.
Calling a sales call a short survey tricks people about the real purpose of the contact, a deceptive practice known as sugging.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in marketing-information management
q.s: Pioneer Research publishes its sample size, questionnaire and data-collection methods along with its findings so that others can review them. This openness mainly increases the research's
q.r: Credibility. Credibility is the degree to which research findings can be trusted. When a research firm openly discloses how a study was conducted, others can judge whether the methods were sound and unbiased, which makes the findings more believable. Publishing methods after the study does not change how many people responded, does not affect the amount of sampling error and does not change the number of people sampled.
w: Response rate is the share of contacted people who answered, and publishing methods after the study is finished cannot change how many responded.
Sharing methods openly lets others judge the study, but it does not change the amount of sampling error that already exists in the results.
Sample size is set when the study is designed, so publishing it afterward does not add any respondents.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in marketing-information management
q.s: A beverage company surveys only its own loyal customers about whether they prefer its drink or a rival's, then advertises that "most people prefer our taste." What makes this practice unethical?
o: The study compared the drink with a competitor's
The company paid for its own research study
The results were used in an advertisement
The sample was picked to favor its product
q.r: The sample was picked to favor its product. Surveying only loyal customers produces biased results, and presenting them as the views of most people misleads consumers. Biased research is commonly misused to promote products in this way. Comparing a product with a competitor's, paying for one's own research and using honest research findings in advertising are all acceptable practices when the study is fair.
w: Comparing a drink with a rival's is a normal and acceptable kind of research when the study is fair, so the comparison itself is not the problem.
Companies commonly pay for their own research, and doing so is acceptable as long as the study is designed fairly and reported honestly.
Using honest research results in an ad is acceptable; the problem here is that the results came from a sample stacked with loyal customers.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in marketing-information management
q.s: Before a moderator begins recording a focus group, she explains the purpose of the study and how the recording will be used, then asks participants to agree. This practice is known as
q.r: Obtaining informed consent. Informed consent is a participant's agreement to take part in research after being told its purpose and how the information will be used. Obtaining it respects participants' rights and is a basic ethical standard in marketing research. Pretesting is a trial run of a questionnaire, coding assigns numbers to responses, and screening determines whether a person qualifies to participate in a study.
w: Pretesting is a trial run of a questionnaire to find problems, not a step where participants are told how recordings will be used and asked to agree.
Coding assigns numbers to responses after data are collected, but the moderator is asking for agreement before the discussion even starts.
Screening checks whether a person qualifies to join a study, while the moderator is explaining the study and asking qualified participants to agree.

q.pt: Describe the regulation of marketing-information management
q.s: An online retailer based in Ohio collects customer data in several U.S. states and in European countries. It finds that it must follow different privacy rules for different customers. This is because consumer-privacy laws
q.r: Differ by jurisdiction. Consumer-privacy laws differ by jurisdiction, the area over which a government has legal authority. Some U.S. states, such as California, have their own privacy laws, and the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to personal data of people in the EU. Industry groups may issue voluntary codes, but laws are set by governments, apply to online data collection and are not optional.
w: Industry groups can publish voluntary codes, but privacy laws are made by governments, which is why the rules change from state to state and country to country.
Privacy laws cover many kinds of data collection, including online shopping, so they are not limited to phone surveys.
Privacy laws are legal requirements that retailers must follow, not voluntary guidelines they can choose to ignore.

q.pt: Describe the regulation of marketing-information management
q.s: A caller tells Dana he is conducting a short survey about home security. After two questions, he begins pitching an alarm system and asks for an appointment. This practice is called
q.r: Sugging. Sugging means selling under the guise of research. The caller pretends to conduct a survey to gain Dana's cooperation and then delivers a sales pitch. Research-industry codes of ethics prohibit it, and it can violate consumer-protection rules that require sellers to disclose a sales purpose promptly. Frugging is fundraising under the guise of research, data mining searches databases for patterns, and cross-selling suggests related products to existing customers.
w: Frugging is asking for donations while pretending to do research, but this caller is pitching an alarm system, which is a sale, not fundraising.
Data mining uses software to find patterns in large databases, not a phone call where someone pretends to survey a person.
Cross-selling suggests related products to someone who is already a customer, while this caller is using a fake survey to start a sales pitch.

q.pt: Describe the regulation of marketing-information management
q.s: An app developer wants to collect email addresses from users younger than 13 for a marketing survey. Under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), the developer must first
o: offer an opt-out after collecting the data.
limit the survey to ten questions.
q.r: Obtain verifiable parental consent. COPPA requires operators of websites and online services directed to children under 13 to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting children's personal information, such as email addresses. The law is enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, not the Federal Communications Commission. Offering an opt-out after the data are collected does not satisfy the requirement for consent beforehand, and the law does not limit the number of survey questions.
w: COPPA is enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, not the Federal Communications Commission, and notifying an agency is not what the law requires first.
COPPA requires a parent's permission before the data are collected, so offering a chance to opt out afterward comes too late.
COPPA controls how children's personal information is collected; it does not set any limit on the number of questions in a survey.

q.pt: Identify data monitored for marketing decision making
q.s: The two-person marketing staff at Riverside Sports Shop wants to track every possible statistic about its customers, competitors and industry. What guideline should the staff follow when planning its data collection?
o: Monitor the data needed for key decisions
Collect as much data as can be found
Rely on competitors to share their data
Wait for a crisis before gathering data
q.r: Monitor the data needed for key decisions. Businesses should monitor the data needed for their key marketing decisions, such as sales, customer and competitor figures, without overextending their time, money and staff. Collecting everything that can be found wastes resources and causes information overload, which makes important facts harder to see. Competitors seldom share their data, and waiting for a crisis means the business cannot spot changes early and adjust.
w: Gathering every bit of data available would overwhelm a two-person staff and bury the important facts under information they do not need.
Competitors rarely share their data, so depending on them would leave Riverside without the information it needs for its own decisions.
Waiting for a crisis means Riverside would miss early warning signs and have no data ready when a quick decision is needed.

q.pt: Identify sources of error in a research project (e.g., response errors, interviewer errors, non-response errors, sample design)
q.s: Only 10 percent of the customers who received Sunbeam Travel Gear's mail survey returned it, and most who responded were frequent buyers. Which source of research error is most likely?
q.r: Non-response error. Non-response error occurs when the people who do not respond differ in important ways from those who do. Here, frequent buyers were far more likely to answer, so the results probably overstate customer enthusiasm. Interviewer error requires an interviewer whose behavior influences answers, which a mail survey lacks. Frame error occurs when the sampling list omits part of the population, and coding error happens when responses are assigned the wrong numbers during processing.
w: Interviewer error comes from an interviewer influencing answers, but a mail survey has no interviewer talking with respondents.
Frame error happens when the list used for sampling leaves out part of the population, but Sunbeam's problem is which customers chose to return the survey.
Coding error happens when responses are given the wrong numbers during processing, but the issue here is that most customers never responded at all.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the marketing-information management function
q.s: Ashford Department Stores uses software to search its large customer database and discovers that shoppers who buy patio furniture often buy outdoor lighting within a month. This use of technology is called
q.r: Data mining. Data mining uses software to search large databases for hidden patterns and relationships, such as products customers tend to buy together. Marketers can use the pattern to time promotions for outdoor lighting. Data entry is keying or importing data into a system, data coding assigns numbers or symbols to responses, and data editing checks data for errors and missing information before analysis.
w: Data entry is just keying or importing data into a system, not searching through a database to uncover buying patterns.
Data coding assigns numbers or symbols to responses so they can be counted, not searching a database for links between purchases.
Data editing checks data for errors and missing information, while Ashford is using software to discover a hidden buying pattern.

q.pt: Monitor/measure customer “buzz”
q.s: A sneaker brand tracks how often it is mentioned on social media compared with the total mentions of all sneaker brands. This measure of customer buzz is called
q.r: Share of voice. Share of voice is a brand's mentions divided by the total mentions of all brands in its category, showing how much of the conversation the brand owns. Monitoring it helps marketers measure customer buzz. Market share compares a firm's sales with total industry sales, response rate is the percentage of contacted people who complete a survey, and Net Promoter Score measures how likely customers are to recommend a brand.
w: Market share compares a company's sales with total industry sales, but the brand is measuring social media mentions, not sales.
Response rate is the percentage of people who complete a survey, which has nothing to do with counting social media mentions of brands.
Net Promoter Score measures how likely customers are to recommend a brand, based on asking them, not on counting its share of online mentions.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the product/service management function
q.s: Bayside Outfitters regularly reviews which jackets and boots to add, update or drop, based on what its customers are requesting. Which marketing function is the company performing?
q.r: Product/service management. Product/service management is the marketing function of obtaining, developing, maintaining and improving a product or service mix in response to market opportunities. Deciding which jackets and boots to add, update or drop is a product-mix decision, so it belongs to this function. Channel management deals with moving products to customers through distribution channels. Marketing-information management gathers and analyzes information for decision making, and promotion communicates with customers to inform, persuade or remind them.
w: Channel management moves products from producers to customers, but Bayside is deciding which jackets and boots to offer, not how to deliver them.
Marketing-information management gathers the customer feedback Bayside uses, but deciding to add, update or drop items is a product-mix decision.
Promotion communicates with customers to inform or persuade them, while Bayside is choosing which products belong in its lineup.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the product/service management function
q.s: A furniture store that delivers and assembles the sofas it sells is providing __________ services.
q.r: Product-related. Product-related services are services a business provides along with the goods it sells, such as delivery, installation, assembly or repair. They add value to the good and help a business stand out from competitors that sell similar products. Pure services, such as a haircut or tax preparation, are sold on their own without a good. Professional and financial services are categories of services that businesses sell by themselves, not services that accompany a good.
w: Pure services, like a haircut, are sold on their own, but delivery and assembly here come along with the sofas the store sells.
Professional services, like legal or accounting advice, are sold by themselves, while delivery and assembly are add-ons to the sofa purchase.
Financial services involve money, such as loans or insurance, but delivering and assembling a sofa is a service tied to the good itself.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the product/service management function
q.s: How do services differ from goods?
o: Services are performed rather than manufactured
Services can be stored in inventory until needed
Services are easier to standardize than goods
Services are priced lower than comparable goods
q.r: Services are performed rather than manufactured. Goods are tangible items that are made or grown, while services are intangible activities that people perform for customers, such as cleaning, repairing or advising. Because services are performed, they cannot be stored in inventory; an unsold appointment time is lost. Services also vary with the person performing them, so they are harder, not easier, to standardize than goods. Services are not necessarily cheaper; many professional services cost more than goods.
w: Services cannot be stored; an unfilled appointment time is simply lost, while goods can sit in inventory until a customer buys them.
Services depend on the person performing them, so they vary more and are harder to standardize than manufactured goods.
Services are not automatically cheaper; many professional services cost more than goods, so price is not what separates the two.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the product/service management function
q.s: Why do businesses continually review and update their product mix?
o: To reduce the need for marketing research
To match competitors' prices on every item
To lower the cost of their promotional activities
To keep offerings in line with customer needs
q.r: To keep offerings in line with customer needs. Customer wants change, competitors introduce new products and technology improves, so a product mix that fit last year may not fit today. Product/service management responds to these market opportunities by adding, improving or dropping products. Reviewing the mix actually depends on marketing research rather than reducing it. Matching competitors' prices is a pricing decision, and lowering promotional costs is a promotion decision.
w: Updating the product mix actually depends on marketing research to learn what customers want, so it increases rather than reduces the need for research.
Matching competitors' prices is a pricing decision, while reviewing the product mix is about which products to add, improve or drop.
Cutting promotional costs is a promotion decision, while reviewing the product mix focuses on keeping the right products available.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the product/service management function
q.s: A product manager's duties would most likely include which of the following tasks:
o: Negotiating shipping rates with a trucking company
Choosing the radio stations that will air an ad
Calculating the sales tax owed to the state
Deciding to drop a slow-selling product line
q.r: Deciding to drop a slow-selling product line. Product/service management includes deciding which products to add, keep, improve or drop from the product mix. Removing a line that no longer sells well keeps the mix profitable and focused on what customers want. Negotiating shipping rates is part of channel management and distribution. Choosing radio stations for an ad is a promotion decision, and calculating sales tax is an accounting task.
w: Negotiating shipping rates is part of channel management and distribution, not deciding which products a business should offer.
Picking radio stations for an ad is a promotion decision, while a product manager focuses on what is in the product mix.
Figuring out sales tax owed is an accounting task, not a decision about which products to add, keep, improve or drop.

q.pt: Identify the impact of product life cycles on marketing decisions
q.s: Product managers know that many new products fail early, while sales are low, promotion costs are high and customers are unfamiliar with the item. In which stage of the product life cycle is the failure rate highest?
q.r: Introduction. In the introduction stage, a product is new to the market, few customers know about it, sales are low and costs for development and promotion are high, so the product usually loses money. Many products never gain enough buyers to survive this stage. In the growth stage, sales are rising quickly. In maturity, sales level off, and in decline, sales fall after the product has already been successful.
w: In the growth stage, sales are rising quickly and customers already know the product, which is the opposite of the low-sales situation described.
In maturity, sales level off after the product is well known, so customers are no longer unfamiliar with it.
Products reach decline only after they have already succeeded, so this stage is not where brand-new, unfamiliar products fail.

q.pt: Identify the impact of product life cycles on marketing decisions
q.s: When almost every potential customer who wants a product already owns one, the product has reached market __________.
q.r: Saturation. Market saturation occurs when nearly all potential buyers of a product have already bought it, so sales level off. It usually happens in the maturity stage of the product life cycle, and marketers respond by finding new uses, new markets or product improvements. Market penetration is a strategy for increasing sales of current products in current markets. Segmentation is dividing a market into groups, and liquidation is selling off remaining inventory.
w: Market penetration is a strategy to increase sales of current products in current markets, not the point where nearly everyone already owns the product.
Segmentation is dividing a market into groups with similar traits, which does not describe a market where almost every buyer already has the product.
Liquidation is selling off leftover inventory, often when a product is dropped, not the condition of a market where nearly everyone owns one.

q.pt: Identify the impact of product life cycles on marketing decisions
q.s: Sales of Tidewell Electronics' portable DVD players have fallen for three straight years. Tidewell stops production and sells its remaining stock to a discount reseller at a reduced price. This is an example of
q.r: Liquidation. In the decline stage of the product life cycle, sales and profits fall, and a business may decide to drop the product. Liquidation is selling off the remaining inventory, usually at reduced prices, so the company can recover some money and free up resources. Trading up is adding higher-priced items to the product mix. Repositioning tries to change a product's image to revive sales, and market penetration aims to increase sales in current markets.
w: Trading up means adding higher-priced items to the product mix, but Tidewell is getting rid of a product, not adding more expensive ones.
Repositioning tries to change a product's image to revive sales, while Tidewell has stopped making the players and is selling off what is left.
Market penetration aims to grow sales in current markets, but Tidewell has stopped production and is clearing out its remaining stock.

q.pt: Identify the impact of product life cycles on marketing decisions
q.s: Six months after Krest Kitchens launched its air-fryer oven, sales are climbing rapidly and several competitors have released similar models. In which stage of the product life cycle is the oven?
q.r: Growth. During the growth stage, sales increase rapidly as more customers learn about and buy the product, and profits rise. Success attracts competitors, who enter the market with similar products. In the introduction stage, sales are low and few competitors exist. In maturity, sales level off and competition is most intense, and in decline, sales fall steadily.
w: In the introduction stage, sales are low and few competitors exist, but the oven's sales are climbing fast and rivals are already copying it.
In maturity, sales level off, but the oven's sales are still climbing rapidly only six months after launch.
In decline, sales fall steadily, which is the opposite of the rapid sales growth the oven is experiencing.

q.pt: Identify the impact of product life cycles on marketing decisions
q.s: Zenna Audio launches new wireless earbuds at a low price so it can win a large share of the market quickly, before competitors respond. Which introduction-stage pricing strategy is Zenna using?
q.r: Penetration pricing. In the introduction stage of the product life cycle, marketers often choose between two pricing strategies. Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to attract many buyers quickly and build market share. Price skimming does the opposite, setting a high initial price to earn profits from eager buyers before lowering it. Prestige pricing keeps prices high to suggest quality, and price lining sets a limited number of price points for a product line.
w: Price skimming starts with a high price to earn profit from eager early buyers, the opposite of Zenna's low launch price.
Prestige pricing keeps prices high to suggest quality and status, while Zenna is pricing low to win many buyers quickly.
Price lining sets a few price points across a product line, but Zenna's goal is a low launch price to gain market share fast.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the product/service management function
q.s: What is a primary purpose of using electronic data interchange (EDI) with vendors?
o: To design new products using 3-D computer models
To monitor online conversations about a brand
To create digital ads for social media sites
To automate product reordering with vendors
q.r: To automate product reordering with vendors. Electronic data interchange (EDI) is the computer-to-computer exchange of business documents, such as purchase orders, invoices and shipping notices, between a business and its vendors. Sharing sales and inventory data this way lets products be reordered quickly and accurately so they stay in stock and product availability is managed. Designing products with 3-D models is done with computer-aided design (CAD) software. Monitoring online conversations is social listening, and creating digital ads is a promotion activity.
w: Building 3-D models of new products is done with computer-aided design software, not with a system for exchanging documents with vendors.
Tracking what people say about a brand online is social listening, while EDI exchanges orders and invoices between a business and its suppliers.
Creating social media ads is a promotion activity, not the computer-to-computer exchange of purchase orders and invoices that EDI handles.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the product/service management function
q.s: Which of the following is a drawback of rapid technological change for product managers:
o: Customers have less information about products
New product designs take longer to create
q.r: Products become obsolete more quickly. When technology advances rapidly, newer and better products replace existing ones sooner, which shortens product life cycles and gives a business less time to earn back its development costs. Product managers must plan for frequent updates and replacements. Technology actually gives customers more product information, not less. Design tools such as CAD software speed up product design, and technologies such as barcodes and RFID make inventory easier to track.
w: Technology actually gives customers more product information, such as online reviews and price comparisons, so less information is not a drawback product managers face.
