Tools like computer-aided design actually speed up product design, so technology change makes new designs faster to create, not slower.
Technologies like barcodes and RFID tags make inventory easier to track, so this is a benefit of technology rather than a drawback.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the product/service management function
q.s: Designers at Northpoint Bikes build and test 3-D models of a new frame on screen before making a physical prototype. Which technology are they using?
q.r: Computer-aided design (CAD). CAD software lets designers create, view and test detailed product designs on a computer, so problems can be found and fixed before money is spent on physical prototypes. This speeds product development and lowers its cost. Radio frequency identification uses radio tags to track items. Electronic data interchange exchanges business documents between companies, and social listening software monitors what people say about a brand online.
w: RFID uses radio tags to track items through inventory, not software to build and test 3-D designs on screen.
EDI exchanges business documents like purchase orders between companies, not design models of a bike frame.
Social listening software tracks what people say about a brand online, which has nothing to do with designing a new frame.

q.pt: Explain business ethics in product/service management
q.s: A maker of phone chargers deliberately uses a cord material it knows will crack within a year so that customers will have to buy replacements. This practice is called
q.r: Planned obsolescence. Planned obsolescence is deliberately designing a product to wear out or become outdated quickly so that customers must replace it. Many people consider it unethical because it wastes customers' money and creates unnecessary waste. Technological obsolescence happens when new technology genuinely improves on a product. Style obsolescence happens when fashions change, and product liquidation is selling off remaining inventory when a product is dropped.
w: Technological obsolescence happens when new technology genuinely improves on a product, while this maker is choosing a material meant to crack.
Style obsolescence happens when fashions change and an item looks outdated, but the charger cord is being designed to physically break.
Product liquidation is selling off leftover stock when a product is dropped, not designing a product to fail so customers must buy again.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the product/service management function
q.s: Brightline's smartwatch still works perfectly, but a competitor's new model with far longer battery life and added health sensors has made it outdated. This is an example of
q.r: Technological obsolescence. Technological obsolescence occurs when a product becomes outdated because new technology has genuinely improved on it, even though the older product still works. The competitor's real improvements in battery life and sensors made Brightline's watch less desirable. Planned obsolescence is a deliberate design choice to make a product wear out early. Style obsolescence results from changing fashions, and market saturation means nearly all potential buyers already own the product.
w: Planned obsolescence is a deliberate choice to make a product wear out early, but Brightline's watch still works and was outdone by a rival's improvements.
Style obsolescence comes from changing fashions, while Brightline's watch became outdated because of real improvements in battery life and sensors.
Market saturation means nearly everyone who wants a product already owns one, which is not what happened when a better competing model came out.

q.pt: Explain business ethics in product/service management
q.s: Which of the following is an argument that supporters of planned obsolescence make:
o: It reduces the waste that goes to landfills
It lowers what consumers spend over time
It makes products last as long as possible
q.r: It encourages ongoing product improvement. Supporters of planned obsolescence argue that regularly replacing products pushes businesses to develop new and better versions and keeps the economy growing. Critics answer that the practice is unethical when products are deliberately made to fail early, because it wastes customers' money and resources. Planned obsolescence increases rather than reduces landfill waste, raises rather than lowers what consumers spend over time and works against making products last as long as possible.
w: Planned obsolescence means products are thrown away sooner, which adds to landfill waste rather than reducing it.
Replacing products more often makes consumers spend more over time, so supporters do not claim it lowers spending.
Planned obsolescence deliberately shortens how long products last, so making products last as long as possible is the opposite of the practice.

q.pt: Explain business ethics in product/service management
q.s: Which of the following labeling practices is ethical:
o: Using an oversized box to make a small product look bigger
Calling a product eco-friendly without evidence to support the claim
Printing a customer-service website and phone number on the package
Listing the ingredients in type too small for most people to read
q.r: Printing a customer-service website and phone number on the package. Ethical labeling is honest and complete, and giving customers a way to contact the company lets them ask questions, report problems or seek help. It shows the business stands behind its product. An oversized box misleads customers about how much they are buying. Unsupported eco-friendly claims are greenwashing, and unreadable ingredient lists hide information customers need.
w: An oversized box tricks shoppers into thinking they are getting more product than they are, which is misleading rather than ethical.
Calling a product eco-friendly without evidence is greenwashing, a misleading claim that deceives customers who care about the environment.
Printing ingredients too small to read hides information customers need, even though the list is technically there.

q.pt: Explain business ethics in product/service management
q.s: Kestrel Cleaning Co. labels its spray "all natural and earth-safe" even though it contains the same harsh chemicals as its regular product. This unethical practice is called
q.r: Greenwashing. Greenwashing is making misleading claims that a product is environmentally friendly in order to attract customers who care about the environment. It is unethical because it deceives customers and can also lead to Federal Trade Commission action against deceptive claims. Planned obsolescence is designing products to wear out early. Trading down is adding lower-priced products to a product mix, and product bundling is selling products together as a package.
w: Planned obsolescence means designing a product to wear out early, while Kestrel's problem is a false environmental claim on its label.
Trading down is adding lower-priced products to a product mix, not falsely labeling a harsh spray as earth-safe.
Product bundling is selling several items together as a package, which has nothing to do with misleading environmental claims.

q.pt: Identify product opportunities
q.s: Which personal trait best helps a marketer identify new product opportunities?
o: Being observant and aware of customers' needs
Being cautious about trying anything new
Being focused only on current best-sellers
Being reluctant to question how things are done
q.r: Being observant and aware of customers' needs. Product opportunities often come from noticing unmet needs, customer complaints, trends and gaps that competitors are not filling. Marketers who pay close attention to what customers say and do are more likely to spot these opportunities. Being overly cautious, focusing only on current best-sellers or refusing to question the way things are done all make a marketer less likely to recognize new product possibilities.
w: Being cautious about anything new makes a marketer less likely to try fresh ideas, which works against spotting new product opportunities.
Focusing only on current best-sellers keeps attention on what already works and makes it easy to miss unmet needs and new trends.
Refusing to question how things are done keeps a marketer stuck in old habits, which hides gaps where new products could succeed.

q.pt: Identify methods/techniques to generate a product idea
q.s: During a Six Thinking Hats session, Dani says, "I can't explain why, but I have a bad feeling about this new flavor." Which hat is Dani wearing?
q.r: Red hat. In the Six Thinking Hats technique, the red hat represents feelings, emotions and intuition, which people may share without having to justify them. Dani's hunch that she cannot explain is red-hat thinking. The black hat represents caution and identifying risks with logical reasons. The white hat focuses on facts and information, and the yellow hat looks for benefits and reasons for optimism.
w: The black hat is used to point out risks with logical reasons, but Dani admits she cannot explain her feeling at all.
The white hat focuses on facts and data, while Dani is sharing an unexplained gut feeling instead of information.
The yellow hat looks for benefits and reasons for optimism, but Dani is expressing a negative hunch about the flavor.

q.pt: Identify methods/techniques to generate a product idea
q.s: What does the Six Thinking Hats technique help a product development team do?
o: Vote anonymously on the most popular idea
Rank ideas by their projected profit
Eliminate weak ideas before anyone discusses them
Examine an idea from one perspective at a time
q.r: Examine an idea from one perspective at a time. Six Thinking Hats sorts thinking into six viewpoints, each represented by a colored hat, such as facts, feelings, caution, benefits, creativity and process control. The whole group focuses on the same viewpoint at the same time, which reduces arguments and makes sure each idea is considered thoroughly. The technique does not involve anonymous voting or profit rankings, and it encourages discussion rather than eliminating ideas before they are explored.
w: Six Thinking Hats is a group discussion method, not an anonymous voting process for picking the most popular idea.
The technique sorts thinking into viewpoints like facts, feelings and caution; it does not rank ideas by projected profit.
Six Thinking Hats encourages the group to discuss each idea from several angles, rather than throwing out ideas before they are talked about.

q.pt: Identify methods/techniques to generate a product idea
q.s: A product team at Lumos Lighting tries to come up with as many ideas as possible for a new desk lamp, with a rule that no one may criticize an idea until the session ends. Which idea-generation technique is the team using?
q.r: Brainstorming. Brainstorming is a group technique for producing a large number of ideas quickly, and judging or criticizing ideas is not allowed during the session so that people feel free to share. Evaluation comes later. Idea screening is the next step, in which ideas are evaluated and weak ones are dropped. Concept testing asks potential customers to react to a product idea, and test marketing sells a finished product in a limited area.
w: Idea screening is the later step that evaluates and drops weak ideas, while the Lumos team has a rule against criticizing ideas during the session.
Concept testing asks potential customers to react to a product idea, but the Lumos team is generating ideas among themselves.
Test marketing sells a finished product in a limited area, while the Lumos team is still coming up with ideas for a lamp that does not exist yet.

q.pt: Generate product ideas
q.s: After generating dozens of possible product ideas, what should the product team at Harbor Snacks do next?
o: Begin full production of the idea the team likes best
Launch a national advertising campaign for each idea
Set final retail prices for every idea on the list
Screen the ideas against company goals
q.r: Screen the ideas against company goals. Idea generation produces many possibilities, and idea screening narrows them by dropping ideas that do not fit the company's goals, abilities, budget or target market. Only the most promising ideas move on to concept testing and development. Beginning full production, advertising nationally or setting final prices all come much later, after an idea has been developed and tested.
w: Starting full production right after generating ideas skips screening, concept testing and development, which would risk money on an untested idea.
Advertising every idea nationally makes no sense before the ideas are screened and developed, since most of them will never become products.
Final prices are set much later, after an idea has been developed and tested, not for every rough idea on the first list.

q.pt: Describe the uses of grades and standards in marketing
q.s: Glenview Market's weekly ad highlights that its steaks are USDA Choice beef. Why would the store promote this grade to shoppers?
o: To show the meat was raised locally
To signal the quality of the meat
To indicate the store's lowest price
To prove the meat is certified organic
q.r: To signal the quality of the meat. Grades rank products by quality level. USDA beef grades, such as Prime, Choice and Select, tell shoppers about qualities like tenderness and flavor, so promoting a high grade builds shoppers' confidence in the quality they are buying. Grading is separate from the safety inspection that meat must pass. A grade does not tell where the meat was raised, does not indicate price and is separate from organic certification, which has its own standards.
w: A USDA grade tells shoppers about quality traits like tenderness and flavor, not where the cattle were raised.
A beef grade ranks quality, not price, so promoting Choice beef does not tell shoppers the store has its lowest price.
Organic certification follows separate standards, so a USDA Choice grade says nothing about whether the meat is organic.

q.pt: Describe the uses of grades and standards in marketing
q.s: How do shared industry standards for product size and performance benefit consumers?
o: They require competing brands to charge the same price
They make it easier to compare similar products
They replace the need for product warranties
They let each seller set its own measurements
q.r: They make it easier to compare similar products. Standards set specific, measurable requirements for size, content, safety or performance. When competing products meet the same standards, consumers can compare them on an equal basis and trust what they are buying. Standards do not set prices; competition and each business's pricing decisions do. They do not replace warranties, which state what a seller will do if a product fails, and shared standards prevent sellers from using their own measurements.
w: Industry standards set requirements for size, content or performance, but they do not set prices; each business still decides what to charge.
Standards describe what a product must meet, while warranties promise what the seller will do if the product fails, so standards do not replace them.
Shared standards mean everyone uses the same measurements, which is the opposite of letting each seller set its own.

q.pt: Describe the uses of grades and standards in marketing
q.s: Labels such as Grade AA and Grade A on cartons of eggs rank products by their level of quality. These rankings are called
q.r: Grades. Grades are ratings that rank products according to their level of quality, such as Grade AA, A and B eggs or Prime, Choice and Select beef. They help buyers know what quality they are getting without inspecting every item. Standards set specific requirements that products must meet rather than ranking them. Specifications are detailed descriptions of required product characteristics, and brand marks are symbols that identify a seller.
w: Standards set requirements that a product must meet, but they do not rank products into levels of quality like Grade AA and Grade A.
Specifications are detailed descriptions of required product characteristics, not a ranking system that labels eggs by quality level.
Brand marks are symbols that identify a seller, like a logo, while Grade AA and Grade A describe the quality of the eggs.

q.pt: Explain warranties and guarantees
q.s: From a business's point of view, what is a key purpose of offering a written warranty?
o: To protect both the producer and the seller
To shift all product risks to the customer
To replace the need for product testing
To exempt the business from consumer protection laws
q.r: To protect both the producer and the seller. A written warranty spells out what the producer or seller will do if a product fails and under what conditions, such as excluding damage from misuse. Stating these responsibilities clearly limits the business's liability and reduces disputes. A warranty does not shift all risk to the customer; it accepts some responsibility. It does not replace product testing, and it does not exempt a business from consumer protection laws.
w: A warranty means the business accepts some responsibility if the product fails, so it does not push all of the risk onto the customer.
Writing a warranty does not replace testing; a business still needs to test products so they work as promised and claims stay low.
A warranty cannot free a business from consumer protection laws, which still apply no matter what the warranty says.

q.pt: Explain warranties and guarantees
q.s: Ridgeline Appliances reviews its warranty claims every month and notices that many involve the same dishwasher pump. How does this information benefit the company?
o: It reduces the company's legal obligations
It allows the company to raise the product's price
It shortens the product's warranty period
It reveals problems to fix in the product
q.r: It reveals problems to fix in the product. When customers use warranties, their claims show the business which parts fail, how often and under what conditions. This feedback helps the company fix design or quality problems and improve future products. Reviewing claims does not reduce the company's legal obligations under its warranty. It also does not justify a higher price, and the warranty period is set by the warranty's terms, not by the number of claims.
w: Reviewing claims does not change what Ridgeline legally promised; the warranty still binds the company no matter how many pump claims it sees.
Repeated pump failures are a sign of a quality problem, which gives customers less reason, not more, to accept a higher price.
The warranty period is set by the warranty's written terms, so counting pump claims is a way to learn about defects, not to cut coverage.

q.pt: Explain warranties and guarantees
q.s: What is a primary benefit of a warranty for consumers?
o: It ensures they pay the lowest price for the product
It lets them return any product for any reason
It gives them legal recourse if the product fails
It entitles them to free upgrades to newer models
q.r: It gives them legal recourse if the product fails. A warranty is a promise about a product's quality or performance, so if the product does not perform as promised, consumers have a legal basis to require repair, replacement or a refund. This gives them confidence when buying. A warranty has nothing to do with getting the lowest price. Returning a product for any reason describes a satisfaction guarantee, and warranties do not promise free upgrades to newer models.
w: A warranty is a promise about how the product will perform, not a promise about price, so it says nothing about whether buyers paid the least.
Returning anything for any reason describes a satisfaction guarantee; a warranty only covers a product that fails to perform as promised.
Warranties promise repair, replacement or a refund when the product fails, but they do not entitle owners to newer models when those come out.

q.pt: Explain warranties and guarantees
q.s: A salesperson at Summit Gear tells a customer that a tent "will keep you dry in heavy rain." This statement creates a(n) __________ warranty.
q.r: Express. An express warranty is a promise about a product's quality or performance that the seller states orally or in writing. The salesperson's spoken statement about keeping the customer dry is a specific promise, so it is an express warranty. An implied warranty is unstated and imposed by law. An extended warranty, or service contract, is purchased separately to lengthen coverage, and a full warranty is a type of written warranty with broad repair or replacement terms.
w: An implied warranty is an unstated promise the law assumes, but this salesperson spoke an actual promise out loud about keeping the customer dry.
An extended warranty is extra coverage bought separately to lengthen protection, while the salesperson's words were a stated promise made at no added cost.
A full warranty is a type of written warranty with broad repair terms, but the question is about a spoken promise of how the tent performs.

q.pt: Explain warranties and guarantees
q.s: Bloom Bakery promises customers their money back if they are not happy with any pastry they buy. This promise is a
q.r: Satisfaction guarantee. A guarantee is a promise that customers will be satisfied with a product or will receive their money back. Bloom's promise covers any unhappy customer, not just a defect, so it is a satisfaction guarantee. A limited warranty covers only certain parts, problems or conditions. An implied warranty is unstated and imposed by law, and an extended service contract is purchased separately to cover repairs.
w: A limited warranty covers only certain parts or defects, while Bloom refunds anyone who is simply unhappy with a pastry, defect or not.
An implied warranty is unstated and set by law, but Bloom openly announces its money-back promise to customers.
An extended service contract is bought separately to pay for repairs, which makes no sense for a pastry and is not what Bloom is offering.

q.pt: Identify consumer protection provisions of appropriate agencies
q.s: How do consumer protection regulations often affect businesses?
o: They add costs for testing, labeling and compliance
They reduce the need for quality control
They lower the cost of bringing products to market
They allow businesses to set prices without competition
q.r: They add costs for testing, labeling and compliance. Consumer protection regulations require businesses to make safe products, label them accurately and advertise honestly. Meeting these rules adds expenses for product testing, record keeping, labeling changes and legal review, although compliance also builds consumer trust. Regulations increase rather than reduce the need for quality control, and they raise rather than lower the cost of bringing products to market. They do not remove competition or let businesses set prices freely.
w: Consumer protection rules require safe, accurately labeled products, so businesses need more quality control to meet them, not less.
Testing, labeling and legal review all cost money, so these regulations usually raise rather than lower the cost of launching a product.
Consumer protection rules aim at safety and honesty; they do not remove competitors or give businesses freedom to set prices without rivals.

q.pt: Identify consumer protection provisions of appropriate agencies
q.s: When a customer and a business cannot settle a dispute, they may agree to let an impartial third party hear both sides and make a decision. This process is called
q.r: Arbitration. In arbitration, an impartial third party, the arbitrator, hears both sides of a dispute and makes a decision, which is often binding. It is usually faster and less expensive than going to court. In mediation, a neutral third party helps the two sides reach their own agreement but does not make the decision. Negotiation involves only the two parties working it out themselves, and litigation is settling a dispute through a lawsuit in court.
w: Mediation also uses a neutral third party, but the mediator only helps the two sides reach their own agreement and does not make the decision.
Negotiation is the customer and business working it out between themselves, with no impartial third party hearing both sides.
Litigation means taking the dispute to court through a lawsuit, which is the formal route that arbitration is often used to avoid.

q.pt: Identify consumer protection provisions of appropriate agencies
q.s: Before releasing a new infant car seat, how can Kinder Motion best determine whether the product is safe for consumers?
o: Survey parents about which seat colors they like best
Compare its price with competitors' seats
Test the product under realistic conditions
Ask the sales team for its opinion
q.r: Test the product under realistic conditions. Product testing shows how a product actually performs, including how it holds up in situations customers are likely to face, so it is the best way to find safety problems before a product reaches the market. Testing also helps a business meet government safety standards and avoid costly recalls. Surveys about colors, price comparisons and sales team opinions provide marketing information but cannot show whether the seat protects a child.
w: A survey about favorite colors tells Kinder Motion what parents find attractive, but it cannot show whether the seat protects a child in a crash.
Comparing prices helps with pricing decisions, but a seat's price says nothing about whether it holds up safely in real use.
The sales team's opinions are guesses from people focused on selling, not evidence from tests showing how the seat actually performs.

q.pt: Identify consumer protection provisions of appropriate agencies
q.s: Which federal agency sets safety standards for toys and household products and works with companies to recall those that are dangerous?
q.r: Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). The CPSC protects the public from unreasonable risks of injury from consumer products such as toys, appliances and furniture. It sets safety standards, investigates hazards and works with businesses on recalls. The FDA regulates the safety and labeling of food, drugs, cosmetics and medical devices. OSHA enforces workplace safety rules for employees, and the EPA protects the environment.
w: The FDA oversees food, drugs, cosmetics and medical devices, not toys and everyday household products like the ones in the question.
OSHA enforces safety rules for workers on the job, while the question asks about the safety of products that consumers buy and use at home.
The EPA protects the environment, such as air and water quality, rather than setting safety standards and recalls for toys.

q.pt: Identify consumer protection provisions of appropriate agencies
q.s: Flexcore advertises that its exercise band "burns 10 pounds of fat a week" but has no evidence to support the claim. Which federal agency handles complaints about deceptive advertising like this?
q.r: Federal Trade Commission (FTC). The FTC protects consumers from unfair and deceptive business practices, including false or unsupported advertising claims. Advertisers must be able to back up claims like the one Flexcore makes. The CPSC deals with the physical safety of consumer products rather than advertising claims. OSHA protects worker safety on the job, and the USDA inspects and grades agricultural products such as meat and poultry.
w: The CPSC deals with whether products are physically dangerous, but Flexcore's problem is an unsupported advertising claim, not a safety hazard.
OSHA protects employees' safety at work and has no role in judging whether an exercise band's ad is truthful.
The USDA inspects and grades farm products such as meat and poultry, so it does not handle false claims in exercise-equipment ads.

q.pt: Explain the concept of product mix
q.s: Pinecrest Tea Co. sells only loose-leaf teas and tea accessories. What is a key benefit of its narrow product mix?
o: It spreads risk across many markets
It protects against falling demand for tea
It allows the company to specialize
q.r: It allows the company to specialize. A narrow product mix has few product lines, so the business can focus its knowledge, buying, staff and promotion on one area and build a reputation as an expert. Spreading risk across many markets and offering one-stop shopping are benefits of a wide product mix. A narrow mix actually increases the risk from falling demand, because the business depends on a small number of related products.
w: Spreading risk across many markets comes from a wide product mix, but Pinecrest sells only tea and tea accessories in one market.
One-stop shopping requires carrying many different product lines, which is the opposite of Pinecrest's tea-only mix.
A tea-only business depends heavily on tea, so a drop in tea demand would hurt it more, not protect it.

q.pt: Explain the concept of product mix
q.s: Larkspur Foods organizes its products into a restaurant line, a school-cafeteria line and a grocery-store line. How is Larkspur grouping its product lines?
q.r: By customer group. A product line is a group of closely related products, and businesses can group lines in different ways. Larkspur's lines are organized by the market each one serves: restaurants, school cafeterias and grocery stores. Grouping by price range would separate budget, mid-priced and premium products. Grouping by product use would organize products by what they do, and production method is not a basis Larkspur is using here.
w: Grouping by price range would separate budget and premium products, but Larkspur's lines are named for restaurants, schools and grocery stores.
Grouping by use would sort products by what they do, such as snacks or entrees, while Larkspur sorts by which buyers each line serves.
Nothing in the question says the lines are made in different ways; each line is defined by the market it sells to.

q.pt: Explain the concept of product mix
q.s: Maple Street Shoes adds a line of premium leather boots priced well above any of its current styles. This product-mix strategy is called
q.r: Trading up. Trading up is adding higher-priced, higher-quality products to the product mix to attract customers willing to pay more and to improve the business's image. The premium boots are priced above Maple Street's current styles, so this is trading up. Trading down is adding lower-priced items. Line contraction is dropping products from the mix, and cannibalization occurs when a new product takes sales away from the company's own existing products.
w: Trading down means adding lower-priced items, but Maple Street's new boots are priced well above its current styles.
Line contraction means dropping products from the mix, while Maple Street is adding a new line of boots.
Cannibalization happens when a new product steals sales from the company's own products, but the question describes adding a pricier line, not lost sales.

q.pt: Describe the nature of product bundling
q.s: How does product bundling benefit the business that offers it?
o: Each item earns a higher profit margin
Products no longer need to be promoted
Customers can buy only the items they want
q.r: Customers compare prices less often. When products are sold together for one price, customers cannot easily compare the price of each item with competitors' prices, so the business faces less direct price comparison. Bundling also increases the size of the average sale. However, each item in a bundle usually earns a smaller profit margin because the package price is discounted. Bundles still need promotion, and buying only the items they want is what customers lose with a bundle.
w: Bundled items are usually priced at a discount, so each item tends to earn a smaller profit margin, not a higher one.
A bundle is still a product offer that customers must hear about, so the business still has to promote it.
Being able to buy only the items you want is what customers give up with a bundle, so it is not a benefit to the business.

q.pt: Describe the nature of product bundling
q.s: Arcadia Games packages a new gaming console with two older games that have been selling slowly. Which business benefit of bundling does this illustrate?
q.r: Moving slow-selling merchandise. Product bundling lets a business pair a popular item with items that are not selling well, so customers who want the popular product also take the slower sellers. This clears inventory and increases the size of each sale. Specialization comes from a narrow product mix, not from bundling. Bundling does not shorten a product's life cycle, and it does not change the need for warranties on the products in the package.
w: Specialization comes from carrying a narrow product mix, while Arcadia is pairing items to sell more of its slow games.
Bundling the games does not make the console or games go through their life cycle faster; it just helps clear the slower sellers.
Packaging items together does not change what each product's warranty covers, so the bundle has nothing to do with warranty needs.

q.pt: Describe the nature of product bundling
q.s: Treeline Mobile offers a phone, case and charger together for $640; bought separately, the three items cost $715. What is the primary benefit of this bundle for customers?
o: A wider choice of individual items
A higher level of product quality
q.r: A lower total price. Product bundling offers two or more products together for one price that is usually lower than the total of their separate prices. Here, customers save $715 - $640 = $75 by buying the bundle, and they also gain the convenience of getting everything at once. Bundling does not lengthen warranties or raise product quality. It actually narrows rather than widens the choice of individual items, because the items come as a set.
w: Selling the items together does not lengthen any warranty; the customer's gain here is the $75 saved compared with buying separately.
A bundle actually narrows choice because the phone, case and charger come as a set rather than letting customers pick each item.
The phone, case and charger are the same products whether bought together or apart, so the bundle does not raise their quality.

q.pt: Explain the nature of corporate branding
q.s: When customers describe a company as friendly, adventurous and caring, they are describing its brand __________.
q.r: Personality. Brand personality is the set of human traits and values that customers associate with a brand. A clear personality helps create an emotional connection between customers and the company. Brand equity is the added value a brand name gives a product. Brand loyalty is customers' tendency to keep buying the same brand, and a brand mark is a symbol or design that identifies the brand.
w: Brand equity is the extra value a brand name adds to a product, not the human traits like friendly or caring that customers describe.
Brand loyalty is customers' habit of buying the same brand again, while the question describes the human qualities they see in the company.
A brand mark is a symbol or design, but words like adventurous and caring describe the company's character, not a visual symbol.

q.pt: Explain the nature of corporate branding
q.s: Halvorsen Group puts its company name and logo on its appliances, power tools and lawn equipment so that customers' trust in the company carries over to every product. Halvorsen is using
q.r: Corporate branding. Corporate branding promotes the company itself as a brand, using the parent company's name across many products or units. Because customers already know and trust the Halvorsen name, that reputation transfers to each product, including new ones. Private branding is a retailer selling products under its own brand. Individual product branding gives each product its own separate name, and co-branding pairs two companies' brands on one product.
w: Private branding is a retailer selling goods under its own store label, while Halvorsen is a maker putting its company name on its products.
Individual product branding gives each product its own separate name, the opposite of putting one company name on every product.
Co-branding pairs two companies' brands on one product, but Halvorsen uses only its own name and logo.

q.pt: Identify customer touch points
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a customer touch point:
o: A company's annual tax return filed with the government
A company's social media reply to a customer
A supplier's invoice for raw materials
q.r: A company's social media reply to a customer. A customer touch point is any point at which a customer interacts with or experiences a brand, including ads, websites, stores, packaging, employees and social media. Each touch point shapes how customers see the company, so businesses try to make every one consistent with their brand. Tax returns, internal training schedules and supplier invoices are internal business records that customers do not experience.
w: A tax return is a record sent to the government, and customers never see or interact with it, so it does not shape their view of the brand.
An internal training schedule is used only inside the company, so customers do not experience it as a contact with the brand.
A supplier's invoice is a bill between the company and its supplier, which customers never see or interact with.

q.pt: Explain the nature of corporate branding
q.s: Vela Market tells customers they will always find fresh produce and get through checkout in under five minutes. This statement of what customers can consistently expect is the company's brand __________.
q.r: Promise. A brand promise is what customers can consistently expect every time they deal with a company. Keeping the promise across every interaction builds trust and loyalty, while breaking it damages the brand. Brand image is the perception customers actually hold of the company. Brand equity is the added value a brand name provides, and brand loyalty is customers' tendency to keep buying the same brand.
w: Brand image is the opinion customers actually hold of a company, while Vela is stating what customers can always count on.
Brand equity is the extra value a brand name adds, not a statement of what customers should expect on every visit.
Brand loyalty is customers' habit of coming back, which a kept promise can build, but Vela's statement itself is the promise.

q.pt: Explain the nature of corporate branding
q.s: What is a risk of corporate branding?
o: Each product must be promoted under a separate brand name
New products cannot benefit from the company's reputation
A problem with one product can hurt all products
Customers cannot tell which company makes the products
q.r: A problem with one product can hurt all products. Corporate branding links all of a company's products to one name, so a safety recall or scandal involving one product can damage customers' trust in all of them. Using separate brand names for each product is individual branding, which avoids this risk. Corporate branding helps new products benefit from the company's reputation and makes it easy for customers to know who makes them.
w: Separate brand names for each product describes individual branding, which corporate branding replaces with one company name.
Corporate branding actually helps new products by letting them borrow the trust customers already have in the company name.
With corporate branding the company name is on every product, so customers can easily tell who makes them.

q.pt: Explain the nature of corporate branding
q.s: What a company says it is and how it wants to be seen, expressed through its name, logo, values and messages, is its brand
q.r: Identity. Brand identity is the set of elements a company controls, such as its name, logo, colors, values and messages, to show who it is and how it wants customers to see it. Brand image is different: it is the perception customers actually hold, which may or may not match the identity. Brand equity is the added value a brand name gives, and brand awareness is how familiar customers are with the brand.
w: Brand image is what customers actually think of the company, which may differ from what the company says about itself.
Brand equity is the added value a brand name brings, not the name, logo and messages a company uses to present itself.
Brand awareness is how familiar customers are with a brand, not the self-description a company creates through its logo and values.

q.pt: Describe factors used by businesses to position corporate brands
q.s: Fernwood Health is deciding how it wants the whole company to be perceived. Which factor should most guide how Fernwood positions its corporate brand?
o: The personal preferences of its executives
The needs and wants of its target market
The colors its competitors use in their logos
q.r: The needs and wants of its target market. Positioning a corporate brand means shaping how target customers perceive the company compared with competitors, so the position must matter to those customers. Businesses also consider competitors, company values and strengths. Executives' personal preferences may not reflect what customers value. Competitors' logo colors are a design detail, and choosing low-cost media is a promotion decision made after the position is set.
w: Executives' personal tastes may not match what customers care about, and positioning only works if it matters to the target market.
Competitors' logo colors are a small design detail, while positioning is about how customers see the whole company compared with rivals.
Choosing cheap advertising media is a promotion decision made after the position is set, so it should not decide the position itself.

q.pt: Describe factors used by businesses to position corporate brands
q.s: Arbor Paper Company highlights its tree-replanting program and recycled materials so it will be seen as the most environmentally responsible paper maker. Which factor is Arbor using to position its corporate brand?
q.r: Corporate social responsibility. Corporate social responsibility is a company's commitment to act in the best interest of society and the environment. Arbor is positioning its whole company around its environmental actions to stand apart from competitors and appeal to customers who share those values. Low prices, product selection and delivery speed are other positioning factors, but Arbor's message focuses on responsible behavior, not price, selection or delivery.
w: Arbor's message is about replanting trees and using recycled materials, and it says nothing about having the industry's lowest prices.
Product selection is a valid positioning factor, but Arbor is promoting its environmental actions rather than how many products it offers.
Delivery speed can set a company apart, but Arbor's message focuses on caring for the environment, not on getting orders out fast.

q.pt: Identify customer touch points
q.s: Lakeshore Furniture wants to strengthen the customer touch points that occur after a sale. Which of the following should it focus on:
o: A billboard advertising its spring sale
A salesperson's demonstration of a sofa in the showroom
A follow-up email checking on customer satisfaction
Online product reviews that shoppers read before buying
q.r: A follow-up email checking on customer satisfaction. Customer touch points are all the moments when customers interact with a business before, during and after a purchase. A follow-up email asking how customers like their furniture reaches them after the sale, shows that the company cares and can lead to repeat business. A billboard and online reviews are touch points that occur before a purchase, and a showroom demonstration takes place during the buying process.
w: A billboard for a spring sale reaches people before they buy, so it does not strengthen Lakeshore's contact with customers after a sale.
A showroom demonstration happens while the customer is still deciding, which is during the buying process rather than after it.
Shoppers read online reviews while deciding what to buy, so they are a before-purchase touch point rather than an after-sale one.

q.pt: Describe factors used by marketers to position products/services
q.s: Which of the following is a valid reason for a business to reposition an existing product:
o: Sales of the product are growing as planned
A new competitor has changed the market
Customers value the product's current image
The product's target market has not changed
q.r: A new competitor has changed the market. Repositioning is changing the image customers hold of an existing product. Businesses reposition when the competitive environment changes, sales decline, customer needs shift or the current image no longer works. A strong new competitor may take over the product's position, so the business needs a new one. Growing sales, a valued image and an unchanged target market all suggest the current position is working.
w: Sales growing as planned signals that the current position is working, which is a reason to keep it rather than change it.
If customers value the product's current image, changing that image would risk losing what already appeals to them.
An unchanged target market means the product still serves the same customers, which by itself gives no reason to change the image they hold of it.

q.pt: Explain the nature of product/service branding
q.s: A cartoon fox that appears on all of Copperline Cereal's boxes and ads to represent the brand is a
q.r: Trade character. A trade character is a brand mark that has human or lifelike qualities, such as a cartoon animal mascot. It gives the brand a personality and makes it easy to recognize, especially for children. A trade name is the legal name under which a company does business. A brand name is the part of a brand that can be spoken, and a slogan is a catchy phrase used in promotion.
w: A trade name is the legal name a company does business under, not a cartoon mascot that appears on boxes and ads.
A brand name is the part of a brand you can say out loud, while the fox is a lifelike picture that represents the brand.
A slogan is a catchy phrase used in promotion, but the fox is a character image rather than a set of words.

q.pt: Explain the nature of product/service branding
q.s: Why does a business register its brand name and logo as a trademark?
o: To qualify for lower business tax rates
To meet government product grading rules
To gain exclusive legal rights to them
To set a minimum retail price for its products
q.r: To gain exclusive legal rights to them. A trademark is a brand name, symbol or design that is legally protected, so competitors cannot use the same or a confusingly similar mark. Registering a trademark helps protect the brand's reputation and the value the business has built in it. Trademarks have no effect on tax rates, are unrelated to product grading and do not set the prices at which products are sold.
w: Trademark registration protects a name and logo from copying; it has no effect on the tax rates a business pays.
Product grading rules deal with quality standards for goods like meat or eggs, and a trademark is about protecting a brand's identity instead.
A trademark keeps rivals from using the brand's name and logo, but it does not control the prices stores charge for the products.

q.pt: Describe the role of customer voice in branding
q.s: Solano Outdoor reads customer reviews and social media posts, then uses customers' own words to shape its new brand message. Which branding practice is Solano using?
o: Using the voice of the customer
q.r: Using the voice of the customer. The voice of the customer is customers' own expressed needs, opinions and language. Brands that listen to reviews and social media and reflect that language in their messages show customers they understand what matters to them. Creating a trade character gives a brand a lifelike mascot. Registering a trademark provides legal protection, and developing a private brand means a retailer sells products under its own name.
w: A trade character is a lifelike mascot, but Solano is studying reviews and posts to borrow customers' words, not creating a cartoon.
Registering a trademark gives legal protection for a name or logo, while Solano is using customer language to shape its message.
A private brand is a retailer's own store label, which has nothing to do with listening to reviews and social media posts.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: Before customers ever visit Lakeview Appliance, many have already seen its ads for a new energy-saving refrigerator and know the model's main features. This shows that promotion helps a business by
q.r: Preselling products. Promotion presells products by informing customers about features and benefits before they ever talk with a salesperson. Customers who arrive already interested and informed are easier and quicker to serve, so the selling job becomes more efficient. Setting product prices is part of the pricing function, not promotion. Product liability depends on product safety and legal responsibility. Promotion supports salespeople, but it does not replace them.
w: Setting prices belongs to the pricing function; the ads in the question are informing customers about the refrigerator before they visit.
Product liability depends on product safety and legal responsibility, while the ads here simply teach customers about features ahead of time.
Promotion makes salespeople's work easier by sending in informed customers, but it does not take the place of the sales staff.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: Which of the following is a way that consumers benefit from promotion:
o: Learning new uses for products they already own
Receiving a promise of the lowest available price
Avoiding the need to read product labels
Buying products that are free from defects
q.r: Learning new uses for products they already own. Promotion informs consumers about new products, new uses for familiar products, prices and places to buy, which helps them make informed buying decisions. Promotion does not promise the lowest available price; pricing is a separate marketing function. Consumers still need to read labels for complete product information. Product quality depends on production and quality control, not on promotion.
w: Promotion tells consumers about products and prices, but it does not guarantee they are getting the lowest price available.
Ads give only some information, so consumers still need labels for complete details such as ingredients, warnings and instructions.
Whether a product is free from defects depends on how well it is made and checked, not on how it is promoted.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: The three basic purposes of promotion are to inform, persuade and __________ customers.
q.r: Remind. Promotion communicates with customers to inform them about products, persuade them to buy, and remind them about products they already know. Reminder messages keep a brand in customers' minds so they continue to buy. To work, promotional messages must be persuasive and relevant to the target audience. Rewarding customers is a goal of loyalty programs, researching customers is part of marketing-information management, and refunds are a customer-service matter.
w: Rewarding customers is the aim of loyalty programs, while promotion's three purposes are to inform, persuade and keep products in customers' minds.
Researching customers is part of marketing-information management, which gathers information rather than sending messages to customers.
Refunds are a customer-service matter after a sale, not one of the basic communication purposes of promotion.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: Harbor Coffee Roasters runs radio spots telling coffee drinkers who buy other brands that its beans are roasted fresher and urging them to switch. The main purpose of this promotion is to
o: inform customers about a new invention.
train employees to describe the product.
q.r: Persuade customers to change brands. Persuasive promotion tries to convince customers that a product is better than competing products so that they will buy it. Harbor's spots compare its freshness with other brands and urge listeners to switch, which is persuasion. Informing customers about a new invention applies to products buyers have never seen, and Harbor's coffee is not new. Training employees is an internal management activity, and gathering research about tastes is part of marketing-information management, not promotion.
w: Informing about a new invention fits products buyers have never seen, but coffee is familiar and Harbor is urging people to switch brands.
Training employees is an internal management task, while Harbor's radio spots speak to coffee drinkers who buy other brands.
Gathering research collects information from customers, but Harbor's spots send a message to customers urging them to act.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: Promotion benefits the economy as a whole by
o: encouraging competition and new product development.
preventing new businesses from entering markets.
keeping the prices of competing products equal over time.
removing the need for consumer protection laws.
q.r: Encouraging competition and new product development. Promotion lets businesses tell customers about better products and better prices, which pushes competitors to improve. Because new products can be introduced to the market quickly through promotion, businesses have more reason to develop them. Promotion makes it easier, not harder, for new businesses to enter markets. It does not keep competing prices equal; competition leads businesses to set different prices. Consumer protection laws remain necessary to prevent deceptive promotion.
w: Promotion helps new businesses tell customers about themselves, so it makes entering a market easier rather than blocking newcomers.
Competition encouraged by promotion leads businesses to set different prices, so it does not keep rivals' prices equal.
Promotion can be misleading, so consumer protection laws are still needed to keep advertising honest.

q.pt: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)
q.s: Pinecrest Grocers runs a newspaper ad featuring its employees volunteering at a local food pantry. The ad does not mention any products or prices. This is an example of __________ promotion.
q.r: Institutional. Institutional promotion builds a favorable image and goodwill for the business itself rather than selling specific goods or services. An ad that highlights employees' community service, with no products or prices, is designed to make the public think well of Pinecrest. Product promotion tries to sell specific goods or services. Sales promotion uses short-term incentives such as coupons. Comparative promotion compares a product with competitors' products.
w: Product promotion aims to sell specific goods, but this ad mentions no products or prices and only shows employees volunteering.
Sales promotion uses short-term incentives like coupons, and Pinecrest's ad offers no deal at all.
Comparative promotion compares a product with rivals' products, while this ad focuses on the store's community service.

q.pt: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)
q.s: What is the main goal of institutional promotion?
o: To clear out excess seasonal inventory
To create a favorable image of the company
To announce a product's limited-time price
To gather data about competitors' prices
q.r: To create a favorable image of the company. Institutional promotion focuses on the business as a whole. It aims to build goodwill, a favorable corporate image and positive public attitudes, which can lead to sales over the long term. Clearing out inventory and announcing a limited-time price are goals of product promotion and sales promotion. Gathering data about competitors' prices is a marketing-research activity, not a type of promotion.
w: Clearing out seasonal inventory is a goal of product or sales promotion, which push specific items rather than the company's overall image.
Announcing a limited-time price is meant to sell a specific product now, while institutional promotion builds goodwill toward the whole company.
Collecting competitors' prices is marketing research, which gathers information instead of sending a message to the public.

q.pt: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)
q.s: Trailmark Sporting Goods posts social media ads announcing 30% off all of its running shoes this weekend. Trailmark is using __________ promotion.
q.r: Product. Product promotion is designed to sell specific goods or services by informing customers about them and persuading them to buy. An ad announcing a discount on running shoes focuses on selling a particular product line. Institutional promotion builds the image of the business itself. Public-service messages support a cause or social issue. Public-relations promotion shapes the public's attitudes toward the company rather than selling a product.
w: Institutional promotion builds the image of the business itself, but Trailmark's ad is pushing a discount on specific shoes.
A public-service message supports a cause like safety or health, while Trailmark's ad is trying to sell running shoes.
Public-relations promotion shapes how people feel about the company, but a 30%-off shoe ad is aimed at making sales this weekend.

q.pt: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)
q.s: When a business uses public-relations promotion, it is mainly trying to
o: persuade customers to buy one product today.
teach salespeople how to handle objections.
shape the public's attitudes toward the business.
lower the cost of shipping its products to stores.
q.r: Shape the public's attitudes toward the business. Public-relations promotion is a form of institutional promotion. It builds goodwill and a favorable image by influencing how the public feels about the organization, often through news coverage, events and community involvement. Persuading customers to buy one product immediately is the goal of product promotion. Teaching salespeople is sales training, and lowering shipping costs is a distribution concern.
w: Persuading customers to buy one product right away is the goal of product promotion, not public relations.
Teaching salespeople to handle objections is sales training, an internal activity rather than a way of reaching the public.
Lowering shipping costs is a distribution concern and has nothing to do with how the public views the business.

q.pt: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a public-service message:
o: A furniture store's ad listing its holiday prices
A bicycle brand's ad urging teens to wear helmets
A phone maker's ad comparing its battery life
A restaurant's ad announcing its new lunch menu
q.r: A bicycle brand's ad urging teens to wear helmets. A public-service message supports a cause or social issue, such as safety or health, rather than selling a product. It is a type of institutional promotion because it builds goodwill toward the sponsor. The furniture store's price list, the phone maker's battery comparison and the restaurant's new menu are all product promotion because each aims to sell specific goods or services.
w: A list of holiday prices is meant to sell furniture, so it is product promotion rather than a message supporting a social cause.
Comparing battery life is meant to win phone sales, so it is product promotion rather than a message about a social cause.
Announcing a new lunch menu aims to sell meals, which makes it product promotion, not a public-service message.

q.pt: Explain types of advertising media
q.s: The general term for all of the channels that carry advertising messages to an audience is
q.r: Promotional media. Promotional media are the channels, such as print, broadcast, direct mail, out-of-home and online media, that carry advertising messages to a target audience. Each medium differs in cost, reach and targeting ability. The promotional mix is the combination of promotional elements a business uses, such as advertising and personal selling. A media kit is a packet of information for journalists. An ad layout is the arrangement of elements within one advertisement.
w: The promotional mix is the combination of tools a business uses, such as advertising and personal selling, not the channels that carry ads.
A media kit is a packet of information given to journalists, not the general term for channels that carry ads to an audience.
An ad layout is how elements are arranged within one ad, not the channels that deliver ads to the audience.

q.pt: Explain types of advertising media
q.s: Velo Cycle Shop pays to display its ads on the sides of city buses and inside train stations. Velo is using __________ media.
q.r: Transit. Transit media are advertisements placed on or inside public transportation vehicles, such as buses, subways and taxis, and in stations and terminals. They are a type of out-of-home media that reach commuters repeatedly. Broadcast media are television and radio. Specialty media are useful items, such as pens or calendars, printed with a business's name. Print media include newspapers and magazines.
w: Broadcast media are television and radio, while Velo's ads are posted on buses and in train stations.
Specialty media are useful items like pens printed with a business's name, not ads placed on public transportation.
Print media are newspapers and magazines, while Velo's ads appear on buses and inside stations.

q.pt: Explain types of advertising media
q.s: Brookside Pet Supply gives customers free leashes and water bottles printed with the store's name and phone number. These items are an example of __________ media.
q.r: Specialty. Specialty media are useful items, such as pens, calendars, tote bags or leashes, that carry a business's name, logo or contact information. Customers keep and use the items, so the advertising message is seen again and again. Transit media appear on buses and in stations. Direct-mail media are printed pieces sent through the mail. Broadcast media are television and radio.
w: Transit media are ads on buses and in stations, while Brookside is handing out useful items printed with its name.
Direct mail is printed material sent through the mail, but Brookside gives its leashes and bottles to customers directly.
Broadcast media are television and radio, not physical items like leashes that customers keep and use.

q.pt: Explain types of advertising media
q.s: Which of the following is an advantage of using radio as an advertising medium:
o: It lets listeners see the product being demonstrated
It can target listeners by station format at low cost
It gives the message a long life since listeners save it
It allows listeners to clip and save coupons
q.r: It can target listeners by station format at low cost. Radio is a broadcast medium. Because stations attract different audiences with formats such as country, sports talk or news, advertisers can reach specific listener groups, and radio time usually costs less than television time. Radio has no visual element, so listeners cannot see a demonstration. Radio messages are short-lived because they cannot be saved and reviewed. Clipping coupons requires a print medium, such as newspapers or magazines.
w: Radio has sound but no pictures, so listeners cannot actually see a product being demonstrated.
Radio ads play and are gone, so listeners cannot save them, which gives radio a short message life rather than a long one.
Coupons need something printed that people can cut out, so clipping them requires print media rather than radio.

q.pt: Explain types of advertising media
q.s: One advantage of direct mail as an advertising medium is that it
o: reaches a mass audience within a few minutes of sending.
costs less per person than online advertising.
is seldom thrown away before it is read.
allows the advertiser to select specific recipients.
q.r: Allows the advertiser to select specific recipients. Direct mail, such as sales letters, postcards and catalogs, is sent to people chosen from a customer database or mailing list, so the message reaches the exact prospects the business wants. Direct mail takes days to prepare and deliver, so it does not reach a mass audience within minutes. Printing and postage usually make it more expensive per person than online advertising. Many recipients discard direct mail as junk mail.
w: Direct mail takes days to print and deliver, so it cannot reach a mass audience within minutes like online messages can.
Printing and postage usually make direct mail more expensive per person than online ads, not cheaper.
Many people toss direct mail as junk mail without reading it, so this is a weakness of the medium rather than an advantage.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: Which of the following is an example of direct-response advertising:
o: A magazine ad offering a free sample to readers who text a code
A billboard showing a soft-drink brand's logo and its new slogan
A news story about a local store's grand opening event
A stadium sign displaying a credit union's name and colors
q.r: A magazine ad offering a free sample to readers who text a code. Direct-response advertising asks the audience to act right away, by calling, texting, scanning or ordering, so the business can measure the response. The texted code lets the business count exactly how many readers responded. A billboard and a stadium sign build awareness but do not ask for an immediate, measurable action. A news story is publicity, which the business does not pay for or control.
w: A billboard showing a logo and slogan builds awareness, but it does not ask people to take an immediate action the business can count.
A news story about a grand opening is publicity, which the business neither pays for nor uses to request a direct response.
A stadium sign keeps a name visible, but it does not ask fans to call, text or order, so responses cannot be measured.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: To reduce complaints and keep its marketing emails from being treated as spam, an online retailer should send promotional emails to customers who have
o: visited one of its physical stores.
q.r: Given permission to receive them. Permission, or opt-in, email marketing sends messages only to people who have agreed to receive them. Recipients who asked for the emails are less likely to report them as spam, and spam filters are less likely to block them. Customers of a competitor or store visitors have not agreed to receive emails. Sending messages to people who have unsubscribed violates their request and federal law.
w: People who bought from a competitor never agreed to get this retailer's emails, so sending them would likely draw spam complaints.
Visiting a store does not mean a shopper agreed to receive emails, so mailing them anyway risks being treated as spam.
People who unsubscribed have asked to stop receiving emails, so sending more would ignore their request and break federal law.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: Mapleton Furniture mails postcards with a unique coupon code to 2,000 past customers so it can count exactly how many customers use the code. This shows that direct marketing is designed to produce a(n)
q.r: Measurable response. Direct marketing communicates straight to targeted individuals to obtain a specific action, such as a purchase, call or visit, that the business can track. The unique coupon code lets Mapleton count responses and judge the mailing's success. A long-term company image is the goal of institutional promotion. An unpaid news story is publicity. General brand awareness is a broad advertising goal that is difficult to measure directly.
w: A long-term company image is the goal of institutional promotion, while Mapleton's coupon code is meant to count specific customer actions.
An unpaid news story is publicity, but Mapleton is paying to mail postcards directly to past customers.
Brand awareness is broad and hard to count, while Mapleton's unique code is designed so every response can be tracked.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: Cedar Lane Books mailed 2,500 catalogs to area residents and received 115 orders from the mailing. What was the catalog's response rate?
q.r: 4.6%. The response rate is the percentage of recipients who respond to a direct-marketing offer. Divide the number of responses by the number of pieces sent and multiply by 100: 115 / 2,500 = 0.046, and 0.046 x 100 = 4.6%. The 1.15% and 11.5% answers simply shift the decimal point in the number of orders instead of dividing by the number of catalogs mailed. The 21.7% answer comes from dividing the catalogs mailed by the orders received, which reverses the formula.
w: The 1.15% answer comes from shifting the decimal in the 115 orders instead of dividing those orders by the 2,500 catalogs mailed.
The 11.5% answer just moves the decimal in 115; the response rate requires dividing the orders by the 2,500 catalogs sent.
The 21.7% answer comes from dividing catalogs by orders, which flips the formula; responses must be divided by pieces mailed.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: Which of the following is a major advantage of email marketing compared with direct mail:
o: Less need for an accurate customer list
A longer life in the recipient's home
q.r: Lower cost per message sent. Email marketing avoids printing and postage, so each message costs far less than a mailed piece, and it can be sent quickly and tracked easily. Delivery is less reliable, because spam filters block many marketing messages. Businesses still need an accurate list, ideally of people who opted in. Printed catalogs stay in homes longer than emails stay in inboxes, so a longer life is an advantage of direct mail.
w: Spam filters block many marketing emails, so delivery is actually less reliable than mail that reaches a physical mailbox.
Email still needs an accurate list, ideally of people who opted in, so it does not reduce the need for good customer data.
Printed mail can sit in a home for weeks while emails get buried in an inbox, so a longer life favors direct mail, not email.

q.pt: Describe the use of business ethics in promotion
q.s: Critics say that paying to have branded products appear in movies and video games raises ethical concerns because viewers
o: cannot afford the products that are shown.
may not realize they are seeing advertising.
must pay extra to watch the content.
are required to buy the products shown.
q.r: May not realize they are seeing advertising. Product placement is the paid inclusion of branded products in shows, films, video games and other media. Because the brand is blended into entertainment, audiences, especially children, may not recognize the message as a paid promotion. Whether viewers can afford a product is not the ethical issue. Product placement does not change the price of the content. Viewers are never obligated to buy products they see.
w: Whether viewers can afford a product shown on screen is not what makes product placement an ethical concern; hidden advertising is.
Product placement is paid for by the brand, not by viewers, so it does not add to the cost of watching the content.
Seeing a product in a movie or game does not require anyone to buy it, so this is not the ethical issue critics raise.

q.pt: Describe the use of business ethics in promotion
q.s: An ad for a phone service portrays all older adults as confused by technology and unable to send a text message. This ad relies on
q.r: A stereotype. A stereotype is an oversimplified, fixed portrayal of a group of people. Showing every older adult as unable to use technology is unfair and can offend the audience, so ethical marketers avoid stereotypes based on age, gender, race or other traits. A testimonial is a statement from a satisfied user. Puffery is obvious, harmless exaggeration about a product. A premium is a free or low-cost item offered as a purchase incentive.
w: A testimonial is a statement from a satisfied user, while this ad unfairly portrays an entire age group as confused by technology.
Puffery is harmless exaggeration about a product, but this ad makes an unfair, fixed claim about a group of people.
A premium is a free or low-cost item given to encourage a purchase, and nothing in this ad offers a gift.

q.pt: Describe the use of business ethics in promotion
q.s: Tonelli's Pizzeria claims in its ads that it serves "the most delicious pizza on the planet." Because no reasonable person would take this statement literally, it is considered
q.r: Puffery. Puffery is exaggerated, subjective praise that no reasonable consumer would treat as a factual claim, such as calling a pizza the most delicious on the planet. It is generally legal because it cannot be proven true or false. Bait and switch lures customers with a bargain and then pushes a pricier item. Corrective advertising is required to fix earlier misleading claims. A testimonial is a statement from a satisfied customer or endorser.
w: Bait and switch lures customers with a bargain and then pushes a pricier item, while Tonelli's is simply boasting about taste.
Corrective advertising is ordered to fix earlier misleading claims, but Tonelli's harmless boast needs no correction.
A testimonial comes from a satisfied customer or endorser, while this boast is the pizzeria's own claim in its ads.

q.pt: Describe the use of business ethics in promotion
q.s: Delmar Electronics advertises a laptop at a very low price. When customers arrive, salespeople criticize the advertised laptop and pressure them to buy a much more expensive model. This deceptive practice is called
q.r: Bait and switch. Bait and switch advertises a bargain the seller does not truly intend to sell, then discourages customers from buying it and pushes a higher-priced item instead. It is unethical and considered a deceptive practice under federal law. Puffery is harmless exaggeration about a product. Product placement puts branded products in entertainment media. Comparative advertising compares a product with competitors' products by name.
w: Puffery is harmless exaggeration that no one takes literally, while Delmar is luring customers with a bargain it does not want to sell.
Product placement puts branded products in movies or games for pay, which has nothing to do with steering store shoppers to pricier laptops.
Comparative advertising compares a product with rival brands by name, but Delmar's salespeople are knocking their own advertised laptop.

q.pt: Describe the use of business ethics in promotion
q.s: A caller tells Andre that she is conducting a short survey about home safety. After two questions, she begins trying to sell him an alarm system. This unethical practice is known as
q.r: Sugging. Sugging means selling under the guise of research: pretending to conduct a survey in order to make a sales pitch. It is unethical because it deceives people about the purpose of the contact and makes consumers distrust legitimate research. Puffery is harmless exaggeration in ads. Product seeding gives products to influencers so others see them in use. Cause marketing links a business's promotion with support for a charitable cause.
w: Puffery is harmless exaggeration in an ad, while this caller is pretending to do research so she can make a sales pitch.
Product seeding gives free products to influencers so others see them in use, not a phone call disguised as a survey.
Cause marketing links a business's promotion with a charity, and nothing about this call involves supporting a cause.

q.pt: Describe the regulation of promotion
q.s: Ridgeway Motors advertises a sedan's low monthly payment but leaves out the fact that the offer requires a $6,000 down payment. Ridgeway's ad could be considered
q.r: Deceptive advertising. Deceptive advertising misleads reasonable consumers about important facts. An ad can be deceptive through false statements or through omissions, such as hiding a large down payment that changes the true cost of the offer. Puffery is obvious, subjective exaggeration that consumers do not take literally. Institutional advertising builds a company's image. Corrective advertising is required to fix earlier misleading ads.
w: Puffery is obvious, subjective exaggeration, while Ridgeway hides a real fact, the $6,000 down payment, that changes the offer's true cost.
Institutional advertising builds a company's overall image, but Ridgeway's ad is pushing a specific sedan deal.
Corrective advertising is run to fix earlier misleading ads, while Ridgeway's ad is the one that misleads in the first place.

q.pt: Describe the regulation of promotion
q.s: After finding that a juice company's ads falsely claimed its drink prevents colds, the Federal Trade Commission ordered the company to run new ads stating that the claim was untrue. This is an example of
q.r: Corrective advertising. Corrective advertising is advertising that a regulator such as the Federal Trade Commission requires a business to run to correct false impressions created by earlier ads. It helps undo the harm deceptive advertising caused consumers. Comparative advertising compares a product with competitors' products. Institutional advertising promotes a company's image. Industry self-regulation occurs when industry groups review ads without government involvement, but here a government agency gave the order.
w: Comparative advertising compares a product with competitors, but these new ads exist to admit the earlier cold-prevention claim was false.
Institutional advertising promotes a company's image by choice, while these ads were ordered by a regulator to correct a false claim.
Self-regulation happens when industry groups review ads without the government, but here the Federal Trade Commission gave the order.

q.pt: Describe the regulation of promotion
q.s: Which federal agency is primarily responsible for regulating deceptive advertising in the United States?
q.r: Federal Trade Commission (FTC). The FTC enforces federal laws against unfair and deceptive advertising. It can require businesses to back up their claims, order them to stop deceptive practices and require corrective advertising. The FCC licenses broadcasters and oversees the airwaves rather than policing the truth of ad claims. OSHA enforces workplace safety standards. The EEOC enforces laws against employment discrimination.
w: The FCC licenses broadcasters and oversees the airwaves, but it is not the main agency that judges whether ad claims are deceptive.
OSHA enforces workplace safety rules for employees and does not police the truth of advertising.
The EEOC enforces laws against job discrimination, which has nothing to do with deceptive advertising.

q.pt: Describe the regulation of promotion
q.s: Before running ads claiming its sunscreen stays effective for eight hours in water, Solara Skincare must have test results that support the claim. This requirement is called
q.r: Substantiation. Substantiation means an advertiser must have reasonable evidence, such as test results, to support objective claims before an ad runs. A claim about how long a sunscreen lasts can be measured, so Solara needs proof. Puffery is subjective exaggeration that does not need proof.
