An endorsement is a statement of support from a person or group. Self-regulation is industry policing of ads without government involvement.
w: Puffery is vague exaggeration that needs no proof, while an eight-hour water claim is measurable and must be backed by tests.
An endorsement is a statement of support from a person or group, not the requirement to have evidence before making a claim.
Self-regulation is industry groups reviewing ads on their own, while the question describes the duty to hold proof before a claim runs.

q.pt: Describe the regulation of promotion
q.s: A fitness influencer receives payment and free supplements from Peak Nutrition in exchange for posting about the products. Under Federal Trade Commission guidelines, the influencer should
o: avoid naming the brand in any posts.
disclose the paid connection to Peak Nutrition.
post reviews that criticize competing supplement brands.
wait a full year before posting about it.
q.r: Disclose the paid connection to Peak Nutrition. Federal Trade Commission guidelines on endorsements require influencers and other endorsers to clearly disclose any material connection, such as payment or free products, with the brand they promote. Disclosure lets followers judge the endorsement fairly. Hiding the brand name would defeat the promotion and does not address the connection. Criticizing competing brands and waiting a year do nothing to inform followers of the paid relationship.
w: Leaving out the brand name would hide the very product being promoted and still would not tell followers about the payment.
Criticizing competing brands does nothing to tell followers that Peak Nutrition is paying the influencer, which is what the guidelines require.
Waiting a year does not tell followers about the paid relationship, which is the information the guidelines say they need.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the promotion function
q.s: A cosmetics brand's mobile app lets users try on lipstick shades virtually with their phone's camera and then buy the shade they like. This promotional technology is valuable mainly because it is
q.r: Interactive. Interactive technology lets customers respond to and control the promotional experience, as when app users try on shades and then make a purchase. Interaction keeps customers engaged and moves them toward buying. A passive or one-way message, such as a traditional print ad, does not let the customer respond. Apps are highly targeted because they reach people who chose to download them, so untargeted does not describe this technology.
w: A passive message just sits there for people to see, but this app lets users try on shades and buy right away.
A one-way message gives customers no way to respond, while this app lets users control the try-on and make a purchase.
An app reaches people who chose to download it, so it is highly targeted, and untargeted is not why it is valuable.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the promotion function
q.s: Compared with a television commercial, a small business's targeted social media ad campaign usually
o: costs less and reaches a more precise audience.
reaches a broader mass audience in the market.
requires a longer lead time for production and approval.
provides fewer ways to measure results.
q.r: Costs less and reaches a more precise audience. Online promotion is often more cost-effective than traditional media because businesses can set small budgets and target users by location, age and interests, so less money is spent on people outside the target market. Television, not a targeted social media campaign, reaches a broad mass audience. Social media ads can be created and changed quickly. Online ads provide detailed measures, such as impressions and click-through rate.
w: Reaching a broad mass audience is a strength of television, while targeted social media ads focus on a narrower group of users.
Social media ads can be made and changed quickly, so they usually need less lead time than a television commercial, not more.
Online ads report clicks, impressions and other detailed measures, so they usually offer more ways to measure results than TV does.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the promotion function
q.s: Rosewood Boutique's online ad was displayed 40,000 times and was clicked 600 times. What was the ad's click-through rate?
q.r: 1.5%. The click-through rate is the percentage of ad impressions that result in a click. Divide clicks by impressions and multiply by 100: 600 / 40,000 = 0.015, and 0.015 x 100 = 1.5%. The 0.15% and 15% answers misplace the decimal point. The 66.7% answer reverses the formula by dividing impressions by clicks. Marketers use click-through rate to compare how well different online ads attract interest.
w: The 0.15% answer misplaces the decimal; 600 divided by 40,000 is 0.015, which equals 1.5% after multiplying by 100.
The 15% answer misplaces the decimal; 600 clicks out of 40,000 views is 0.015, which is 1.5%, not 15%.
The 66.7% answer comes from dividing impressions by clicks, which flips the formula; clicks must be divided by impressions.

q.pt: Explain communications channels used in public-relations activities
q.s: Oak Hollow Garden Center writes a ready-to-print article on fall planting tips and sends it to local newspapers, which may run it when they need extra content. This article is a
q.r: Matte release. A matte release is a feature article written by a business and supplied to media outlets in ready-to-print form. Newspapers often use matte releases as filler, which gives the business free exposure and publicity. A media kit is a packet of background facts, photos and contacts for journalists. A paid advertisement is placed and paid for by the business. A press conference is a live event where an organization announces news to reporters.
w: A media kit is a packet of background facts, photos and contacts for journalists, not a finished article ready to print.
Oak Hollow gives the article to newspapers for free to use as filler, so it is not an ad the business pays to place.
A press conference is a live event where reporters hear an announcement, while Oak Hollow sent a written article.

q.pt: Explain communications channels used in public-relations activities
q.s: Summit Athletic Apparel sponsors its city's annual charity 5K run, and local television stations mention the company during their race coverage. Summit's main public-relations goal is to
q.r: Obtain publicity and goodwill. Sponsoring community events is a public-relations activity that earns favorable media coverage, or publicity, and builds goodwill with the community. Publicity is unpaid, so the business gains exposure without buying airtime. Collecting direct-response orders is a goal of direct marketing. Testing a product's price is a pricing or marketing-research activity. Training sales staff is an internal management function.
w: Direct-response orders come from offers asking people to buy right away, but sponsoring a charity run is about image and media mentions.
Testing a price is a pricing or research activity, and sponsoring a 5K does not involve trying out any product's price.
Training sales staff is an internal management task, while sponsoring a public charity event aims to win favor with the community.

q.pt: Explain communications channels used in public-relations activities
q.s: Fernwood Outfitters sends a written news announcement about its new downtown store to newspapers, radio stations and local news websites. Which public-relations channel is Fernwood using?
q.r: Press release. A press release, or news release, is a written announcement of newsworthy information that an organization sends to media outlets in hopes that they will report it. A store opening is news, so a press release is the right channel. A matte release is a ready-to-print feature article, such as a how-to piece, rather than a news announcement. An infomercial is a long paid television ad. A testimonial is a satisfied customer's statement.
w: A matte release is a ready-to-print feature article such as a how-to piece, while Fernwood is announcing news about a new store.
An infomercial is a long paid television ad, while Fernwood is sending a written announcement for the media to report.
A testimonial is a satisfied customer's statement, not a news announcement a business sends to reporters.

q.pt: Describe word-of-mouth channels used to communicate with targeted audiences
q.s: Before launching a new trail-running shoe, Arcway sends free pairs to running coaches with large social media followings, hoping followers will notice the coaches wearing them. This is called
q.r: Product seeding. Product seeding is a word-of-mouth tactic in which a business gives products to influencers or opinion leaders so others see them using the products and start talking about them. Product placement is paying to feature branded products in shows, films or games. Sugging is selling under the guise of research. Direct mail is printed advertising sent through the mail to selected prospects.
w: Product placement means paying to feature products in shows, films or games, not giving free shoes to coaches with followings.
Sugging is selling while pretending to do research, which has nothing to do with sending free shoes to influencers.
Direct mail is printed advertising sent to prospects, while Arcway is relying on coaches being seen wearing the shoes.

q.pt: Describe word-of-mouth channels used to communicate with targeted audiences
q.s: Why is word-of-mouth promotion often more persuasive than advertising?
o: The business usually pays people to share it
The business controls what customers say about it
Consumers view it as coming from people they trust
It reaches a nationwide audience almost instantly
q.r: Consumers view it as coming from people they trust. Word-of-mouth is communication about a product passed from person to person in conversation, reviews or social media. Because it comes from friends, family or trusted influencers rather than the business, consumers find it highly credible. Most word-of-mouth is not paid for by the business. The business cannot control what people say, which is its main risk. Word-of-mouth usually spreads gradually from person to person rather than reaching a nationwide audience almost instantly.
w: Most word-of-mouth is not paid for, and it is persuasive precisely because it seems to come from people rather than the business.
Businesses cannot control what customers say about them, which is actually the main risk of word-of-mouth, not why it persuades.
Word-of-mouth usually spreads gradually from person to person, so instant nationwide reach is not what makes it persuasive.

q.pt: Explain the components of advertisements
q.s: In a print ad for Lumen Lighting, the large bold line at the top reads, "Light Up Every Room for Less." This part of the ad is the
q.r: Headline. The headline is the main attention-getting statement in an advertisement, usually set in large type at the top. It should draw readers into the rest of the ad. The signature identifies the sponsor with its name, logo and often a slogan. The copy is the main written selling message. The illustration is the photograph or artwork that shows the product or creates a mood.
w: The signature identifies the sponsor with its name and logo, usually near the bottom, not the large attention-getting line at the top.
Copy is the main body of selling text, while the large bold line at the top is meant to grab attention first.
An illustration is a photo or artwork, but the line described in the question is bold text at the top of the ad.

q.pt: Explain the components of advertisements
q.s: The copy in a magazine ad for Everfresh dish soap says, "Cuts through grease twice as fast as before." This copy is mainly
o: identifying the ad's sponsor and its slogan.
making a claim about the product's performance.
q.r: Making a claim about the product's performance. Ad copy is the written selling message of an advertisement. Copy that states what a product does, such as cutting grease faster, makes a claim, and that claim must be truthful and supported by evidence. Identifying the sponsor and slogan is the job of the signature. A testimonial quotes a satisfied user, and nothing here is attributed to a customer. A short-term incentive, such as a coupon, is sales promotion.
w: The signature names the sponsor and slogan, but this line describes what the soap does to grease.
A testimonial quotes a satisfied user, but this line is not credited to any customer; it is the company's own statement.
A short-term sales incentive would be a coupon or deal, and this copy offers no discount at all.

q.pt: Explain the importance of coordinating elements in advertisements
q.s: A designer notices that the headline, copy, illustration and signature in a print ad for Fairview Bakery all compete equally for the reader's attention. To unify the ad, the designer should
o: make the elements equal in size.
q.r: Create one dominant focal point. Coordinating ad elements means making the headline, copy, illustration and signature work together as one message. A single dominant focal point gives the reader a clear starting place and guides the eye through the rest of the ad. Making the elements equal in size adds to the competition for attention. More photos create clutter. Removing the signature would leave readers unsure who the sponsor is.
w: Making the elements equal in size would keep them competing for attention, which is the very problem the designer noticed.
Adding more photos would create clutter and give the reader even more things competing for attention.
Removing the signature would leave readers unsure who the ad is from, and it would not fix the lack of a focal point.

q.pt: Discuss internal and external audiences for public-relations activities
q.s: Which of the following is an internal audience for a retail chain's public-relations activities:
q.r: The chain's store employees. Internal audiences are the people inside an organization, chiefly its employees, who need to be informed, motivated and loyal. Businesses reach them through employee newsletters, intranets and meetings. Newspaper reporters, community shoppers and suppliers' representatives are all outside the organization, so they are external audiences for the chain's public-relations activities.
w: Newspaper reporters work outside the retail chain, so they are an external audience for its public-relations activities.
Shoppers in the community are customers outside the organization, which makes them an external audience, not an internal one.
Suppliers' sales representatives work for other companies, so they are outside the chain and count as an external audience.

q.pt: Identify the elements of the promotional mix
q.s: For one week, Glenmore Market hands out free samples of a new salsa and offers a buy-one-get-one-free coupon on it. Which element of the promotional mix is Glenmore using?
q.r: Sales promotion. Sales promotion uses short-term incentives, such as samples, coupons, contests and premiums, to encourage immediate buying. Free samples and a one-week coupon fit this element of the promotional mix. Personal selling is direct, two-way communication between a salesperson and a customer. Public relations builds goodwill and a favorable image. Advertising is a paid, nonpersonal message from an identified sponsor carried by promotional media.
w: Personal selling is a salesperson talking one-on-one with a customer, while Glenmore is using samples and coupons to spark quick buying.
Public relations builds goodwill and a favorable image, but free samples and a one-week coupon are incentives to buy now.
Advertising is a paid message carried by media, while handing out samples and coupons offers shoppers a direct reason to buy.

q.pt: Identify communications channels used in sales promotion
q.s: A cereal company places a small free toy inside each box to encourage children's families to buy the cereal. This sales promotion is called a
q.r: Premium. A premium is a free or low-cost item offered as an incentive to purchase a product, such as a toy packed inside a cereal box. A rebate is a partial refund paid after the purchase. A sweepstakes is a game of chance in which participants enter to win prizes. A loyalty program rewards customers for repeat purchases over time rather than for a single purchase.
w: A rebate is a partial refund paid after the purchase, while the toy is a free item packed inside the box.
A sweepstakes is a game of chance where people enter to win prizes, but every box here contains a toy.
A loyalty program rewards repeat purchases over time, while the toy comes with a single box of cereal.

q.pt: Identify types of public-relations activities
q.s: Public-relations activities that build positive relationships with a company's shareholders and potential investors are called
q.r: Investor relations. Investor relations is a public-relations activity that keeps shareholders and potential investors informed about a company's performance and plans, building confidence in the business. Employee relations builds positive relationships with workers. Community relations builds goodwill with people in the areas where the business operates. Media relations builds relationships with journalists to earn favorable news coverage.
w: Employee relations builds good relationships with workers, not with shareholders and potential investors.
Community relations builds goodwill with people where the business operates, not specifically with those who own or may buy its stock.
Media relations builds ties with journalists to earn news coverage, while the question is about shareholders and potential investors.

q.pt: Acquire product information for use in selling
q.s: Dante just started selling running shoes at Stride Athletics. Which of the following would give him the most firsthand knowledge of how the store's shoes perform:
o: Wearing several models on his own runs
Reviewing the store's weekly sales reports
q.r: Wearing several models on his own runs. Personal use is the most direct, firsthand source of product information because the salesperson experiences the product's performance for himself. Dante can then describe fit, comfort and support with confidence. Manufacturers' catalogs and competitors' advertisements are secondhand materials written by others. Sales reports show how many shoes sold, not how the shoes perform.
w: Catalogs are useful, but they are secondhand descriptions written by the makers rather than Dante's own experience of how the shoes perform.
Competitors' ads describe other stores' products in their own favor, so they tell Dante little firsthand about Stride's shoes.
Sales reports show how many shoes sold, not how the shoes actually feel and perform during a run.

q.pt: Acquire product information for use in selling
q.s: A salesperson at a kitchen-appliance store calls shoppers who bought a blender last month to ask how they use it and what they like about it. The salesperson is gathering product information from
q.r: Customers. People who have bought and used a product are a valuable firsthand source of product information. Their experiences reveal real uses, likes and problems that salespeople can share with future shoppers. Trade publications are industry magazines and websites. Manufacturers' representatives are the producer's employees who provide training and specifications. Product labels list printed facts; none of these is the buyer's own experience.
w: Trade publications are industry magazines and websites, but the salesperson is calling the people who bought the blender.
Manufacturers' representatives are the producer's employees, while the salesperson here is talking with shoppers who used the blender.
Product labels list printed facts, but the salesperson is asking buyers about their own experience using the blender.

q.pt: Acquire product information for use in selling
q.s: Marcus needs to explain to a shopper the exact differences between two similar laptop models. The most reliable source of this information is
o: the opinions of other shoppers in the store.
the prices charged by nearby competitors.
q.r: The manufacturers' published specifications. Product materials such as specification sheets, manuals and labels list each model's exact features, which makes them the best source for comparing similar items side by side. Opinions of other shoppers vary and may be inaccurate. Competitors' prices show what rivals charge, not how the models differ. An advertising circular highlights sale prices and a few selling points rather than complete product details.
w: Other shoppers' opinions vary and may be wrong, so they are not a reliable source for exact differences between two laptop models.
Competitors' prices show what rivals charge, but they do not explain how the two laptop models differ in features.
An ad circular highlights sale prices and a few selling points, not the complete details Marcus needs to compare models.

q.pt: Acquire product information for use in selling
q.s: A cosmetics brand sends a representative to show retail salespeople how its new skin-care line works and which customers it suits best. The salespeople are acquiring product information through
q.r: Manufacturer training. Producers often provide training sessions, demonstrations and representatives so that the salespeople who sell their products understand features, uses and the right customers for each item. Personal use means the salesperson tries the product himself or herself. Competitive shopping means visiting rival businesses to see what they carry. Customer satisfaction surveys collect information from buyers, not from the producer.
w: Personal use means a salesperson tries the product personally, but here the brand's representative is teaching them about it.
Competitive shopping means visiting rival stores, while these salespeople are learning from the maker of the skin-care line.
Satisfaction surveys collect opinions from buyers, but this information comes from the brand's representative, not from customers.

q.pt: Acquire product information for use in selling
q.s: A salesperson at Lakeside Furniture visits a rival store to see which sofas it carries and how it prices them. This source of product information is
q.r: Competitive shopping. Visiting or browsing competitors helps salespeople learn what other businesses offer, how they price it and how their own products compare. That knowledge lets the salesperson point out real advantages to customers. Manufacturer training comes from the producer of the products. Customer feedback comes from people who bought the products. Personal use means trying the product yourself rather than studying a competitor.
w: Manufacturer training comes from the company that makes the products, not from visiting a rival store to check its sofas.
Customer feedback comes from people who bought the products, while this salesperson is studying a competitor's selection and prices.
Personal use means trying a product yourself, but the salesperson is looking at what a rival store carries and charges.

q.pt: Analyze product information to identify product features and benefits
q.s: What is the main reason salespeople study the characteristics of the products they sell?
o: To write the company's advertising slogans
To set the products' selling prices
To lower the store's inventory costs
q.r: To answer customers' questions accurately. When salespeople understand a product's features, they can explain what each one does for the customer and respond to questions with confidence. This builds trust and helps match the product to the customer's needs. Writing slogans is an advertising task, setting prices is a pricing decision, and lowering inventory costs is an operations goal; none is the main reason salespeople learn product details.
w: Slogans are written by the advertising team, so learning product details is not mainly about creating them.
Prices are set through pricing decisions, while salespeople study products so they can explain them to customers.
Lowering inventory costs is an operations goal, and knowing product features helps with customers, not with storage costs.

q.pt: Analyze product information to identify product features and benefits
q.s: Northpoint Bikes is the only shop in town that offers free lifetime tune-ups with every bicycle it sells. For Northpoint's salespeople, the free tune-ups are a
q.r: Unique feature. A unique feature is a characteristic or service that competitors do not offer, so it gives customers a strong reason to choose one business over another. Salespeople should stress unique features and their benefits. A standard feature is one that most competing products also have. A buying motive is the customer's reason for buying. A trade discount is a price reduction given to channel members.
w: A standard feature is one most competitors also offer, but Northpoint is the only shop in town with free lifetime tune-ups.
A buying motive is the customer's own reason for buying, while the tune-ups are something the shop offers.
A trade discount is a price cut given to channel members, not a free service offered to bicycle buyers.

q.pt: Analyze product information to identify product features and benefits
q.s: Which of the following statements describes a product benefit rather than a feature:
o: The jacket is made of waterproof nylon
The jacket keeps you dry during heavy rain
The jacket has four zippered pockets
The jacket comes in six different color options
q.r: The jacket keeps you dry during heavy rain. A benefit is what a product characteristic does for the customer, the advantage that gives the customer a reason to buy. Staying dry is the result the customer enjoys. Waterproof nylon, four zippered pockets and six colors are features: physical or factual characteristics of the jacket. Salespeople turn features like these into benefits for each customer.
w: Waterproof nylon is a fact about what the jacket is made of, which is a feature; the benefit is what that material does for you.
Four zippered pockets describe a physical part of the jacket, which is a feature rather than a result the customer enjoys.
Six color options is a fact about the jacket's choices, which is a feature rather than what the jacket does for the customer.

q.pt: Analyze product information to identify product features and benefits
q.s: A salesperson tells a shopper, "This vacuum has a HEPA filter, which means you'll breathe cleaner air at home." The salesperson is
o: translating a feature into a benefit.
q.r: Translating a feature into a benefit. The HEPA filter is a feature, a physical characteristic of the vacuum. Cleaner air at home is the benefit, what the feature does for the customer. Linking the two shows customers why a product matters to them. Responding to objections addresses a customer's concerns. Closing asks for the purchase. Suggestion selling recommends additional, related items.
w: Responding to objections addresses a customer's concern, but the shopper here has not raised any worry about the vacuum.
Closing means asking for the purchase, while the salesperson is only explaining what the filter does for the shopper.
A suggestion sale recommends additional related items, but the salesperson is describing the vacuum itself, not adding products.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: To explain how a smartphone's long battery life will help a busy commuter get through the day, a salesperson must have strong
q.r: Product knowledge. Turning a product's features into benefits requires a solid understanding of what the product does and how it can help a particular customer. Product knowledge lets the salesperson connect the battery's capacity to the commuter's long day. Negotiation skills help settle terms, time-management skills help organize a salesperson's work, and computer skills help with technology; none of them explains the product's benefits.
w: Negotiation skills help a salesperson settle terms like price or delivery, but they don't help explain how a battery feature makes a commuter's day easier.
Time-management skills help a salesperson organize calls and schedules, yet knowing how to plan your day says nothing about what the phone's battery can do for the buyer.
Computer skills help with sales technology, but describing why long battery life benefits a commuter depends on understanding the phone itself, not on using a computer.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: Which personal trait most helps a salesperson appear credible to customers?
q.r: Self-confidence. Salespeople who believe in themselves and in the products they sell come across as knowledgeable and trustworthy, which gives them credibility. Customers are more willing to accept recommendations from someone who speaks with confidence. Competitiveness drives a salesperson to win but does not build trust by itself. Spontaneity and independence are useful in some situations but do not convey credibility.
w: Competitiveness pushes a salesperson to win sales, but a drive to beat others does not by itself make customers trust what the salesperson says.
Spontaneity can help a salesperson react quickly, but acting on impulse does not signal the knowledge and steadiness that make customers believe a recommendation.
Independence lets a salesperson work without close supervision, which is useful on the job but does not make customers see the salesperson as believable.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: Selling is best described as
o: informing the public about a business through paid mass media.
determining customer needs and satisfying them with products.
setting prices that cover costs and earn a profit.
moving products from producers to final users.
q.r: Determining customer needs and satisfying them with products. Selling is the marketing function that identifies what each customer needs or wants and responds with goods or services that satisfy those needs in a way that benefits both the customer and the business. Informing the public through paid mass media describes advertising, a promotion activity. Setting prices is the pricing function. Moving products to final users is channel management.
w: Informing the public through paid mass media describes advertising, a promotion tool that speaks to many people at once rather than meeting individual customers' needs.
Setting prices that cover costs and earn a profit is the pricing function, which decides what to charge rather than identifying and satisfying a customer's needs.
Moving products from producers to final users is the job of distribution, or channel management, not the person-to-person work of matching products to customer needs.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: Amira, a sales representative for a packaging manufacturer, meets with buyers at food companies to recommend boxes that fit their production needs. This is an example of
q.r: Business-to-business selling. Amira sells to other businesses that will use the packaging in their operations, so her customers are organizational buyers rather than final consumers. Business-to-business sales often involve larger orders and long-term relationships. Retail selling is selling to ultimate consumers for personal use, and direct-to-consumer selling means a producer sells straight to final consumers; Amira's buyers are neither. Mass-media advertising is paid, nonpersonal promotion rather than direct selling.
w: Retail selling means selling to final consumers for their own personal use, but Amira's buyers are food companies that will use the boxes in production.
Direct-to-consumer selling means a producer sells straight to individual shoppers, while Amira sells packaging to other businesses for their operations.
Mass-media advertising is paid, nonpersonal promotion aimed at large audiences, but Amira meets face to face with specific company buyers to recommend products.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the selling function
q.s: Which type of software would a sales manager most likely use to total each salesperson's weekly sales volume and compare it with sales quotas?
q.r: Spreadsheet. Spreadsheet software organizes numbers in rows and columns and performs calculations quickly, so it is ideal for tracking sales volume, totaling results and comparing them with quotas. It can also turn the figures into charts. Word-processing software creates letters and reports. Presentation software creates slide shows. Desktop-publishing software designs printed materials such as brochures; none of these is built for numerical analysis.
w: Word-processing software is built for writing letters and reports, so it is a poor tool for totaling sales figures and comparing them with quotas.
Presentation software creates slide shows, which could display results but is not designed to calculate weekly totals and compare them with quotas.
Desktop-publishing software designs printed pieces like brochures and flyers, so it lacks the calculation features a manager needs to total and compare sales numbers.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the selling function
q.s: Instead of flying to a client's office, Imani, a sales representative, presents a new product line to the client through a videoconference. A key advantage of this technology for Imani is that it
o: lets her skip the approach step.
cuts her travel time and costs.
q.r: Cuts her travel time and costs. Videoconferencing lets salespeople meet with clients face to face on screen from anywhere, so they spend less time and money traveling and can reach more clients in a day. Technology supports, rather than replaces, the steps of the selling process. Imani still needs to approach the client and build rapport, still needs to prepare a strong presentation, and still needs to follow up after the sale to keep the relationship strong.
w: Videoconferencing changes where the meeting happens, but Imani still has to open the meeting and build rapport, so the approach step does not disappear.
Presenting on screen still requires a well-planned presentation, so the technology does not remove Imani's need to prepare for the client meeting.
Follow-up after a presentation keeps the client relationship strong whether the meeting happened in person or by video, so the technology does not make it unnecessary.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the selling function
q.s: Tessa uses software that stores each client's contact information, purchase history and preferences and reminds her when to follow up. Tessa is using
q.r: Customer relationship management software. CRM software keeps detailed records on each customer and prompts salespeople to follow up, which helps them personalize their service and build long-term relationships. Warehouse inventory management software tracks the quantity of goods on hand. Presentation software creates slide shows for sales presentations. Electronic data interchange software sends business documents, such as purchase orders and invoices, between companies' computers; none of these is built to manage relationships with individual clients.
w: Warehouse inventory software tracks how many goods are on hand, while Tessa's software keeps records about individual clients and reminds her when to contact them.
Presentation software creates slides for sales talks, but it does not store each client's purchase history or remind Tessa to follow up.
Electronic data interchange sends business documents like orders and invoices between companies' computers, not personal client records and follow-up reminders for a salesperson.

q.pt: Explain company selling policies
q.s: Brightline Office Supply's written rules on quantity discounts, credit terms and delivery charges are examples of
q.r: Terms-of-sale policies. Terms-of-sale policies spell out the conditions under which a business sells, such as prices, discounts, credit and delivery charges, so every customer receives consistent treatment. Selling-activity policies guide how salespeople do their jobs, such as call reports and territories. Customer-service policies cover returns, exchanges and warranties. Personnel policies deal with employees' hiring, pay and conduct.
w: Selling-activity policies guide how salespeople do their jobs, such as call reports and territories, while discounts, credit and delivery charges are conditions customers receive.
Customer-service policies cover returns, exchanges and warranties after a purchase, not the discounts, credit terms and delivery charges that set the conditions of a sale.
Personnel policies deal with employees' hiring, pay and conduct, but Brightline's rules describe what customers pay and how they can buy.

q.pt: Explain company selling policies
q.s: Which of the following is an external factor that can lead a business to change its selling policies:
o: The skill level of its sales staff
A shortage of the raw materials used in its products
The public image its owners want the business to have
q.r: A shortage of the raw materials used in its products. External factors are conditions outside the business's control, such as raw-material availability, competition, the economy and laws. A shortage might force a business to change delivery terms, limit discounts or raise prices. Profit goals, the sales staff's skills and the desired image are internal factors, because the business itself sets or controls them.
w: Long-term profit goals are set by the company itself, so they are an internal factor rather than an outside condition the business cannot control.
The sales staff's skill level is something the business can shape through hiring and training, which makes it an internal factor, not an external one.
The public image the owners want is a choice the business makes for itself, so it is an internal factor rather than an outside force.

q.pt: Explain company selling policies
q.s: Harbor Paper Co. requires its sales representatives to submit weekly call reports and to contact only accounts within their assigned territories. These rules are
q.r: Selling-activity policies. These policies guide how salespeople carry out their work, including reporting, territories, dress and expenses, so the sales effort is organized and consistent. Terms-of-sale policies cover the prices, discounts and delivery conditions customers receive. Customer-service policies cover returns, exchanges and warranties. Credit policies set rules for letting customers buy now and pay later.
w: Terms-of-sale policies spell out prices, discounts and delivery conditions for customers, but call reports and territories govern how salespeople do their work.
Customer-service policies cover returns, exchanges and warranties, while Harbor Paper's rules are about salespeople's reporting and which accounts they may contact.
Credit policies set rules for letting customers buy now and pay later, which has nothing to do with weekly call reports or assigned territories.

q.pt: Explain key factors in building a clientele
q.s: A clothing boutique's generous return policy costs it money on some returned items. How does the policy most likely benefit the boutique?
o: It lowers the boutique's operating costs
It reduces the need for product knowledge
It allows the boutique to raise prices freely
It builds customer trust and repeat business
q.r: It builds customer trust and repeat business. Fair, easy return policies show customers that the business stands behind its products, so shoppers feel safe buying and return again. Over time, this helps the business build a loyal clientele that is worth far more than the cost of returns. Returns add costs rather than lowering them. Salespeople still need product knowledge, and a return policy does not let a business raise prices freely.
w: Accepting returns adds costs, such as refunds and unsellable items, so the policy raises rather than lowers the boutique's operating costs.
A return policy does not replace knowing the merchandise; salespeople still need product knowledge to help shoppers choose items that fit their needs.
Generous returns may make shoppers more comfortable buying, but they do not give the boutique freedom to raise prices without losing customers.

q.pt: Explain key factors in building a clientele
q.s: Building a clientele depends most on a salesperson's ability to
o: identify and satisfy each customer's needs.
make as many sales calls as possible.
match the lowest prices offered by competitors.
q.r: Identify and satisfy each customer's needs. A clientele is a base of regular customers who return because they trust the salesperson to recommend what is right for them. Every sales presentation should be built around the customer's need for the product. Pushing high-priced items can damage trust. Making many calls without meeting needs does not create loyalty. Competing only on price attracts bargain hunters rather than loyal clients.
w: Pushing the most expensive items first puts the sale ahead of the customer, which can damage the trust that brings clients back.
Making many sales calls may find new prospects, but customers will not keep coming back unless their needs are actually met.
Matching competitors' lowest prices tends to attract bargain hunters who switch stores for a better deal, not loyal clients who return to one salesperson.

q.pt: Explain key factors in building a clientele
q.s: After buying a car from Luis, a satisfied customer sends her brother and two coworkers to him for help. These new prospects are
q.r: Referrals. A referral is a prospective customer recommended by an existing, satisfied customer. Referrals are one of the best ways to build a clientele because the new prospects already trust the salesperson's reputation. Walk-ins are customers who enter a business on their own without a recommendation. Cold calls are contacts a salesperson makes without a prior relationship. Impulse buyers make unplanned purchases on the spot.
w: Walk-ins come into a business on their own without anyone recommending it, but these prospects were sent to Luis by a satisfied customer.
Cold calls are contacts a salesperson starts with people he has no prior connection to, while these prospects came to Luis through his customer's recommendation.
Impulse buyers make unplanned purchases on the spot, but these prospects were recommended to Luis before they ever arrived, and nothing says they will buy on impulse.

q.pt: Explain the role of customer service as a component of selling relationships
q.s: Which of the following actions best helps a salesperson maintain a long-term relationship with a business customer:
o: Calling only when a new product launches
Responding promptly to the customer's complaints
Offering a discount on every order
Limiting contact with the customer after the sale closes
q.r: Responding promptly to the customer's complaints. Customer service after the sale shows the customer that the salesperson values the relationship. Handling problems quickly and fairly builds trust and keeps the customer buying. Calling only about new products makes the relationship feel one-sided. Discounting every order cuts profit without addressing service. Limiting contact after the sale weakens the relationship instead of maintaining it.
w: Calling only when a new product launches makes contact feel like a sales pitch, so the customer may feel the salesperson cares only about making the next sale.
Discounting every order cuts the seller's profit and does nothing to solve problems or show the customer that the salesperson values the relationship.
Pulling back contact after the sale closes weakens the relationship, since long-term customers expect ongoing attention and help with problems.

q.pt: Explain the role of customer service as a component of selling relationships
q.s: A week after a customer buys a sofa, the salesperson mails a handwritten thank-you note and asks whether the delivery went smoothly. This is an example of
q.r: Follow-up. Follow-up is contact with the customer after the sale to make sure the customer is satisfied and to keep in touch. Thank-you notes and check-in calls show that the salesperson cares and encourage repeat business and referrals. Prospecting is looking for new potential customers. The approach is the first contact with a customer. Suggestion selling recommends related items during the sale.
w: Prospecting means searching for new potential customers, but this salesperson is contacting someone who has already bought a sofa.
The approach is the first contact that opens a sale, while the thank-you note comes a week after the purchase is complete.
Suggestion selling recommends related items during a sale, but the note simply thanks the customer and checks on the delivery after the sale.

q.pt: Explain the role of customer service as a component of selling relationships
q.s: Customer service is an important part of selling relationships because it
o: replaces the need for product knowledge.
lets the business raise its prices.
shortens the selling process for new products.
q.r: Encourages repeat business and referrals. Help and attention given before, during and after a sale build trust, so satisfied customers buy again and recommend the business to others. Strong service turns single sales into long-term relationships. Service does not replace product knowledge; salespeople need both. Good service does not by itself justify higher prices, and it does not change the steps of the selling process.
w: Good service and product knowledge work together; a salesperson who serves customers well still needs to understand what the products can do.
Strong service may support a business's reputation, but by itself it does not give the business permission to raise prices; its main payoff is customers who return.
Customer service happens before, during and after a sale, but it does not remove or shorten the steps a salesperson follows with a new product.

q.pt: Discuss motivational theories that impact buying behavior
q.s: Jordan buys the same brand of headphones his friends wear because he wants them to approve of his style. Jordan's purchase is driven by
q.r: External motivation. Externally motivated buyers act to gain a reward from other people, such as approval, praise or acceptance by peers. Jordan wants his friends' approval, so the reward comes from outside him. Internal motivation comes from within, such as personal satisfaction. Rational motives are based on reasoning, such as price or quality. Patronage motives explain why a customer chooses one business over another.
w: Internal motivation comes from inside a person, like personal satisfaction, while Jordan buys the headphones to win his friends' approval.
Rational motives are based on logical reasons like price, quality or durability, but Jordan chooses the brand to fit in with his friends.
Patronage motives explain why a customer chooses one store or business over another, not why Jordan picked a particular brand to impress friends.

q.pt: Discuss motivational theories that impact buying behavior
q.s: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, a customer who buys a home security system to protect her family is satisfying a(n) __________ need.
q.r: Safety. Maslow's hierarchy of needs ranks human needs from physiological needs at the base, through safety, social and esteem needs, to self-actualization at the top. Safety needs involve protection from harm and security for oneself and one's family, which a home security system provides. Esteem needs involve respect and recognition. Social needs involve belonging and friendship. Self-actualization is reaching one's full potential.
w: Esteem needs involve respect, status and recognition from others, but a security system is bought to keep the family protected from harm.
Social needs involve belonging, love and friendship, while a home security system meets the need to feel protected and secure.
Self-actualization means reaching your full potential through growth and achievement, a much higher level than protecting a family from danger.

q.pt: Explain the selling process
q.s: During the closing stage of a sale, what should a salesperson do if the customer still seems hesitant?
o: Restart the approach with a new greeting
Leave the customer alone to decide
q.r: Answer any remaining objections. Hesitation near the close usually means the customer still has a concern. Uncovering and answering that objection removes the last barrier and lets the salesperson ask for the sale again. Restarting the approach wastes the progress already made. Prospecting for others abandons a customer who is close to buying. Leaving the customer alone gives up the chance to resolve the concern.
w: Restarting with a new greeting throws away the progress already made, when the customer's hesitation really signals a concern that still needs an answer.
Starting to prospect for other customers abandons a buyer who is close to purchasing instead of resolving the concern that is holding him or her back.
Walking away leaves the customer's unspoken concern unresolved, so the salesperson loses the chance to address it and ask for the sale again.

q.pt: Explain the selling process
q.s: A camera salesperson asks a customer, "What will you mainly use this camera to photograph?" Which step of the selling process is the salesperson performing?
q.r: Determining needs. In this step, the salesperson asks open-ended questions, listens and observes to learn what the customer wants, so the right product can be presented. Knowing whether the customer shoots sports, landscapes or family events shapes the recommendation. Approaching the customer is the greeting that opens the sale. Closing the sale obtains the customer's agreement to buy. Following up takes place after the sale.
w: Approaching the customer is the greeting that opens the sale, but this question digs into what the customer plans to do with the camera.
Closing the sale means asking the customer to buy, while this question is gathering information before any product is recommended.
Following up happens after the purchase is made, but this question comes before the salesperson has even shown a camera.

q.pt: Explain legal and ethical considerations in selling
q.s: A salesperson knows that a less expensive model fully meets a customer's needs but would earn her a smaller commission. What is the ethical action?
o: Recommend the model that pays the larger commission
Mention the lower-priced model only if the customer asks
Recommend the model that best fits the customer's needs
Describe the lower-priced model as less reliable
q.r: Recommend the model that best fits the customer's needs. Ethical salespeople ask, "What is the right thing to do?" and put the customer's interests ahead of their own commissions. Honest recommendations build trust and a loyal clientele. Pushing the higher-commission model or hiding the cheaper one puts the salesperson's interest first. Calling the cheaper model unreliable when it is not is misrepresentation, which is unethical and can be illegal.
w: Recommending the higher-commission model when a cheaper one fully meets the need puts the salesperson's earnings ahead of the customer's interests.
Mentioning the cheaper model only if asked hides an option the salesperson knows is a better fit, which is not honest with the customer.
Calling the cheaper model less reliable when it is not misrepresents the product, which is unethical and can even be illegal.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: Glow Beauty sends one set of promotions to customers who buy its skin care every month and a different set to customers who buy only once a year. Glow is segmenting its market on the basis of
q.r: Behavioral characteristics. Behavioral segmentation groups customers by how they act toward a product, such as usage rate, benefits sought, brand loyalty or purchase occasion. Glow separates frequent buyers from occasional buyers, so it is using usage rate. Demographic characteristics are population traits such as age and income. Geographic characteristics describe where customers live. Psychographic characteristics are lifestyles, values and interests.
w: Demographic segmentation uses population traits like age or income, but Glow is grouping customers by how often they buy its skin care.
Geographic segmentation groups customers by where they live, while Glow divides its customers by monthly versus yearly buying.
Psychographic segmentation looks at lifestyles, values and interests, but Glow's two groups are based only on how often customers purchase.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: A sporting-goods brand targets people who value adventure, spend their weekends outdoors and care deeply about protecting the environment. The brand is using __________ segmentation.
q.r: Psychographic. Psychographic segmentation groups customers by lifestyles, values, attitudes, interests and personality. Valuing adventure, spending free time outdoors and caring about the environment are all lifestyle and value traits. Demographic segmentation uses measurable population traits such as age or income. Behavioral segmentation uses how customers act toward the product. Geographic segmentation uses customers' locations.
w: Demographic segmentation uses measurable traits like age, gender or income, but this brand targets people by what they value and how they spend free time.
Behavioral segmentation groups people by how they buy or use the product, such as how often they purchase, while this brand targets shared values and lifestyle.
Geographic segmentation groups people by location, while this brand's target is defined by values like adventure and environmental concern, not by where people live.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: Which of the following is an example of demographic segmentation:
o: Targeting households that earn more than $100,000 a year
Targeting customers who live in coastal cities
Targeting shoppers who value eco-friendly living
Targeting customers who buy the brand at least once a week
q.r: Targeting households that earn more than $100,000 a year. Demographic segmentation divides a market by population traits such as income, age, gender, education and family size. Household income is a demographic characteristic. Targeting coastal cities is geographic segmentation. Targeting shoppers who value eco-friendly living is psychographic segmentation. Targeting weekly buyers is behavioral segmentation because it is based on usage rate.
w: Targeting people who live in coastal cities groups them by location, which is geographic segmentation rather than a population trait like income or age.
Valuing eco-friendly living is a lifestyle and belief, which makes this psychographic segmentation instead of a measurable population trait.
Grouping customers who buy weekly is based on usage rate, which is behavioral segmentation, not a population trait like income.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: Northern Gear Co. markets its heaviest parkas only in regions with long, cold winters. This is an example of
q.r: Geographic segmentation. Geographic segmentation divides a market by location factors such as region, climate and population density. Northern Gear targets customers based on the climate where they live. Behavioral segmentation is based on how customers act toward the product. Demographic segmentation uses traits such as age and income. Mass marketing uses one marketing mix for the entire market rather than targeting particular regions.
w: Behavioral segmentation is based on how customers act toward a product, such as how often they buy, but Northern Gear chooses markets by climate.
Demographic segmentation uses traits like age and income, while Northern Gear decides where to sell parkas based on regions with cold winters.
Mass marketing offers one marketing mix to everyone, but Northern Gear limits its heaviest parkas to certain regions, which is targeting rather than mass marketing.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: Market segments are formed by grouping potential customers who
o: have bought from the business before.
earn the highest incomes in the market.
q.r: Share similar characteristics or needs. A market segment is a group of customers who are alike in ways that make them respond similarly to a marketing mix. Segments can be based on similarities in demographics, geography, lifestyles or behavior. Past purchases are only one possible basis, and segments include new prospects. Income and location can define segments, but neither is required for every segment.
w: Past buying can be one way to group customers, but segments also include new prospects who have never bought from the business.
Income can be used to form a segment, but segments can also be built on lifestyle, location or behavior, so high earners are only one example.
Location can define a segment, but segments are not tied to a sales territory; they are groups of people who are alike in ways that matter to buying.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channel-member relationships
q.s: Which of the following is an example of vertical channel conflict:
o: A grocery chain's store brand competes with a producer's brand
Two hardware stores in one small town compete for the same shoppers
A manufacturer adds a second shift to meet growing demand
Two wholesalers agree to share a warehouse to cut their costs
q.r: A grocery chain's store brand competes with a producer's brand. Vertical conflict is disagreement between channel members at different levels, such as a retailer and the producer whose products it carries. When the retailer promotes its own private brand against the producer's national brand, their goals clash. Two competing hardware stores are at the same level, which is horizontal conflict. Adding a shift is an internal decision, and sharing a warehouse is cooperation.
w: Two hardware stores in the same town compete at the same level of the channel, so their clash would be horizontal rather than vertical conflict.
Adding a second shift is an internal production decision, and it involves no disagreement with any other channel member.
Two wholesalers sharing a warehouse are cooperating to save money, which is the opposite of conflict, and they sit at the same channel level anyway.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channel-member relationships
q.s: Two franchised Brew Haven coffee shops argue because one has started advertising heavily inside the other's assigned territory. This is an example of
q.r: Horizontal channel conflict. Horizontal conflict occurs between channel members at the same level, such as two retailers or two franchisees. Both Brew Haven shops are franchised outlets at the retail level. Vertical conflict occurs between members at different levels, such as a franchisor and a franchisee. Channel cooperation is the opposite of conflict. Exclusive distribution is a coverage strategy that uses one outlet per area.
w: Vertical conflict happens between channel members at different levels, such as a franchisor and franchisee, but these two shops are both at the retail level.
Channel cooperation means members work together toward shared goals, while these two shops are arguing over territory, which is conflict.
Exclusive distribution is a coverage strategy that uses one outlet per area, not a disagreement between two outlets over advertising.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channel-member relationships
q.s: A strong channel captain can reduce conflict among channel members because it
o: sets prices lower than its competitors do.
has the authority to require cooperation.
sells directly to every final consumer.
q.r: Has the authority to require cooperation. A channel captain is the member, often the one with the most power, that leads and coordinates the channel. Because other members depend on it, a strong captain can settle disagreements and insist that members work toward shared goals. Channel captains coordinate intermediaries rather than eliminating them. Low prices and direct selling do not give a member authority over the channel.
w: A channel captain keeps intermediaries in the channel and coordinates their work, so it reduces conflict by leading those members rather than by getting rid of them.
Charging lower prices than competitors may win sales, but it does not give a member the power to settle disputes among other channel members.
A captain usually works through wholesalers and retailers rather than selling to every consumer itself, and direct selling would not give it authority over other members.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channel-member relationships
q.s: A sporting-goods manufacturer gives retailers free display racks and a cash bonus for every 100 units they sell. The manufacturer is using
q.r: Reward power. Reward power is the ability to influence channel members by offering incentives, such as allowances, free displays, extra discounts or bonuses for meeting goals. The manufacturer encourages retailers to sell more by rewarding them. Expert power comes from special knowledge. Legitimate power comes from a contract or recognized right to decide. Referent power comes from a strong brand or reputation that others want to be associated with.
w: Expert power comes from special knowledge others rely on, while this manufacturer influences retailers by giving them displays and cash bonuses.
Legitimate power comes from a contract or recognized right to make decisions, not from offering incentives like free racks and bonuses.
Referent power comes from a strong brand or reputation others want to be linked with, but here the manufacturer is offering retailers rewards for selling.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channel-member relationships
q.s: Retailers follow Delmar Electronics' advice on store layouts because Delmar's research team understands shopper behavior better than anyone else in the channel. Delmar has
q.r: Expert power. Expert power comes from having special knowledge or skills that other channel members value and rely on, such as market research or technical expertise. Retailers accept Delmar's advice because of its knowledge of shoppers. Coercive power relies on threats or penalties. Reward power relies on incentives such as bonuses. Legitimate power comes from a contract or formal right, such as a franchise agreement.
w: Coercive power relies on threats or penalties, but retailers follow Delmar's advice willingly because they trust its knowledge of shoppers.
Reward power relies on incentives like bonuses or allowances, while Delmar's influence comes from understanding shopper behavior better than others.
Legitimate power comes from a contract or formal right to decide, but nothing requires retailers to follow Delmar; they choose to because of its research.

q.pt: Describe ethical considerations in channel management
q.s: Bennett Pharmacy buys a popular brand of sunscreen from an overseas distributor that is not authorized to sell the brand in the U.S., then resells it below the usual price. Bennett is participating in the
q.r: Gray market. The gray market is the sale of genuine branded goods through distributors the producer has not authorized, often after the goods are imported. It raises ethical concerns because it undercuts authorized channel members and may bypass warranties or quality controls. The black market involves illegal goods or illegal trading. A free market is an economic system. A target market is a group of customers a business aims to reach.
w: The black market involves illegal goods or illegal trading, while Bennett is selling genuine sunscreen that simply came through an unauthorized distributor.
A free market is an economic system where buyers and sellers set prices, not a term for reselling genuine goods bought from unauthorized distributors.
A target market is the group of customers a business aims to reach, which does not describe buying goods from an unauthorized overseas source.

q.pt: Describe ethical considerations in channel management
q.s: A powerful retail chain threatens to stop carrying a small producer's products unless the producer pays for the chain's advertising. This unethical use of channel power is
q.r: Coercion. Coercion occurs when a powerful channel member uses threats or penalties to force another member to act against its own interests. Threatening to drop the producer unless it pays for the chain's advertising is unfair pressure. Cooperation means working together toward shared goals. Reward power uses incentives rather than threats. Expert power comes from special knowledge that others rely on.
w: Cooperation means channel members work together toward shared goals, but the chain is using threats to force the producer to pay.
Reward power uses incentives to encourage cooperation, while this chain is threatening to drop the producer, which is a penalty rather than a reward.
Expert power comes from special knowledge that others choose to rely on, but the chain's pressure here comes from a threat, not from expertise.

q.pt: Describe ethical considerations in channel management
q.s: Which of the following is an ethical concern in channel management:
o: Sharing detailed sales forecasts with wholesalers ahead of a product launch
Giving a buyer's purchasing agent expensive gifts to win the account
Training retail staff to explain the product's features
Putting delivery schedules into written agreements
q.r: Giving a buyer's purchasing agent expensive gifts to win the account. Personal gifts meant to influence a buyer's decision can amount to bribery, an ethical concern because the agent may choose a supplier for personal gain rather than for the employer's benefit. Sharing forecasts, training retail staff and putting delivery schedules in writing are sound channel practices that build trust and cooperation among members.
w: Sharing sales forecasts with wholesalers before a launch helps them plan inventory, which builds trust and cooperation rather than raising an ethical problem.
Training retail staff to explain features helps them serve customers well, which is a normal, honest way to support a product in the channel.
Putting delivery schedules in writing makes expectations clear for everyone, which is a sound business practice rather than an ethical concern.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: Why must a marketing strategy consider the elements of the marketing mix together?
o: Each element must receive an equal budget
Each element affects how well the others work
Changing one element requires a new target market
Customers consider price before anything else
q.r: Each element affects how well the others work. The marketing mix of product, price, place and promotion must fit together to appeal to the target market. A luxury product, for example, needs a price, distribution and promotion that support its image. Budgets are set by need, not split equally. A change in one element does not require a new target market, and customers weigh many factors besides price.
w: Marketing money is spent where each element needs it, so equal budgets are not required, and budget size does not explain why the elements must work together.
Changing one element, like adjusting price, does not mean the business must find a new target market; it means the other elements must still fit together.
Customers weigh many things such as quality, convenience and image, so price is not always their first concern, and this does not explain why elements must fit together.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: Which of the following decisions is part of the product element of the marketing mix:
o: Choosing which stores will carry the new line
Setting the new line's introductory price
Choosing which brand names to use for a new line
Planning the new line's social media advertising
q.r: Choosing which brand names to use for a new line. Product decisions cover what the business will sell, including features, quality, packaging and branding. Choosing brand names is therefore a product decision. Choosing which stores will carry the line is a place (distribution) decision. Setting the introductory price is a price decision. Planning social media ads is a promotion decision.
w: Choosing which stores will carry the line decides where customers can buy it, which is a place, or distribution, decision rather than a product decision.
Setting an introductory price decides how much customers will pay, which belongs to the price element, not the product element.
Planning social media ads decides how the business communicates with customers, which is a promotion decision rather than a product decision.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: Alder Outdoor's marketing strategy aims to increase its share of the camping-equipment market from 12% to 15% within two years. This target is an example of a
q.r: Business goal. Marketing strategies are built to reach business goals, such as increasing sales, profit or market share by a certain date. A target of moving from 12% to 15% market share is a measurable goal. A target market is the group of customers the business wants to reach. The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place and promotion. A competitive advantage is something that makes a business better than its rivals.
w: A target market is the group of customers a business wants to reach, but Alder's 12% to 15% figure is a measurable result it wants to achieve.
The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place and promotion, which are tools used to reach a goal rather than the goal itself.
A competitive advantage is something that makes a business better than rivals, while gaining three points of market share is a target Alder hopes to hit.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: A marketing strategy consists of a __________ and a __________.
q.r: Target market; marketing mix. A marketing strategy identifies the specific group of customers the business will focus on, the target market, and the combination of product, price, place and promotion it will use to reach them, the marketing mix. A sales forecast and budget support the marketing plan. A mission statement and logo express company identity. A product line and price list cover only parts of the mix.
w: A sales forecast and a marketing budget support a marketing plan, but a strategy itself is built from who the business targets and how it will reach them.
A mission statement and logo express a company's identity, but they do not name the customers to target or the mix used to reach them.
A product line and price list cover only parts of the marketing mix and leave out the target market a strategy must identify.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: When Brightwell Tea decides to sell its products through grocery stores rather than only on its own website, it is making a decision about which element of the marketing mix?
q.r: Place. The place element covers how and where products are distributed to customers, including which channels and outlets to use. Moving from a company website to grocery stores is a distribution decision. Product decisions involve the goods themselves, such as flavors, packaging and brands. Price decisions involve how much to charge. Promotion decisions involve how the business communicates with customers, such as advertising.
w: Product decisions involve the goods themselves, such as flavors and packaging, but Brightwell is deciding where customers can buy its tea.
Price decisions set how much customers pay, while choosing grocery stores over a website only changes where the tea is sold.
Promotion decisions involve how a business communicates with customers, but adding grocery stores is a choice about distribution, not advertising.

q.pt: Describe the role of business ethics in pricing
q.s: Which of the following is an example of an unethical pricing practice:
o: Marking down last season's leftover merchandise to clear space
Charging more for an express delivery option
Pricing below cost to force a new competitor out of business
Offering students a discount on weekday visits
q.r: Pricing below cost to force a new competitor out of business. This is predatory pricing: a business sets prices below its costs to drive rivals away, intending to raise prices once competition is gone. It harms competitors and, eventually, customers. Marking down leftover merchandise, charging more for faster service and offering student discounts are common, honest pricing practices that customers can understand.
w: Marking down last season's leftover merchandise is an honest way to clear space that customers easily understand, not an unfair tactic.
Charging more for express delivery is fair because customers pay extra for a faster service they choose to buy.
Offering students a weekday discount is a common, open promotion that does not mislead anyone or harm competitors.

q.pt: Describe the role of business ethics in pricing
q.s: A pricing practice is most likely to be considered unethical when it
o: earns a higher profit margin than its competitors earn.
is designed to confuse customers about the real cost.
changes prices based on the time of the year.
gives quantity discounts to large business buyers.
q.r: Is designed to confuse customers about the real cost. Ethical pricing is honest and clear, so customers can understand what they will pay and compare offers. Deliberately hiding fees or making prices hard to figure out takes advantage of customers and damages trust. Earning a higher margin than competitors, using seasonal prices and offering quantity discounts are legitimate business decisions when they are communicated honestly.
w: Earning a higher margin than competitors is a legitimate business result as long as prices are communicated honestly to customers.
Changing prices with the seasons is a normal response to shifts in demand and is not unethical when the prices are clear.
Quantity discounts for large buyers are a common, legitimate practice that rewards big orders, as long as they are offered fairly and honestly.

q.pt: Explain legal considerations for pricing
q.s: The three largest concrete suppliers in a region secretly agree on the prices they will quote to builders. This is an example of
q.r: Price fixing. Price fixing occurs when competitors agree on the prices or terms of sale they will offer instead of competing. It is illegal under the Sherman Antitrust Act because it removes competition and raises costs for buyers. Price lining offers products at a few set price levels. Price skimming sets a high introductory price. Penetration pricing sets a low introductory price to gain market share.
w: Price lining means one seller offers products at a few set price levels, while these suppliers are secretly agreeing with each other on prices.
Price skimming is one company setting a high introductory price for a new product, not competitors agreeing on the prices they will charge.
Penetration pricing is setting a low introductory price to gain market share, which has nothing to do with rivals secretly agreeing on prices.

q.pt: Describe the role of business ethics in pricing
q.s: An electronics store advertises a television at a very low price, stocks only two units, and then pushes shoppers toward a more expensive model. This practice is known as
q.r: Bait and switch. In bait and switch, a business advertises an item it does not intend to sell in reasonable quantities to lure customers, then pressures them to buy something more expensive. The practice is deceptive and unethical. Loss leader pricing honestly sells an item below cost to attract shoppers. Price bundling sells several items together for one price. Odd-even pricing uses prices such as $19.99 to suggest value.
w: A loss leader is honestly sold below cost and kept available to draw shoppers, while this store stocks only two sets so it can push a pricier model.
Price bundling sells several items together for one price, but this store is luring shoppers with one cheap TV and steering them to another.
Odd-even pricing uses prices like $19.99 to suggest a bargain, which does not describe advertising a deal the store doesn't intend to honor.

q.pt: Describe the role of business ethics in pricing
q.s: Why is ethical pricing important to a business's long-term success?
o: It reduces the cost of producing goods
It eliminates the need to study competitors
It allows prices to stay the same for years
It builds customer trust and loyalty
q.r: It builds customer trust and loyalty. Customers who believe a business prices honestly and fairly are more likely to keep buying from it and recommend it to others. Unethical pricing may produce short-term gains but damages the business's reputation. Ethical pricing does not lower production costs. Businesses must still study competitors, and prices must continue to adjust to changing conditions.
w: Honest pricing affects how customers feel about a business, but it does nothing to lower the cost of making the goods.
Even an ethical business must still watch its competitors' prices and offers, so fair pricing does not remove that need.
Ethical prices still change as costs and market conditions change, so honesty in pricing does not mean prices stay frozen for years.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: A cotton farmer sells raw cotton to a textile mill, which weaves it into fabric. The channel of distribution for the raw cotton ends when
o: the farmer finishes harvesting the cotton.
the fabric is sold to a clothing maker.
the mill changes the cotton into fabric.
the finished clothing reaches a store.
q.r: The mill changes the cotton into fabric. A channel of distribution ends when the product is consumed or changed into a different product. Once the mill weaves the cotton, the fabric becomes a new product that begins its own channel. Harvesting happens before the cotton enters the channel. Selling fabric to a clothing maker and shipping clothing to stores are parts of the channels for the fabric and the clothing.
w: Harvesting happens before the cotton is sold, so it is the start of the cotton's journey rather than the end of its channel.
Selling fabric to a clothing maker is part of the fabric's channel, which begins only after the mill has already turned the cotton into something new.
Clothing reaching a store is part of the finished clothing's channel; the raw cotton's channel ended long before, when it became fabric.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Which channel of distribution is most commonly used for consumer goods?
o: Producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer
Producer directly to the final consumer
Producer to agent to industrial user
Producer to industrial distributor to industrial user
q.r: Producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer. Most consumer goods, such as packaged foods and household products, move from producers to wholesalers, which sell to many retailers, which sell to final consumers. Selling directly to consumers is used by some producers but is less common. Channels that end with an industrial user, whether through an agent or an industrial distributor, are used for industrial goods.
w: Some producers sell straight to consumers, but most everyday consumer goods pass through wholesalers and retailers instead.
A channel that ends with an industrial user moves goods to businesses for their operations, not to consumers buying for personal use.
