Industrial distributors sell to businesses that use goods in their operations, so this channel serves industrial goods rather than consumer goods.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Which channel members sell products directly to ultimate consumers for their personal use?
q.r: Retailers. Retailers buy products and sell them to ultimate consumers, the people who use the products themselves. Department stores, supermarkets and online stores are examples. Wholesalers buy in large quantities and sell to retailers or other businesses. Agents bring buyers and sellers together without taking ownership. Industrial distributors sell goods to businesses that use them in their operations.
w: Wholesalers buy in large quantities and usually resell to retailers or other businesses, not to people using products themselves.
Agents bring buyers and sellers together for a commission without owning the goods, rather than selling products to consumers for personal use.
Industrial distributors sell to businesses that use the goods in their operations, not to individual consumers for personal use.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Patel Brokerage brings food producers and grocery wholesalers together and earns a commission on each sale, but it never takes ownership of the goods. Patel is a(n)
q.r: Agent. An agent is an intermediary that helps buyers and sellers reach agreements and is paid a fee or commission, but does not take title to the goods. Patel never owns the food it helps sell. A wholesaler buys goods and resells them to retailers or businesses. A retailer buys goods and sells them to final consumers. An industrial user buys goods to use in its own operations.
w: A wholesaler buys goods and then resells them, but Patel never takes ownership of the food it helps sell.
A retailer buys goods and sells them to final consumers, while Patel only connects producers with wholesalers for a commission.
An industrial user buys goods to use in its own operations, but Patel uses nothing; it just helps others make sales.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Ridgeview Orchards sells all of its apples at its own farm market next to the orchard. Ridgeview is using a(n)
q.r: Direct channel. A direct channel moves products from the producer straight to the final consumer with no intermediaries. Ridgeview grows the apples and sells them to the people who eat them. An indirect channel uses one or more intermediaries, such as wholesalers or retailers. An industrial channel serves businesses that use products in their operations. A multichannel strategy uses several channels at once.
w: An indirect channel uses one or more intermediaries, but Ridgeview sells its apples itself with no wholesaler or retailer in between.
An industrial channel serves businesses that use products in their operations, while Ridgeview sells apples to people who eat them.
A multichannel strategy uses several channels at once, but Ridgeview sells all of its apples through just one outlet, its own farm market.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the channel management function
q.s: A trucking company wants its dispatchers to see the exact location of each delivery truck at any moment. Which technology should it use?
q.r: Global positioning system (GPS). GPS uses satellite signals to pinpoint the location of vehicles and shipments, so dispatchers can track deliveries, reroute trucks and give customers accurate arrival times. Electronic data interchange exchanges documents such as orders and invoices between computers. A point-of-sale system records sales at checkout. A Universal Product Code is a bar code that identifies a product.
w: Electronic data interchange exchanges documents like orders and invoices between computers, but it cannot show where a truck is on the road.
A point-of-sale system records sales at the checkout counter, so it has no way of tracking trucks out on deliveries.
A Universal Product Code is a bar code that identifies a product, which tells nothing about the location of a moving truck.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the channel management function
q.s: What is the main benefit of using technology in channel management?
q.r: Increased efficiency. Technologies such as GPS, bar codes, RFID and electronic ordering help channel members move products faster, with fewer errors and lower costs. Efficiency is the main reason businesses invest in channel technology. Technology is not intended to raise retail prices. It may support larger assortments in some cases, but that is not its main benefit, and it does not reduce the need to promote products.
w: Channel technology aims to move products faster and at lower cost, so raising retail prices is not its purpose.
Technology may help some businesses manage bigger assortments, but its main benefit is moving goods faster with fewer errors and lower costs.
Tracking and ordering technology helps move products through the channel, but customers still need promotion to learn about and want those products.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the channel management function
q.s: A small distributor delays adopting new inventory software because so many competing systems are available that its managers cannot decide which one fits best. This barrier to adopting technology is
q.r: Too many technology options. When many competing systems are available, businesses can struggle to evaluate them and may delay a decision for fear of choosing the wrong one. Cost and training needs are other common barriers. The distributor's delay is not caused by low customer demand or by government rules. A lack of product information is not the issue, since the managers are comparing many available systems.
w: Nothing in the situation says customers lack interest; the managers are stuck choosing among many systems, not worrying about demand.
No government rule is blocking the software; the delay comes from managers being unable to pick among so many competing systems.
The managers are not short on information, since they are comparing many available systems; having too many choices is what stalls them.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the channel management function
q.s: A warehouse attaches tags that transmit product information by radio waves, so pallets can be counted without scanning each one by hand. The warehouse is using
q.r: Radio frequency identification. RFID tags store product information and send it by radio waves to readers, so items can be identified and counted quickly without a direct line of sight. This speeds up inventory tracking in warehouses. Global positioning systems locate vehicles. Electronic data interchange exchanges business documents between computers. Customer relationship management software organizes information about customers.
w: Global positioning systems use satellites to locate vehicles and shipments, not tags that let a warehouse count pallets by radio signal.
Electronic data interchange sends business documents between companies' computers, but it does not use tags to identify pallets on a warehouse floor.
Customer relationship management software organizes information about customers, which has nothing to do with counting pallets in a warehouse.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the channel management function
q.s: When stock runs low, Rivera Grocers' computer system automatically sends purchase orders directly to its suppliers' computer systems. This technology is
q.r: Electronic data interchange. EDI is the computer-to-computer exchange of business documents, such as purchase orders and invoices, between channel members. It reduces paperwork, errors and delays in reordering. Radio frequency identification uses tags to track items. A global positioning system tracks the location of vehicles. Point-of-sale advertising is promotion placed where purchases are made, not an ordering technology.
w: Radio frequency identification uses tags to identify and track items, but it does not send purchase orders from one company's computer to another's.
A global positioning system tracks where vehicles are, not the exchange of purchase orders between Rivera's computers and its suppliers.
Point-of-sale advertising is promotion placed where customers buy, so it is not a technology for sending orders to suppliers.

q.pt: Explain the nature of sales forecasts
q.s: Fans have preordered so many copies of a popular video game sequel that the publisher's website crashed. When preparing the sales forecast for the launch period, the publisher should most likely predict
o: sales equal to last year's average.
sales that decline after reviews appear.
q.r: High sales. A sales forecast predicts future sales for a specific period based on past sales, market conditions and signs of demand. Heavy preorders show strong interest, so the publisher should forecast high sales and plan production, inventory and staffing to match. Predicting low or average sales would ignore clear evidence of demand. Nothing suggests reviews will cause sales to fall.
w: Predicting low sales would ignore the clearest evidence available, since enough preorders to crash the website show very strong demand.
Using last year's average ignores the record preorders, which signal that this launch will likely sell far more than a typical period.
Nothing in the situation suggests reviews will hurt sales, so a forecast should be based on the strong preorder demand already shown.

q.pt: Explain the nature of sales forecasts
q.s: How does a retailer use its sales forecast?
o: To plan how much merchandise to purchase
To record last month's actual sales
To set its employees' hourly wage rates
To choose the design of its company logo
q.r: To plan how much merchandise to purchase. A sales forecast predicts future sales, so retailers use it to decide how much inventory to buy, how many employees to schedule and how to budget. Buying too little loses sales; buying too much ties up money. Recording last month's sales is record keeping, not forecasting. Wage rates and logo designs are not based on a sales forecast.
w: Recording last month's actual sales is record keeping about the past, while a forecast predicts future sales to guide planning.
Hourly wage rates depend on the job market and pay policies, not on a forecast of how much the store will sell.
Designing a company logo is a branding decision, and a prediction of future sales does not help choose what the logo looks like.

q.pt: Explain the nature of sales forecasts
q.s: The sales manager at Cobalt Industrial Supply asks each sales representative to estimate next year's sales in his or her territory and then combines the estimates. This forecasting method is
q.r: The sales force composite. In this method, each salesperson estimates future sales for his or her territory, and the estimates are combined into a company forecast. Salespeople know their customers well, which makes their input valuable. The jury of executive opinion combines the judgments of top managers. Trend analysis projects future sales from past sales patterns. A test market tries a product in a limited area before full launch.
w: The jury of executive opinion combines the judgments of top managers, but Cobalt is gathering estimates from its sales representatives.
Trend analysis projects future sales from past sales patterns, while Cobalt asks each representative for a territory estimate and adds them up.
A test market tries a product in a limited area before a full launch, which is not the same as combining salespeople's territory estimates.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing plans
q.s: Which section of a marketing plan explains the action steps, schedule, people responsible and budget for carrying out the plan?
q.r: Implementation. The implementation section turns strategies into action by listing the specific tasks, deadlines, people responsible and budget considerations. Without it, a plan stays on paper. The situation analysis describes where the business stands now. The executive summary briefly overviews the whole plan. Evaluation and control describes how results will be measured against objectives and how the plan will be adjusted.
w: The situation analysis describes where the business stands now, not the tasks, deadlines and people that will put the plan into action.
The executive summary gives a brief overview of the whole plan, so it does not lay out detailed action steps, schedules and responsibilities.
Evaluation and control explains how results will be measured and adjusted, which comes after the action steps the implementation section lists.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing plans
q.s: The evaluation and control section of a marketing plan describes how the business will
o: analyze its current strengths and weaknesses.
choose the target market for its products.
summarize the plan for top executives.
q.r: Measure results against its objectives. Evaluation and control explains how the business will track performance, compare actual results with the plan's objectives and make adjustments when results fall short. Analyzing current strengths and weaknesses is the job of the situation analysis. Choosing the target market is part of the marketing strategies section. Summarizing the plan for executives is the purpose of the executive summary.
w: Analyzing current strengths and weaknesses is the job of the situation analysis, which looks at where the business stands before the plan starts.
Choosing the target market belongs to the marketing strategy section, while evaluation and control checks whether the plan is working.
Summarizing the plan for top executives is the purpose of the executive summary, not of the section that measures results.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing plans
q.s: What is the main purpose of a written marketing plan?
o: To record the business's daily sales and expense transactions
To list each employee's job duties, schedule and pay
To satisfy a legal filing requirement
To guide marketing activities toward specific objectives
q.r: To guide marketing activities toward specific objectives. A marketing plan is a written document that describes the current situation, objectives, strategies, action steps, budget and evaluation methods for a set period, so everyone works toward the same goals. Recording daily transactions is an accounting task. Job duties and pay are listed in job descriptions and personnel records. Marketing plans are management tools, not legal filings.
w: Recording daily sales and expense transactions is an accounting task, while a marketing plan looks ahead to set objectives and strategies.
Employees' duties, schedules and pay belong in job descriptions and personnel records, not in a plan that directs marketing activities.
Businesses write marketing plans as management tools to guide their work, not because a law requires them to file one.

q.pt: Explain factors affecting pricing decisions
q.s: After a mild winter, Frostline Outfitters has far more snow shovels in stock than customers want to buy. To move the extra inventory, Frostline should most likely
o: lower the price of the shovels.
raise the price of the shovels.
keep the price and stop advertising.
q.r: Lower the price of the shovels. When supply is greater than demand, prices usually fall. Lowering the price makes the shovels more attractive to the few buyers in the market and helps the business turn overstocked inventory into cash. Raising the price would reduce sales further. Ordering more shovels would increase the overstock. Keeping the price and stopping advertising would leave the extra inventory unsold.
w: Raising the price when shoppers already don't want the shovels would make them even harder to sell and leave more inventory on the shelves.
Ordering more shovels would add to a supply that is already far greater than demand, making the overstock problem worse.
Keeping the price and cutting advertising does nothing to attract the few buyers out there, so the extra shovels would likely stay unsold.

q.pt: Explain factors affecting pricing decisions
q.s: A market in which many sellers offer nearly identical products and no single seller can control the price is
q.r: Pure competition. In pure competition, so many sellers offer such similar products that no one seller can influence the market price; each must accept the going price. Farm products such as wheat are a common example. Monopolistic competition has many sellers with differentiated products. An oligopoly has a few large sellers. A monopoly has a single seller that controls the supply of a product.
w: Monopolistic competition does have many sellers, but they offer differentiated products, so each has some control over its own price.
An oligopoly has only a few large sellers whose pricing affects one another, not many sellers of nearly identical products.
A monopoly has a single seller that controls supply and price, the opposite of a market where no seller can set the price.

q.pt: Explain factors affecting pricing decisions
q.s: In one country, three large firms produce nearly all of the cement sold, so each firm watches the others' prices closely before changing its own. This market structure is
q.r: An oligopoly. This is a market dominated by a few large sellers. Because each firm's pricing affects the others, the firms watch one another closely and often match price changes. A monopoly has only one seller. Pure competition has many sellers of identical products, none of which controls price. Monopolistic competition has many sellers offering similar but differentiated products.
w: A monopoly has only one seller, but this market has three large cement firms that must watch each other's prices.
Pure competition has many sellers, none able to affect price, while this market is dominated by just three large firms.
Monopolistic competition has many sellers offering differentiated products, not three firms that control nearly all of the cement sold.

q.pt: Explain the role of situation analysis in the marketing planning process
q.s: Why do marketers continually monitor the external environment?
o: To set the company's long-term mission
To measure the final results of the marketing plan
To control the company's operating costs
To spot changes that may create opportunities
q.r: To spot changes that may create opportunities. Environmental scanning tracks external factors such as the economy, competitors, technology, laws and social trends. Spotting changes early lets the business take advantage of opportunities and prepare for threats. Setting the mission is a leadership decision. Measuring final results is part of evaluation and control. Controlling operating costs is an internal management task.
w: The company's mission is set by leadership based on its purpose, not by ongoing tracking of outside changes like trends and competitors.
Measuring final results is part of evaluation and control, which looks back at the plan, while scanning the environment looks for coming changes.
Controlling operating costs is an internal management task, but monitoring the external environment looks outside the company at trends and competitors.

q.pt: Explain the role of situation analysis in the marketing planning process
q.s: Lena's marketing plan includes a section describing her company's current position, its main competitors, and each competitor's strengths and weaknesses. This section is the
q.r: Situation analysis. The situation analysis studies the business's internal and external environments to show where it stands now, including a review of competitors' strengths and weaknesses. It provides the foundation for setting objectives and strategies. The executive summary is a brief overview of the plan. The implementation plan lists action steps and the budget. Evaluation and control explains how results will be measured.
w: The executive summary is a brief overview of the whole plan, not the detailed study of the company's position and its competitors.
The implementation plan lists action steps, schedules and budgets, while Lena's section describes where the business stands right now.
Evaluation and control explains how results will be measured, but Lena's section reviews the current situation and competitors' strengths and weaknesses.

q.pt: Explain the role of situation analysis in the marketing planning process
q.s: During a SWOT analysis, the marketing team at Pinecrest Furniture notes that a large competitor plans to open a store nearby next year. This factor is a(n)
q.r: Threat. In a SWOT analysis, threats are external factors outside the business's control that could harm it, such as a new competitor entering the market. Strengths and weaknesses are internal factors, such as staff skills or product quality, that the business controls. Opportunities are external factors the business could use to its advantage, such as a growing customer group.
w: Weaknesses are internal problems the business controls, like poor staff skills, but a competitor's new store is an outside factor.
Strengths are internal advantages the business controls, while a large rival opening nearby is an outside factor that could hurt Pinecrest.
An opportunity is an outside factor that could help the business, but a big competitor moving in is more likely to take customers away.

q.pt: Explain employment opportunities in marketing
q.s: Which field of study helps marketers understand how people think, feel and make buying decisions?
q.r: Psychology. Psychology is the study of human behavior and mental processes, so it helps marketers understand motivation, perception and the decisions consumers make. Many marketing careers, especially in research and advertising, draw on it. Accounting records and reports financial information. Statistics helps analyze data but does not explain why people feel as they do. Geography studies places and their features.
w: Accounting records and reports financial information, so it explains a business's money rather than how people think and feel when buying.
Statistics helps marketers analyze data about buyers, but it measures what people do rather than explaining the thoughts and feelings behind decisions.
Geography studies places and their features, which may help with location decisions but does not explain how people think or feel.

q.pt: Explain employment opportunities in marketing
q.s: Jobs in marketing research and marketing operations most require strong __________ skills.
q.r: Analytical. Marketing research and operations employees gather data, look for patterns, solve problems and turn numbers into recommendations, all of which depend on analytical skills. Artistic skills are most important in creative jobs such as graphic design. Mechanical skills apply to repairing and operating equipment. Negotiation skills matter most in buying and selling positions that involve reaching agreements.
w: Artistic skills matter most in creative jobs like graphic design, while research and operations work centers on studying data and solving problems.
Mechanical skills apply to operating and repairing equipment, not to gathering data and turning it into recommendations.
Negotiation skills matter most in buying and selling jobs that involve reaching agreements, while research work depends on analyzing information.

q.pt: Explain employment opportunities in marketing
q.s: Rosa collects and interprets data on consumer preferences so her company can decide which new products to develop. Rosa most likely works as a
q.r: Marketing research analyst. Marketing research analysts gather and study information about consumers, competitors and markets to help businesses make decisions, such as which products to develop. A logistics manager oversees the movement and storage of goods. A sales representative sells products directly to customers. A public relations specialist manages a business's image and communication with the public and the media.
w: A logistics manager oversees moving and storing goods, while Rosa studies consumer preferences to guide product development.
A sales representative sells products directly to customers, but Rosa's job is gathering and interpreting data, not making sales.
A public relations specialist manages a company's image and media communication, not research on what consumers want in new products.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: The interest a bank charges on a car loan, the tuition a college charges and the fee a dentist charges are all forms of
q.r: Price. Price is the value of a good or service expressed in money, and it goes by many names, such as interest, tuition, fees, rent and premiums. Each names what a customer pays to receive something of value. Profit is the money left after a business pays all of its expenses. Overhead is the ongoing cost of running a business, such as utilities and insurance. Promotion communicates with customers to inform, persuade or remind them.
w: Profit is the money a business keeps after paying expenses, while interest, tuition and fees are what customers pay to receive something.
Overhead is a business's ongoing operating costs, like utilities, but interest, tuition and fees are amounts that customers pay.
Promotion is how a business informs or persuades customers, while interest, tuition and fees are the money customers pay for value received.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: When is a business most likely able to raise its prices without losing many customers?
o: When competitors are cutting their prices
When demand for its product is falling
When a recession is reducing incomes
q.r: When economic conditions are strong. In good economic times, employment and incomes are higher and consumers are more willing to spend, so a business can often raise prices with little loss of sales. When competitors cut prices, customers may switch to them. Falling demand calls for lower, not higher, prices. During a recession, consumers have less money and are more sensitive to price increases.
w: When competitors are cutting prices, a business that raises its own risks losing customers who switch to the cheaper rivals.
Falling demand means fewer people want the product, so raising the price would likely drive even more customers away.
During a recession, people have less money and watch prices closely, so a price increase would likely cost the business many sales.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: Which element of the marketing mix directly produces revenue for a business?
q.r: Price. Price is the only element of the marketing mix that directly brings money into the business; the other elements create costs. Because of this, pricing decisions have a major effect on sales and profit. Product decisions involve developing and improving what the business sells. Place decisions involve distributing products. Promotion decisions involve communicating with customers. Each supports sales but costs money to carry out.
w: Product decisions develop what the business sells, which costs money to carry out, while price is what brings money in.
Place decisions get products to customers, which supports sales but creates distribution costs rather than directly bringing in revenue.
Promotion helps persuade customers to buy, but advertising and other promotion cost money; only price directly brings revenue in.

q.pt: Explain the nature of affinity partner relationships
q.s: An insurance company agrees to offer discounted auto insurance to the members of a statewide teachers' association, and the association earns a fee for each policy sold. This arrangement is an example of a(n)
q.r: Affinity partnership. In an affinity partnership, a business teams up with an organization whose members share a common bond and offers those members special products or deals. The insurer gains access to loyal teachers, and the association earns fees and a new member benefit. An exclusive dealing agreement requires a dealer to carry only one supplier's products. A joint venture creates a new, jointly owned business. A franchise agreement licenses a business model.
w: An exclusive dealing agreement requires a dealer to carry only one supplier's products, which is not what happens between the insurer and the teachers' group.
A joint venture creates a new business owned by both partners, but here the insurer simply offers deals to an existing group's members.
A franchise agreement licenses a business model to another operator, while this deal gives a teachers' association's members special insurance offers.

q.pt: Explain the nature of affinity partner relationships
q.s: Which of the following is an example of affinity marketing:
o: A discount coupon mailed to every household in a single ZIP code
A buy-one-get-one sale on store-brand cereal
A credit card that features a university's logo for its alumni
A billboard advertising a new car model
q.r: A credit card that features a university's logo for its alumni. Affinity marketing targets a group of people who share a common bond, such as alumni of a school or fans of a team, through a partnership with the organization they support. The card issuer reaches loyal alumni, and the university often earns money. Mass-mailed coupons, store-brand sales and billboards target general audiences rather than an affinity group.
w: A coupon mailed to every household in a ZIP code targets everyone in an area, not a group connected by a shared bond.
A buy-one-get-one sale on store-brand cereal is a general price promotion, not a partnership aimed at members of a group.
A billboard speaks to anyone who drives by, so it does not target a group with a common bond through a partner organization.

q.pt: Explain the nature of affinity partner relationships
q.s: In an affinity partnership, the business benefits mainly by gaining access to
o: a loyal group that shares a common interest.
lower costs for its raw materials.
exclusive rights to use the partner's patents.
q.r: A loyal group that shares a common interest. Affinity partnerships let a business reach members, fans or supporters of an organization who feel strong loyalty to it. That loyalty can transfer to the business's products. The partner organization usually gains money, services or exposure. Affinity partnerships do not usually involve sharing production facilities, lowering raw-material costs or transferring patent rights.
w: Affinity partnerships give a business access to a group's loyal members, not to the partner's factories or production equipment.
These partnerships are about reaching people with a shared interest, not about getting cheaper raw materials for production.
An affinity partner may lend its name or logo, but the main benefit is reaching its loyal members, not gaining rights to its patents.

q.pt: Explain the need for professional and ethical standards in marketing
q.s: Why do professional marketing associations develop codes of ethics for their members?
o: To set the prices that member firms must charge
To limit the number of marketing jobs
To build trust with customers and the public
q.r: To build trust with customers and the public. Ethical standards describe honest, fair and responsible conduct, so customers, business partners and the public can trust marketers and the profession as a whole. A code also guides members when they face difficult decisions. Setting members' prices would be illegal price fixing. Codes of ethics do not limit jobs, and they add to, rather than replace, laws.
w: A code that set members' prices would amount to illegal price fixing, so ethical codes guide conduct rather than telling firms what to charge.
Ethical codes describe honest and fair conduct, and they are not designed to reduce how many marketing jobs exist.
Codes of ethics add guidance on top of the law, but marketers must still obey federal advertising laws, so codes do not replace them.

q.pt: Explain the need for professional and ethical standards in marketing
q.s: Darnell, a marketing manager, refuses to approve an ad that exaggerates his product's test results, even though the ad might increase sales. Darnell is demonstrating
q.r: Integrity. Integrity means adhering to moral and ethical principles, being honest and doing what is right even when another choice might bring a reward. Refusing to approve a misleading ad follows professional and ethical standards in marketing. Initiative is starting tasks without being told. Flexibility is adapting to change. Creativity is developing new ideas; none of these describes choosing honesty over sales.
w: Initiative means starting tasks without being told, but Darnell is turning down a misleading ad because it is dishonest.
Flexibility means adapting to change, while Darnell's choice is about staying honest even when a dishonest ad might boost sales.
Creativity means coming up with new ideas, but Darnell's decision is about refusing to approve something misleading, not inventing something new.

q.pt: Explain legal considerations in channel management
q.s: A paint manufacturer requires its dealers to stop carrying competing paint brands if they want to keep selling its products. This practice, which can restrict competition, is
q.r: Exclusive dealing. Exclusive dealing requires a dealer to sell only one supplier's products and not those of competitors. It can be illegal under antitrust law when it substantially lessens competition by shutting rivals out of the market. A tying agreement requires buying an unwanted product to get a wanted one. Price discrimination charges competing buyers different prices. An exclusive territory gives a dealer sole rights to sell in an area.
w: A tying agreement forces a buyer to purchase an unwanted product to get a wanted one, but here dealers are told to drop competing brands.
Price discrimination means charging competing buyers different prices, which is not what happens when dealers must stop carrying rival paints.
An exclusive territory gives a dealer sole rights to sell in an area, while this manufacturer limits which brands its dealers may carry.

q.pt: Explain legal considerations in channel management
q.s: A printer manufacturer tells office-supply wholesalers they can buy its popular printers only if they also buy its slow-selling scanners. This is a(n)
q.r: Tying agreement. A tying agreement requires a buyer to purchase an unwanted product in order to get a product it wants. Forcing wholesalers to take scanners to get printers can restrict competition and may violate antitrust laws. Exclusive dealing requires a dealer to carry only one supplier's products. An affinity partnership links a business with an organization's loyal members. Price lining offers products at a few set price levels.
w: Exclusive dealing requires a dealer to carry only one supplier's products, but the manufacturer here forces wholesalers to buy scanners to get printers.
An affinity partnership links a business with a group's loyal members, not a supplier forcing wholesalers to buy one product to get another.
Price lining means offering products at a few set price levels, which has nothing to do with requiring scanner purchases along with printers.

q.pt: Coordinate channel management with other marketing activities
q.s: Lakeshore Candles decides to sell only through upscale gift boutiques instead of discount stores. To coordinate with this channel decision, Lakeshore should most likely
o: cut prices to match discount stores.
set prices that fit an upscale image.
q.r: Set prices that fit an upscale image. Channel decisions must be coordinated with the other marketing activities. Upscale boutiques attract customers who expect quality and are willing to pay for it, so prices, packaging and promotion should support that image. Cutting prices to discount-store levels would clash with the boutiques' image. Advertising in discount stores' flyers and using plainer packaging would also send mixed signals to the target market.
w: Cutting prices to discount-store levels would clash with the upscale image boutique shoppers expect and send a mixed message.
Advertising in discount stores' flyers would reach bargain shoppers instead of the upscale customers who visit gift boutiques.
Plainer, cheaper packaging would undercut the quality image boutique shoppers expect, working against the channel Lakeshore chose.

q.pt: Coordinate channel management with other marketing activities
q.s: A snack company plans a national TV ad campaign for a new flavor. Why should it coordinate the timing of the campaign with its channel members?
o: So individual stores can set the product's national retail price
So wholesalers can write the ads' scripts
So the ads can run only inside retail stores
So stores have the product in stock when the ads run
q.r: So stores have the product in stock when the ads run. Promotion and distribution must work together. If ads create demand before the product reaches store shelves, customers leave empty-handed and sales are lost. Coordinating with wholesalers and retailers ensures the product is available when customers look for it. The producer, not stores, sets suggested national pricing. Wholesalers do not write ads, and TV ads run on television, not in stores.
w: The producer, not individual stores, usually suggests a national retail price, and coordinating the campaign's timing is about having the product in stock, not about pricing.
Wholesalers move and store products, but writing ad scripts is not their role, and the timing issue is about stock, not ad content.
This is a national TV campaign, so the ads run on television rather than inside stores, and that is not why timing must be coordinated.

q.pt: Explain legal considerations for pricing
q.s: Why is deceptive pricing illegal?
o: It sets prices below what competitors charge
It changes prices more than once in a single season
It uses prices that end in 99 cents
It misleads customers about a product's true value
q.r: It misleads customers about a product's true value. Deceptive pricing, such as advertising a fake "regular" price to make a sale look bigger, misrepresents what customers are getting. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) acts against deceptive pricing because it harms consumers and honest competitors. Pricing below competitors, changing prices often and using prices that end in 99 cents are legal practices when they are honest.
w: Charging less than competitors is legal as long as the prices are honest, so low prices alone do not make pricing deceptive.
Changing prices several times in a season is a normal, legal practice when each price is stated honestly to customers.
Prices ending in 99 cents are a common, legal technique that customers can see clearly, not an attempt to mislead them about value.

q.pt: Explain legal considerations for pricing
q.s: A manufacturer sells the same goods to two competing retailers in the same market but charges one retailer much more, with no difference in costs or order size. This may violate laws against
q.r: Price discrimination. Charging competing business buyers different prices for the same goods, when cost differences do not justify it, can be illegal under the Robinson-Patman Act because it gives one competitor an unfair advantage. Price fixing is an agreement among competitors on prices. Predatory pricing sets prices below cost to drive rivals out. Bait and switch lures customers with an item the seller does not intend to sell.
w: Price fixing requires competitors to agree on prices together, but here one manufacturer acted alone in charging two retailers different amounts.
Predatory pricing means pricing below cost to drive rivals out, while this manufacturer is simply charging one retailer more than another for identical goods.
Bait and switch is a tactic that lures shoppers with an item the seller won't really sell, which has nothing to do with charging two retailers unequal prices.

q.pt: Explain the use of technology in the pricing function
q.s: An online retailer uses software that automatically changes its prices throughout the day based on customer demand and competitors' prices. This use of technology is called
q.r: Dynamic pricing. Pricing software can monitor demand, inventory and competitors' prices and adjust prices automatically, sometimes many times a day. This lets businesses respond to the market far faster than they could by hand. Prestige pricing uses high prices to suggest quality. Price lining sets a few fixed price levels for a product category. Odd-even pricing uses prices such as $9.99 or $10.00 to influence how customers see value.
w: Prestige pricing keeps prices high to signal quality, but this retailer's software moves prices up and down all day in response to demand and rivals.
Price lining sets a few fixed price levels for a product group, the opposite of software that keeps changing prices throughout the day.
Odd-even pricing picks endings like $9.99 to shape how a price looks, but it does not involve software reacting to demand and competitors in real time.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of channel management
q.s: Deciding which wholesalers and retailers will carry a product, and how the product will be stored and shipped, is part of which marketing function?
q.r: Channel management. Channel management involves selecting and working with the intermediaries that move products from producers to users, along with the storage and transportation activities that get products to the right place at the right time. Product/service management decides what to offer. Marketing-information management gathers and uses information for decisions. Promotion communicates information about products to customers.
w: Product/service management decides what products to offer and how to improve them, not which wholesalers and retailers carry them or how they are shipped.
Marketing-information management gathers and analyzes data for decisions; choosing intermediaries and planning storage and shipping are channel decisions, not research.
Promotion communicates with customers about a product, but picking the wholesalers and retailers and arranging storage and shipping is about getting the product to them.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing planning
q.s: Which of the following is the best example of a SMART marketing objective:
o: Become the best-known brand in the industry
Increase online sales by 10% by the end of June
Improve customer satisfaction as much as possible
Attract more young customers in the future
q.r: Increase online sales by 10% by the end of June. SMART objectives are specific, measurable, attainable, realistic and time-bound. This objective names what will change, by how much and by when, so the business can tell whether it succeeded. Becoming the best-known brand is not measurable or time-bound. Improving satisfaction "as much as possible" lacks a measurable target, and attracting more young customers "in the future" has no deadline.
w: Becoming the best-known brand sounds ambitious, but it gives no number to measure and no deadline, so the business could never tell if it succeeded.
Improving satisfaction "as much as possible" names a goal area but sets no measurable target or deadline, so it fails the SMART test.
Attracting more young customers "in the future" has no specific amount and no due date, so it is not measurable or time-bound.

q.pt: Describe the nature of legally binding contracts
q.s: In a legally binding contract, the something of value that each party gives or promises to the other is called
q.r: Consideration. A legally binding contract requires an offer and acceptance, consideration, competent parties (capacity) and a legal purpose. Consideration is what each party exchanges, such as money, goods, services or a promise to act. Capacity is the legal ability to enter a contract, acceptance is agreeing to the terms of an offer, and legality means the contract's purpose must be lawful.
w: Capacity is a party's legal ability to enter a contract, such as being of age and sound mind, not the thing of value each side exchanges.
Acceptance is agreeing to the terms of an offer; it is a separate contract element from the money, goods or promises the parties trade.
Legality means the contract's purpose must be lawful, which is a requirement about the deal's purpose rather than the value each party gives.

q.pt: Explain types of business ownership
q.s: Which form of business ownership is a separate legal entity whose owners' liability is generally limited to the amount they invested?
q.r: Corporation. A corporation is a business that is legally separate from its owners, the stockholders. It can own property, sue and be sued, and its owners usually risk only what they invested, which is called limited liability. Owners of a sole proprietorship and partners in a general partnership have unlimited liability for business debts, and a joint venture is a temporary arrangement between parties to complete a specific project.
w: A sole proprietorship is not separate from its owner, and that one owner has unlimited personal liability for all business debts.
In a general partnership the partners are personally responsible for business debts, so their liability is not limited to what they invested.
A joint venture is a temporary arrangement for a specific project, not a permanent separate legal entity defined by its owners' limited liability.

q.pt: Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
q.s: A company discovers a loophole that lets it legally dump waste in a way that still harms a nearby river. The company is complying with the letter of the law but violating its
q.r: Spirit. The spirit of a law is its purpose or intent, such as protecting a river from pollution, while the letter of the law is its exact wording. Responsible businesses comply with both, because following only the wording while defeating the purpose is unethical and often leads to stricter regulation. Wording is another name for the letter of the law, jurisdiction is a court's authority, and precedent is an earlier court decision used as a guide.
w: Wording is the letter of the law, which the company is actually following; the question asks what it violates, which is the law's purpose.
Jurisdiction is a court's or government's authority over an area or case, not the purpose behind a law that the company is undermining.
Precedent is an earlier court decision used as a guide in later cases, not the intent of a law like protecting a river from pollution.

q.pt: Describe methods used to protect intellectual property
q.s: A songwriter wants legal protection that prevents others from copying and selling an original song she wrote and recorded. Which form of intellectual property protection applies?
q.r: Copyright. A copyright protects original creative works, such as music, books, art, films and software, giving the creator exclusive rights to copy, sell and perform the work. A patent protects inventions and processes, a trademark protects words, names and symbols that identify a brand, and a trade secret is confidential business information, such as a formula, that is protected by keeping it private.
w: A patent protects inventions and new processes, not creative works like a song she wrote and recorded.
A trademark protects names, words and symbols that identify a brand, not the original music itself from being copied and sold.
A trade secret is protected by keeping information confidential, but a recorded song meant to be released can't stay secret and needs a different protection.

q.pt: Explain types of business ownership
q.s: Ava and Rob open a bike repair shop together. They share profits equally and are each personally responsible for all of the business's debts. Their business is a
q.r: General partnership. A general partnership is a business owned by two or more people who share in its management, profits and losses, and each partner has unlimited liability for business debts. In a limited partnership, at least one partner's liability is limited to his or her investment. A corporation's owners generally have limited liability, and a sole proprietorship has only one owner.
w: A limited partnership has at least one partner whose liability is limited, but here both Ava and Rob are personally responsible for all the debts.
A corporation is a separate legal entity whose owners usually have limited liability, which does not match two owners personally responsible for every debt.
A sole proprietorship has only one owner, but this shop is owned and run by two people who share the profits.

q.pt: Explain the nature of staff communication
q.s: Rumors about possible layoffs spread quickly among employees through informal conversations before management makes any announcement. This informal network is called the
q.r: Grapevine. The grapevine is the informal, unofficial network through which information and rumors travel among employees. It moves quickly but is often incomplete or inaccurate, so managers should communicate openly to limit rumors. The chain of command is the formal line of authority. Downward communication flows from managers to employees through official channels, and an open-door policy is a management practice that invites employees to bring concerns directly to supervisors.
w: The chain of command is the formal line of authority in an organization, not the unofficial conversations where these layoff rumors spread.
Downward communication is official messages from managers to employees, but these rumors travel informally before management says anything.
An open-door policy invites employees to bring concerns to supervisors, which is a management practice, not the informal rumor network described.

q.pt: Demonstrate active listening skills
q.s: While a frustrated customer explains how a late delivery disrupted her weekend event, Terrence tries to understand the situation from her point of view before he responds. Terrence is practicing
q.r: Empathetic listening. Empathetic listening means trying to understand a situation from the speaker's point of view and recognizing the feelings behind the words. It helps the listener respond with sensitivity and builds trust with customers. Selective listening is hearing only the parts of a message that interest the listener. Critical listening is evaluating a message to judge its accuracy or logic. Passive listening is receiving a message without engaging or responding.
w: Selective listening means hearing only the parts that interest you, while Terrence is trying to understand the whole situation from the customer's view.
Critical listening judges whether a message is accurate or logical, but Terrence is focused on seeing things from the customer's point of view.
Passive listening means taking in a message without engaging, yet Terrence is actively working to understand the customer's feelings before he responds.

q.pt: Follow oral directions
q.s: After her supervisor explains how to process an exchange, Leah says, "So I check the receipt, scan the returned item and then ring up the new one?" Why is Leah's response helpful?
o: It shows that she disagrees with the process
It confirms that she understood the directions correctly
It allows her to skip steps she already knows
It shifts responsibility for errors to the supervisor
q.r: It confirms that she understood the directions correctly. Restating oral directions gives the speaker feedback and a chance to correct any misunderstanding before the listener begins the task. This simple check reduces mistakes and rework. Leah's restatement does not signal disagreement, and it does not permit her to skip steps; it actually reinforces every step. Employees remain responsible for completing tasks correctly, so restating directions does not shift blame to the supervisor.
w: Leah repeats the steps back in order without objecting to any of them, so her response shows she is checking her understanding, not disagreeing.
Leah restates every step, including ones she might already know, so her response reinforces the full process rather than letting her skip parts of it.
Restating directions gives the supervisor a chance to correct her, but Leah is still responsible for doing the exchange correctly.

q.pt: Ask relevant questions
q.s: A customer tells a sales associate she wants a laptop "for school." The associate replies, "What kinds of programs will you use for your classes?" The associate is asking a(n)
q.r: Probing question. A probing question is a follow-up that digs deeper into a previous answer to uncover more specific information. Here, the associate builds on the customer's general need to find the right product. A leading question is worded to suggest a particular answer. A closed question can be answered with yes, no or a brief fact, and a rhetorical question is asked for effect, without expecting an answer.
w: A leading question is worded to push the customer toward a certain answer, but the associate's open question lets her describe her own needs.
A closed question can be answered with yes, no or a short fact, while asking what programs she will use invites a detailed answer.
A rhetorical question is asked for effect without expecting an answer, but the associate truly wants to know which programs she will use.

q.pt: Write informational messages
q.s: A store manager emails employees that the break room will be repainted next Tuesday and will be closed from 8 a.m. until noon. This is a(n) __________ message.
q.r: Informational. An informational message shares routine facts, such as announcements, schedules or policy updates, that readers are expected to accept with a neutral or positive reaction. The manager is simply telling employees what will happen and when. A persuasive message tries to convince readers to act or agree. A bad-news message delivers disappointing information, and an inquiry requests information from the reader.
w: A persuasive message tries to convince readers to do or believe something, but the manager is only announcing when the break room will be closed.
A short break-room closure for painting is routine news readers should accept neutrally, not disappointing information that calls for a bad-news approach.
An inquiry asks the reader for information, but the manager's email gives employees facts instead of requesting anything from them.

q.pt: Write business letters
q.s: In a business letter, the phrase "Sincerely," that appears just before the writer's signature is called the
q.r: Complimentary close. The complimentary close is the polite ending phrase, such as "Sincerely," or "Respectfully," placed between the body of the letter and the signature. The salutation is the greeting, such as "Dear Mr. Chen:". The inside address contains the recipient's name, title, company and mailing address. Reference initials identify the person who typed or prepared the letter.
w: The salutation is the greeting at the start of the letter, such as "Dear Ms. Lopez:", not the closing phrase before the signature.
The inside address lists the recipient's name and mailing address near the top of the letter, not the polite phrase that comes before the signature.
Reference initials identify who typed or prepared the letter and appear below the signature block, not as the closing phrase like "Sincerely,".

q.pt: Select and utilize appropriate formats for professional writing
q.s: In a full-block business letter, every part of the letter, including the date and the closing, begins at the
q.r: Left margin. In full-block (block) format, all letter parts are aligned at the left margin and paragraphs are not indented; a blank line separates paragraphs. This clean, efficient layout is the most widely used business letter style. No standard business letter format aligns its parts at the right margin or centers them. Modified-block format moves only the date and closing to the center point, and indenting to a tab stop is not used in full-block style.
w: Centering the date and closing is not part of full-block style; even modified-block style only moves those parts to the center point.
No standard business letter format lines its parts up at the right margin, and full-block style puts every part on the left.
Full-block style does not indent anything to a tab stop; every part, including the date and closing, starts at the same margin.

q.pt: Choose and use appropriate channel for workplace communication
q.s: A manager needs to tell an employee that his position is being eliminated. Which channel is most appropriate?
o: A notice on the break room bulletin board
A brief email sent after hours
q.r: A private face-to-face meeting. Sensitive or emotional messages require a rich channel that carries both verbal and nonverbal cues and allows immediate two-way discussion. A private face-to-face meeting shows respect, lets the manager answer questions and helps prevent misunderstanding. A group text and a bulletin board notice violate the employee's privacy. A brief email is a lean channel that seems impersonal for such serious news.
w: A group text exposes very private, upsetting news to other people and gives the employee no real chance to talk it through.
Posting a job elimination on the break room board makes private news public and gives the employee no way to ask questions.
An email is quick, but sending such serious news briefly and after hours feels cold and leaves the employee with no one to talk to.

q.pt: Write inquiries
q.s: What is the most important quality of an effective written inquiry?
o: It describes the writer's company history in detail
It avoids mentioning a response deadline
It states exactly what is needed and by when
It uses general wording to keep options open
q.r: It states exactly what is needed and by when. An inquiry is a written request for information, products, services or action. To get a useful and timely reply, it should be specific about exactly what the writer needs, why it is needed and the date by which a response is required. A detailed company history adds unnecessary length. Omitting a deadline and using vague wording make it hard for the reader to respond accurately.
w: A long company history adds length without telling the reader what information is needed, which makes the inquiry harder to answer.
Leaving out a deadline makes it more likely the reply comes too late, since the reader doesn't know when the information is needed.
General wording might seem flexible, but vague requests leave the reader guessing and lead to incomplete or inaccurate replies.

q.pt: Select and use appropriate graphic aids
q.s: A coffee shop owner wants to show how drinks, pastries, sandwiches and merchandise each contributed to total monthly sales. Which graphic aid is most appropriate?
q.r: Pie chart. A pie chart is a circle divided into slices that show how each part contributes to a whole, so it clearly displays each category's share of total sales. A line graph is best for showing changes or trends over time. A flowchart shows the steps in a process, and an organizational chart shows the structure and reporting relationships within a business.
w: A line graph shows how values change over time, but the owner wants to show each category's share of one month's total sales.
A flowchart shows the steps in a process, not how drinks, pastries, sandwiches and merchandise each contributed to total sales.
An organizational chart shows a company's structure and who reports to whom, not how sales are divided among product categories.

q.pt: Analyze company resources to ascertain policies and procedures
q.s: A company's employee handbook states, "All new employees must complete safety training within 30 days of hire." This statement is an example of a
q.r: Policy. A policy is a general rule or guideline that directs employees' decisions and actions. The handbook statement sets a requirement but does not explain how to complete it. A procedure is a step-by-step method for carrying out a task, such as how to sign up for training. A job description outlines one position's duties, and a mission statement expresses the organization's overall purpose.
w: A procedure gives step-by-step instructions for doing a task, but this statement only sets a requirement without explaining how to complete the training.
A job description lists the duties of one position, while this rule applies to all new employees regardless of their job.
A mission statement expresses the organization's overall purpose, not a specific workplace rule like a training deadline.

q.pt: Make oral presentations
q.s: While rehearsing a presentation for store managers, Devon notices that he often says "um" and "like" between sentences. To improve, Devon should
o: speak faster so the pauses are shorter.
read his entire speech directly from notes.
add more slides to distract from the sounds.
pause silently instead of using filler words.
q.r: Pause silently instead of using filler words. Filler words distract listeners and make a speaker seem unprepared or unsure. A brief silent pause gives the speaker time to think and sounds confident. Speaking faster makes the presentation harder to follow. Reading word for word reduces eye contact and audience connection, and extra slides do not correct the underlying delivery problem.
w: Speaking faster doesn't remove the filler words and makes the presentation harder for the store managers to follow.
Reading the whole speech from notes may reduce fillers but cuts eye contact and connection with the audience, so it trades one problem for another.
More slides don't change how Devon speaks, so the "um" and "like" sounds would still be there.

q.pt: Write persuasive messages
q.s: In a persuasive sales letter, which element tells the reader exactly what to do next, such as calling to schedule a free consultation?
q.r: Call to action. A call to action is a specific request near the end of a persuasive message that tells the reader exactly what action to take and often how to take it easily. Without it, interested readers may not respond. A buffer is a neutral opening used to soften bad news. The inside address identifies the recipient, and an attention-getter opens the message to spark interest.
w: A buffer is a neutral opening used to soften bad news, not the part of a sales letter that tells the reader what to do next.
The inside address identifies the recipient at the top of the letter and does not ask the reader to take any action.
An attention-getter opens the message to spark interest, but the question asks for the element that tells the reader exactly what step to take next.

q.pt: Prepare simple written reports
q.s: A shift supervisor writes a one-page memo summarizing the number of customers served, problems encountered and tasks planned for the next day. This document is a(n)
q.r: Informal report. An informal report is a short, routine report, often written as a memo or email, that shares information within an organization. Daily activity reports like this one help managers track operations. A formal report is longer and researched, with sections such as a title page and table of contents. A business proposal recommends a plan to win approval, and an executive summary condenses a longer document.
w: A formal report is long and researched, with parts like a title page, while this is a short, routine one-page memo about the day's work.
A business proposal recommends a plan to win approval, but this memo just summarizes the day's activity and next day's tasks.
An executive summary condenses a longer document, but this memo stands on its own as a short daily report.

q.pt: Explain communication techniques that support and encourage a speaker
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a verbal encourager that supports a speaker:
o: Checking the time on your phone
Changing the subject to your own story
q.r: Saying "Go on, I'm following you". Verbal encouragers are brief comments, such as "I see," "Really?" or "Go on," that show the listener is paying attention and invite the speaker to continue. They make the speaker feel heard and valued. Checking a phone signals boredom. Changing the subject shifts attention away from the speaker, and finishing the speaker's sentences is a form of interrupting that discourages the speaker from sharing.
w: Checking the time on your phone is a nonverbal sign of boredom, not a spoken comment that encourages the speaker to keep going.
Changing the subject to your own story pulls attention away from the speaker instead of inviting them to continue.
Finishing someone's sentences is a form of interrupting, which discourages the speaker rather than showing you're following along.

q.pt: Explain the nature of effective verbal communications
q.s: Instead of telling a new employee to "restock the shelf soon," Gina says, "Restock shelf 4 with the 12-ounce cans by 3 p.m." Gina is improving her verbal communication by
q.r: Using precise language. Precise speech means choosing specific words that convey your exact meaning so the listener does not have to guess. Gina names the shelf, the product and the deadline, which leaves little room for misunderstanding. Technical jargon consists of specialized terms that outsiders may not understand. Gina's revision is not more informal, and it does not depend on gestures or other nonverbal cues.
w: Technical jargon is specialized terms outsiders may not understand, but Gina used plain, specific details like a shelf number and a time.
Gina's revision isn't more casual; she simply replaced a vague request with exact details about what, where and when.
Gina's improvement is in her words, which now name the shelf, product and deadline, not in gestures or other nonverbal cues.

q.pt: Interpret others' nonverbal cues
q.s: Why should a salesperson avoid drawing a conclusion from a single nonverbal cue, such as a customer's crossed arms?
o: Nonverbal cues are usually meant to mislead others
Body language changes too quickly to observe
Nonverbal cues can be misinterpreted when viewed alone
Spoken words carry more meaning than body language
q.r: Nonverbal cues can be misinterpreted when viewed alone. A single nonverbal cue can have several meanings; crossed arms might signal defensiveness, or the customer might simply be cold. Skilled communicators look for cue clusters, several signals that point to the same meaning, and compare them with what the person says. Most nonverbal cues are not intended to mislead, body language can be observed throughout a conversation, and much of a message's meaning is carried by nonverbal behavior rather than by words alone.
w: Most nonverbal cues are not meant to mislead; the problem is that one cue like crossed arms can have several innocent meanings.
Body language can be watched throughout a conversation, so the issue isn't that it changes too fast but that one cue alone is unreliable.
Body language actually carries much of a message's meaning, so the reason for caution is that a single cue can be misread, not that it matters less.

q.pt: Apply written directions to achieve tasks
q.s: A new team member is assembling a display fixture using a printed instruction sheet. Which approach will most likely produce the correct result?
o: Look at the finished picture and assemble from memory
Complete the easiest steps first and return to the rest
Skim the sheet once and start building
Read each step and complete it before moving to the next
q.r: Read each step and complete it before moving to the next. Written directions are designed to be followed in sequence, so reading one step, completing it and then moving on reduces errors and missed details. Building from a picture or from memory skips information that the directions provide. Completing steps out of order can make later steps impossible or require rework. Skimming once does not give the reader enough attention to each step to complete the task accurately.
w: Building from the picture and memory skips details the written steps provide, making errors more likely on a fixture assembly.
Doing the easiest steps first breaks the intended order, which can make later steps impossible or force the new team member to redo work.
Skimming the sheet once gives only a general idea and misses details needed to assemble the fixture correctly.

q.pt: Extract relevant information from written materials
q.s: Jamal needs to find the return deadline in a 10-page supplier agreement, so he quickly searches the document for the words "return" and "days." Jamal is
q.r: Scanning. Scanning is moving your eyes quickly over text to locate a specific piece of information, such as a name, number or key word. It lets a reader extract exactly what is needed without reading everything. Skimming is reading quickly to get the general idea of a document. Proofreading is checking writing for errors, and summarizing is restating the main points in a shorter form.
w: Skimming is reading quickly to get the general idea, but Jamal is hunting for one specific detail, the return deadline.
Proofreading checks writing for errors, but Jamal isn't correcting the agreement; he's searching it for a specific fact.
Summarizing means restating main points in shorter form, but Jamal is only trying to locate the return deadline.

q.pt: Provide legitimate responses to inquiries
q.s: A customer asks a drugstore clerk whether a cold medicine is safe to take with her prescription. The clerk is not sure. What is the most legitimate response?
o: Guess based on what other customers have said
Explain that he will ask the pharmacist to answer
Tell her the products are probably fine together
Suggest that she search for the answer online
q.r: Explain that he will ask the pharmacist to answer. A legitimate response to an inquiry is honest, accurate and complete. When an employee does not know the answer, he should say so and connect the customer with someone who does, especially when health or safety is involved. Guessing or offering a reassuring but unverified answer could harm the customer and the business. Sending the customer to search online fails to address her question.
w: Guessing based on other customers' comments could give her wrong information about a health and safety question.
Telling her the products are "probably fine" sounds reassuring but is an unverified guess that could put her health at risk.
Pointing her to an online search avoids the question instead of getting her an accurate answer from the pharmacist who can help.

q.pt: Identify sources that provide relevant, valid written material
q.s: When evaluating a website for a research report, Hannah checks whether the author is a recognized expert and whether the site cites its sources. Hannah is evaluating the website's
q.r: Credibility. Credibility is the trustworthiness and expertise of a source. An author's qualifications and a list of cited sources are strong signals that the information is valid and can be verified. Readability refers to how easy the text is to understand. Popularity, such as the number of visitors, does not prove accuracy, and an attractive design does not guarantee reliable content.
w: Readability is how easy the text is to understand, but Hannah is checking the author's expertise and sources to decide if the information is trustworthy.
Popularity measures how many people visit a site, which doesn't show whether the author is an expert or the information is supported.
Design is how the site looks, and an attractive layout says nothing about whether the author is qualified or the facts are cited.

q.pt: Give verbal directions
q.s: Before sending a new hire to the stockroom alone, Ms. Brandt explains the route and then asks him to describe it back to her. Ms. Brandt is
q.r: Checking for understanding. When giving verbal directions, the speaker should confirm that the listener can restate them correctly. Asking the listener to repeat or describe the directions reveals any confusion before the person sets out. Ms. Brandt is not demonstrating, which would involve showing the task, and her directions are spoken rather than written. Signal words show the order of steps but do not confirm understanding.
w: Demonstrating would mean showing the new hire the task, but Ms. Brandt explains the route and has him describe it back.
Ms. Brandt's directions are spoken, not written, and asking him to repeat them is a way to confirm he understood.
Signal words like "first" and "next" show the order of steps, but having him describe the route back is a check on his understanding.

q.pt: Utilize note-taking strategies
q.s: Sofia must take notes during a fast-paced vendor presentation. Which strategy will help her keep up while still recording accurate information?
o: Use abbreviations and symbols for common words
Write down every sentence the speaker says
Wait until the end and summarize from memory
Copy the slides word for word instead of listening
q.r: Use abbreviations and symbols for common words. Abbreviations and symbols, such as "w/" for with or an arrow for increase, let a note-taker record key ideas quickly without falling behind. Trying to write every sentence is impossible at a fast pace and causes the listener to miss ideas. Relying on memory leads to forgotten details. Copying slides word for word replaces listening, and speakers often explain important points that are not on the slides.
w: Writing every sentence is impossible in a fast presentation, so Sofia would fall behind and miss key ideas.
Waiting until the end and relying on memory means many details will be forgotten before she writes them down.
Copying slides word for word keeps her from listening, and speakers often explain important points that aren't on the slides.

q.pt: Defend ideas objectively
q.s: Nadia proposes switching the store to an online scheduling app. When a coworker says the app costs too much, which response best defends her idea objectively?
o: Remind the coworker that she has worked there much longer
Say that the coworker always resists new ideas
Share data on the time and overtime the app would save
Insist on the app because she personally likes it
q.r: Share data on the time and overtime the app would save. Defending an idea objectively means supporting it with facts, logic and evidence rather than emotion or personal attacks. Showing projected time and overtime savings addresses the cost concern directly and lets others judge the idea on its merits. Pointing to seniority and criticizing the coworker are personal, not factual, arguments. Personal preference is subjective and does not explain why the idea benefits the business.
w: Pointing to how long she has worked there is about her status, not facts showing the app is worth its cost.
Saying the coworker always resists new ideas attacks the person instead of answering the concern about cost.
Liking the app personally is a subjective feeling that doesn't show how the app would benefit the store or justify its cost.

q.pt: Handle phone calls in a businesslike manner
q.s: Before placing a business caller on hold, an employee should
o: transfer the call to a manager right away.
mute the line without saying anything to the caller.
ask the caller's permission and explain why.
tell the caller to call back later.
q.r: Ask the caller's permission and explain why. Telephone etiquette calls for asking whether the caller can hold, giving a brief reason and waiting for an answer. When returning, the employee should thank the caller for waiting. Transferring to a manager is unnecessary unless the manager is needed. Muting the line without explanation confuses the caller, and asking the caller to call back shifts the burden to the customer.
w: Transferring to a manager is unnecessary unless the manager is actually needed, and it skips asking the caller whether holding is okay.
Muting the line without a word leaves the caller confused about what is happening, which is poor telephone etiquette.
Telling the caller to call back pushes the burden onto the caller instead of politely asking to place the call on hold.

q.pt: Explain the nature of positive customer relations
q.s: Satisfied customers of a local bike shop recommend it to their friends and post positive reviews online. This customer-to-customer promotion is called
q.r: Word-of-mouth. Word-of-mouth is promotion that occurs when customers share their experiences with others. It is one of the most believable forms of promotion because it comes from customers, not the business, and it costs the business little. Positive customer relations create favorable word-of-mouth. Sales promotion, personal selling and direct marketing are all forms of promotion that the business itself plans and pays for.
w: Sales promotion is short-term incentives like coupons that the business itself plans and pays for, not customers recommending the shop to friends.
Personal selling is a salesperson talking directly with a customer, while here satisfied customers are doing the promoting on their own.
Direct marketing is the business reaching customers directly through mail, email or ads, not customers praising the shop to each other.

q.pt: Identify company's brand promise
q.s: A traveler reads a hotel's online reviews, calls to book a room and later receives a thank-you email from the hotel. Each of these points of contact between the customer and the business is called a
q.r: Touchpoint. A touchpoint is any interaction or point of contact between a customer and a business, before, during or after a purchase. Every touchpoint is a chance for the business to keep its brand promise and shape the customer's experience. A brand mark is the symbol or design part of a brand, a slogan is a short memorable phrase, and a market segment is a group of customers with similar characteristics.
w: A brand mark is the symbol or design part of a brand, not the moments when the traveler interacts with the hotel.
A slogan is a short, memorable phrase used in promotion, not each contact like reading reviews, calling or getting an email.
A market segment is a group of customers with similar traits, not the individual points where one customer interacts with the hotel.

q.pt: Demonstrate a customer service mindset
q.s: Mia is restocking shelves when a shopper walks up with a question about a product. Which action best shows a customer service mindset?
o: Answering while she keeps stocking the shelf
Telling the shopper to find another employee
Pausing to give the shopper her full attention
Asking the shopper to wait until she finishes
q.r: Pausing to give the shopper her full attention. A customer service mindset is an attitude that puts the customer first. Giving customers full attention shows they are more important than routine tasks such as stocking, and it helps the employee understand and meet their needs. Continuing to work while answering, sending the shopper elsewhere or making the shopper wait all signal that the task matters more than the customer.
w: Answering while still stocking divides Mia's attention and signals that the shelf matters more than the shopper's question.
Sending the shopper to another employee passes the customer off when Mia could help, which does not put the customer first.
Making the shopper wait until she finishes stocking treats a routine task as more important than the customer.

q.pt: Handle customer/client complaints
q.s: A customer comes to the service desk upset that her new blender stopped working after two days. What should the employee do first?
o: Offer her a full refund right away
Explain the store's return policy to her
Call a manager to take over the problem
q.r: Listen carefully without interrupting. The first step in handling a complaint is to let the customer explain the problem fully.
